q: A solid dissolves well in hot ethanol but also fairly well in cold ethanol, and it is insoluble in water. How can a mixed-solvent recrystallization be done?
o: Dissolve in minimal hot ethanol, add hot water until cloudy, then cool
Dissolve in cold water, add hot ethanol until clear, then heat
Dissolve in hot water, add ice-cold ethanol, then filter right away
Dissolve in hot ethanol, then evaporate all of the ethanol away
e: Ethanol is the 'good' solvent and water (miscible with ethanol) is the 'poor' solvent.
Adding water until the hot solution turns cloudy makes it just saturated; slow cooling then gives crystals. Evaporating to dryness keeps the impurities too.
w: Insoluble in water.
The compound is insoluble in water, so it can't be dissolved in hot water first; ethanol must be the dissolving solvent.
Evaporating all the ethanol leaves the impurities in the solid too, so nothing is purified.

q: An ideal liquid mixture is 50 mol% A (pure vapor pressure 600 torr) and 50 mol% B (pure vapor pressure 200 torr). Its vapor is condensed, and the condensate is vaporized again, as on two ideal plates of a fractional column. What is the mole fraction of A in the second vapor?
e: Second vapor from a 0.75 : 0.25 liquid: P(A) = 450, P(B) = 50 → x(A) = 450 ÷ 500 = 0.90. Each cycle enriches the more volatile component.
w: That's the first vapor.
0.56 comes from multiplying 0.75 × 0.75; instead, recompute partial pressures from the 0.75 liquid: 450 ÷ 500 = 0.90.
That's the liquid.

q: A carboxylic acid streaks badly on silica TLC. Adding about 1% acetic acid to the eluent gives a tight spot. Why?
o: It keeps the compound fully protonated, so it moves as one form
It converts the compound into a less polar ester on the plate
It deprotonates the compound so it binds the silica less
It makes the silica nonpolar, so every compound moves faster
e: Without added acid, some molecules are neutral (RCOOH) and some are ionized (RCOO⁻); the two forms have very different R<sub>f</sub> values, so the spot smears.
Excess acetic acid suppresses ionization (Le Châtelier), so the compound runs as neutral RCOOH in one compact spot.
w: Acetic acid in the eluent doesn't esterify the acid on the plate; it suppresses ionization instead.
This is reversed: added acetic acid suppresses deprotonation, keeping the compound neutral as RCOOH.
Silica stays polar.

q: After recrystallization, crystals collected by vacuum filtration are rinsed with a small amount of ice-cold solvent. Why ice-cold?
o: It rinses off impure solution while dissolving little product
It dissolves the remaining impurities trapped deep inside the crystal lattice
It makes the crystals grow larger during filtration
It reacts with leftover impurities and removes them
e: The liquid clinging to the crystals (mother liquor) holds the dissolved impurities.
The product is least soluble in cold solvent, so a cold rinse removes that liquid while losing little product.
w: A quick rinse only reaches the crystal surfaces; impurities trapped inside stay put.
Crystal growth happens during slow cooling, not during a brief rinse.
A recrystallization solvent is chosen to be unreactive.

q: An organic amine in an ether layer is shaken with aqueous HCl. Where does the amine go?
o: Into the aqueous layer, as an ammonium salt
It stays in the ether layer as the free amine
It evaporates
It forms an insoluble solid at the interface
e: Protonation makes it charged and water-soluble.
w: It becomes charged.
It's a salt.
The protonated ammonium salt is charged and dissolves in the aqueous layer rather than precipitating.

q: On a silica TLC plate developed in hexane, all the spots stay near the baseline. Which change should move them farther up the plate?
o: Add ethyl acetate to make the eluent more polar
Use pure pentane to make the eluent less polar
Use a longer plate with the same hexane
Spot a larger amount of the sample
e: A more polar mobile phase competes better with the silica for the compounds, so they spend more time moving.
All R<sub>f</sub> values rise. A longer plate does not change R<sub>f</sub>.
w: Less polar slows them.
Rf is a ratio of distances, so a longer plate with the same hexane leaves the spots at the same relative position.
Spotting more sample doesn't change how strongly compounds stick to silica, and it tends to make spots streak.

q: A compound's solubility is 5.0 g per 100 mL of a solvent at its boiling point and 0.50 g per 100 mL at 0 °C. A student dissolves 5.0 g in 100 mL of the hot solvent and cools it to 0 °C. What is the maximum mass of crystals that can be recovered?
e: At 0 °C, 0.50 g stays dissolved in the 100 mL and is lost in the filtrate.
Maximum recovery = 5.0 − 0.50 = 4.5 g (90%).
w: Some stays dissolved.
That's what's lost.
Recheck: 5.0 − 0.50.

q: A mixture of pentane, hexane and heptane is analyzed by GC on a nonpolar column. In which order do they elute?
o: Pentane, then hexane, then heptane
Heptane, then hexane, then pentane
Hexane, then pentane, then heptane
All three at the same retention time
e: On a nonpolar column, alkanes separate mainly by volatility (boiling point).
Pentane (bp 36 °C) spends the most time in the gas phase, so it elutes first; heptane (bp 98 °C) elutes last.
w: This reverses the order: heptane has the highest boiling point, so it elutes last on a nonpolar column.
Not this order.
The three alkanes have different boiling points, so they separate and elute at different times.
t: In GC, the more volatile compound (lower boiling point) usually comes out first.

q: Which method is best for separating pentane (bp 36 °C) from toluene (bp 111 °C)?
o: Simple distillation
Recrystallization from water
Extraction with aqueous HCl
Size-exclusion chromatography
e: Both are neutral liquids, so acid–base extraction won't separate them, and neither is a solid to recrystallize.
Their boiling points differ by 75 °C (well over 25 °C), so simple distillation works: pentane distills first.
w: Both are liquids.
Both are neutral.
Not for small molecules.

q: Acid chlorides must be stored away from moisture because they react with water. What are the products?
o: A carboxylic acid and HCl
A ketone and chloride ion
A primary alcohol and HCl
An ester and Cl₂ gas
e: Water attacks the C=O, and Cl⁻ (a very good leaving group) leaves; the lost H⁺ and Cl⁻ make HCl.
RCOCl + H₂O → RCOOH + HCl. The fumes of HCl are why acid chlorides 'smoke' in moist air.
w: No ketone forms.
Water substitutes for Cl at the carbonyl; there is no reducing agent to give a primary alcohol.
No Cl₂ forms.

q: N-Phenylpropanamide, CH₃CH₂CONHC₆H₅, is heated in aqueous NaOH until hydrolysis is complete. Which products form?
o: Sodium propanoate and aniline
Propan-1-amine and sodium benzoate
Propanoic acid and phenol
Propanamide and benzene
e: Amide hydrolysis breaks the bond between the carbonyl carbon and nitrogen.
The acyl side becomes propanoate (as its sodium salt in base); the nitrogen side becomes aniline, C₆H₅NH₂.
w: This puts the carbonyl on the wrong fragment; the C=O stays with the propanoyl group.
The nitrogen leaves as an amine, so no phenol forms.
Hydrolysis breaks the C–N bond, not the N–phenyl bond.

q: Why are β-lactam antibiotics (like penicillin) especially reactive toward bacterial enzymes?
o: The strained four-membered ring makes the amide unusually reactive
The fused benzene ring strongly activates the amide carbonyl toward attack
The strained ring makes the amide nitrogen strongly basic
Their large size lets them bind many enzyme sites at once
e: Ring strain and reduced amide resonance help them acylate the bacterial enzyme.
w: The β-lactam is fused to a thiazolidine ring, not a benzene ring; strain causes the reactivity.
Ring strain reduces nitrogen lone-pair donation, making the carbonyl more electrophilic, not the N more basic.
Size and multi-site binding don't explain it; the strained, poorly resonance-stabilized amide does.

q: Saponification of a triglyceride with NaOH gives:
o: Glycerol and three fatty acid carboxylate salts
Glycerol and three fatty acid methyl esters
Glycerol and three neutral fatty acids (RCOOH)
Three fatty alcohols and glyceric acid
e: These carboxylate salts are soaps.
w: Methyl esters come from transesterification with methanol (biodiesel), not NaOH hydrolysis.
In excess NaOH, fatty acids are deprotonated to carboxylate salts, not neutral acids.
The glycerol backbone is released intact; fatty acyl groups become carboxylates, not alcohols.

q: N,N-Dimethylbenzamide, C₆H₅CON(CH₃)₂, is treated with LiAlH₄ and then water. What is the product?
o: N,N-Dimethylbenzylamine, C₆H₅CH₂N(CH₃)₂
Benzyl alcohol and dimethylamine, C₆H₅CH₂OH + (CH₃)₂NH
Benzaldehyde and dimethylamine, C₆H₅CHO + (CH₃)₂NH
Benzoic acid and dimethylamine, C₆H₅COOH + (CH₃)₂NH
e: LiAlH₄ reduces amides differently from esters: the C=O oxygen is removed, and the C–N bond stays.
C=O → CH₂, so the tertiary amide becomes the tertiary amine C₆H₅CH₂N(CH₃)₂.
w: LiAlH₄ removes the amide C=O oxygen while keeping the C–N bond, so the amine isn't cleaved off.
C=O goes to CH₂.
LiAlH₄ reduces rather than hydrolyzes the amide, so the C–N bond stays and no benzoic acid forms.
t: LiAlH₄ + amide keeps the nitrogen: C=O simply becomes CH₂.

q: Alkyl chlorides react with nucleophiles by backside SN2 attack, but acyl chlorides (RCOCl) react by addition–elimination. Why the difference?
o: The planar C=O lets the nucleophile add to its π*, forming a tetrahedral intermediate
Acyl chlorides have a stronger C–Cl bond, so Cl⁻ can't leave in one step
The carbonyl carbon is sp³, so backside attack is blocked by the oxygen and both other groups
Acyl chlorides react only through a free acylium ion, as in SN1
e: The acyl carbon is sp² with a low-lying, empty π* orbital, so a nucleophile can simply add to it.
This gives a tetrahedral intermediate, which then expels Cl⁻ and re-forms the C=O.
Adding to the π bond is much easier than pushing out Cl⁻ by backside attack.
w: The acyl C–Cl bond isn't the issue; Cl⁻ leaves readily from the tetrahedral intermediate.
The acyl carbon is sp², not sp³, before the nucleophile adds.
Typical acyl substitutions pass through a tetrahedral intermediate, not a free acylium ion.

q: Transesterification is:
o: Exchanging an ester's alkoxy group for that of a different alcohol
Hydrolyzing an ester into a carboxylic acid and an alcohol with water
Converting an ester into an amide by reaction with an amine
Reducing an ester to two alcohols using LiAlH₄
e: Biodiesel is made this way from fats and methanol.
w: That's hydrolysis; transesterification uses an alcohol, not water.
That's aminolysis to an amide; transesterification keeps an ester with a new alkoxy group.
That's LiAlH₄ reduction; transesterification is substitution, not reduction.

q: 4-Aminobutanoic acid (GABA), H₂NCH₂CH₂CH₂COOH, loses water on strong heating to form a lactam. How many atoms are in the lactam ring?
e: The amine N attacks the carboxyl carbon and forms a cyclic amide.
Ring atoms: N, the carbonyl carbon and the three CH₂ carbons = 5 (2-pyrrolidinone).
w: 4 leaves out either the nitrogen or the carbonyl carbon, but both are in the ring.
6 counts the carbonyl oxygen, which sits outside the ring.
The chain has only four carbons and one nitrogen, so it can't make seven ring atoms.

q: Why are acid anhydrides more reactive toward nucleophiles than esters?
o: A carboxylate leaves more easily than an alkoxide does
Anhydride carbonyls are less polarized than ester carbonyls
An alkoxide leaves more easily than a carboxylate does
Esters are sterically more crowded at the carbonyl carbon
e: Leaving-group ability follows conjugate-acid strength: RCOO⁻ comes from RCOOH (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 5); RO⁻ comes from ROH (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 16).
Also, the central oxygen shares its lone pairs between two carbonyls, so each C=O gets less resonance donation and stays more electrophilic.
w: They're more polarized.
This is reversed: a carboxylate (from an acid, pKa ≈ 5) is a weaker base and leaves more easily than an alkoxide.
Not the reason.

q: Reducing an amide with LiAlH₄ gives:
o: An amine
An alcohol
An ester
A carboxylic acid
e: The C=O becomes CH₂, keeping the nitrogen.
w: Unlike esters, amides keep nitrogen; LiAlH₄ converts C=O to CH₂, giving an amine.
Reduction cannot form an ester; no alcohol oxygen is introduced.
A carboxylic acid would be a hydrolysis product, not a reduction product.

q: Which product forms when acetic anhydride reacts with ethanol?
o: Ethyl acetate and acetic acid
Ethyl acetate and water only
Acetic acid and ethane gas
Ethanal
e: One acetyl group transfers to ethanol; the other leaves as acetic acid.
w: Missing a product; the second acetyl group leaves as acetate/acetic acid.
Ethane isn't formed; ethanol becomes ethyl acetate, not an alkane.
Ethanal requires oxidizing ethanol; anhydrides acylate alcohols instead.

q:
Using the conjugate-acid pKa values of the leaving groups, predict the order of reactivity toward hydrolysis for acetic anhydride, phenyl acetate and ethyl acetate.
Leaving groupConjugate acid pKa
CH₃COO⁻4.8
C₆H₅O⁻10.0
CH₃CH₂O⁻16
o: Acetic anhydride > phenyl acetate > ethyl acetate
Ethyl acetate > phenyl acetate > acetic anhydride
Phenyl acetate > acetic anhydride > ethyl acetate
All three react at about the same rate
e: All three are acetyl derivatives, so the leaving group decides.
A weaker base (lower conjugate-acid pKa) is a better leaving group: acetate > phenoxide > ethoxide.
So the anhydride reacts fastest and the alkyl ester slowest.
w: This reverses the trend; ethoxide is the strongest base and the worst leaving group.
Phenoxide (pKa 10) is a stronger base than acetate (pKa 4.8), so phenyl acetate is less reactive than the anhydride.
The leaving groups span over 11 pKa units, so the rates differ a lot.

q: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃?
o: Butan-2-ol
Butan-3-ol
2-Hydroxybutane
Butan-1-ol
e: Number from the end giving –OH the lowest number: C2.
w: Use the lower number.
Use the -ol suffix.
–OH is on C2.

q: Which name matches the substituent –CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃?
o: sec-Butyl (butan-2-yl)
Isobutyl (2-methylpropyl)
tert-Butyl (2-methylpropan-2-yl)
Butyl (butan-1-yl)
e: The group is an unbranched 4-carbon chain.
It attaches through C2 of that chain (the CH), so it is butan-2-yl, also called sec-butyl.
w: Branch at the far end.
Attached at a tertiary C.
Attached at C1.
t: iso = branch at the far end; sec = attached at a secondary carbon; tert = attached at a tertiary carbon.

q: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CHBrCH₂CHClCH₃?
o: 2-Bromo-4-chloropentane
4-Bromo-2-chloropentane
2-Chloro-4-bromopentane
1-Bromo-3-chloropentane
e: Both numbering directions give locants {2, 4}: a tie.
Break the tie alphabetically: bromo comes first, so Br gets the lower number (C2).
w: Alphabetize: bromo gets 2.
Alphabetize: bromo first.
Halogens are on C2 and C4.

q: CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂C≡N is named pentanenitrile, but a cyclohexane ring carrying –C≡N is named cyclohexanecarbonitrile. Why do the endings differ?
o: The –C≡N carbon can't be part of the ring, so it isn't counted in the parent name
Ring compounds take the -carbonitrile ending for every functional group they carry
Pentanenitrile's chain has five carbons, so it needs the shorter ending
The -carbonitrile ending is used only when the nitrile is on an aromatic ring
e: In a chain, the nitrile carbon is C1 of the chain, so -nitrile is added to the full chain name.
In a ring, the nitrile carbon sits outside the ring, so -carbonitrile names that extra carbon.
w: Rings do not use a '-carbo-' ending for every group; cyclohexanol, for example, has no such ending.
The ending depends on whether the C≡N carbon is in the parent, not on chain length.
Cyclohexanecarbonitrile is not aromatic, so the ending is not limited to aromatic rings.

q: What is the IUPAC name of (CH₃)₂CHCH₂CH₃?
o: 2-Methylbutane
Isopentane-2
3-Methylbutane
2-Ethylpropane
e: Longest chain: 4 carbons (butane).
A methyl branch sits on C2 (number from the end closer to the branch).
w: "Isopentane-2" mixes a common name with a locant, which isn't valid IUPAC; the parent chain is butane.
Number from the closer end.
Longest chain is four.

q: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃OOC–CH₂–CH₂–COOCH₃?
o: Dimethyl butanedioate
Dimethyl ethanedioate
Methyl butanedioate
Dimethyl hexanedioate
e: The parent acid is HOOC–CH₂–CH₂–COOH: four carbons counting both carbonyls, butanedioic acid.
Both acid groups are methyl esters, so each '-oic acid' becomes '-oate' with two methyl groups: dimethyl butanedioate.
w: Ethanedioate counts only the two CH₂ carbons; the carbonyl carbons belong to the parent chain too.
There are two ester groups, so the alkyl part must be 'dimethyl'.
The methyl groups are on oxygen, so they are not counted in the parent chain.

q: What is the common name of propan-2-ol?
o: Isopropyl alcohol
Propyl alcohol
Ethyl alcohol
Methyl alcohol
e: The –OH is on the middle carbon of a 3-carbon chain.
w: –OH on the end.
Ethyl alcohol is the two-carbon alcohol, but propan-2-ol has a three-carbon chain.
Methyl alcohol has just one carbon, but propan-2-ol has a three-carbon chain.

q: What is the IUPAC name of (CH₃CH₂)₂NH?
o: N-Ethylethanamine
N-Ethylethanamide
Butan-1-amine
1-Ethylethanamine
e: In a secondary amine, the larger (or either identical) alkyl group is the parent: ethanamine.
The other group on nitrogen gets the locant N → N-ethylethanamine (common name diethylamine).
An amide would need a C=O.
w: Amide needs C=O.
N has two ethyls, not one butyl.
N gets the locant.

q: What is the IUPAC name of HOCH₂CH₂OH?
o: Ethane-1,2-diol
Ethanol
Ethan-1-ol-2-ol
Glycerol
e: Two –OH groups on a two-carbon chain (common name: ethylene glycol).
w: Only one –OH.
Not proper form.
Glycerol is a three-carbon triol (propane-1,2,3-triol), but HOCH₂CH₂OH has two carbons and two –OH groups.

q: On a benzene ring, the prefix meta- (m-) indicates two substituents at which positions?
o: 1 and 3
1 and 2
1 and 4
1, 3 and 5
e: ortho = 1,2 (adjacent); meta = 1,3 (one carbon between); para = 1,4 (directly across).
These prefixes apply only to disubstituted rings.
w: Positions 1 and 2 are adjacent, which is the ortho relationship, not meta.
Positions 1 and 4 are directly across the ring, which is the para relationship, not meta.
Meta describes just two substituents at 1 and 3; listing 1, 3 and 5 requires three substituents.
t: O-M-P goes 2-3-4: ortho 1,2; meta 1,3; para 1,4.

q: Which compound is a constitutional isomer of cyclopentane?
o: Pent-2-ene
Cyclopentene
Pentane
Methylcyclopentane
e: Cyclopentane is C₅H₁₀: one ring, so one degree of unsaturation.
Pent-2-ene is also C₅H₁₀, with a C=C instead of a ring, so it is a constitutional isomer.
w: Cyclopentene is C₅H₈, with a ring and a C=C, so its formula differs.
Pentane is C₅H₁₂, with no ring or π bond.
Methylcyclopentane is C₆H₁₂, with one more carbon.
t: A ring and a π bond each count as one degree of unsaturation.

q: What is the common name of propanone?
o: Acetone
Acetaldehyde
Propionaldehyde
Acetic acid
e: CH₃COCH₃ is the simplest ketone.
w: Acetaldehyde is the two-carbon aldehyde (ethanal), but propanone is a three-carbon ketone.
Propionaldehyde is propanal, the three-carbon aldehyde; propanone has its C=O in the middle, making it a ketone.
Acetic acid is ethanoic acid, a carboxylic acid, while propanone is a ketone.

q: Breaking a C=C bond completely takes about 610 kJ mol⁻¹, while breaking a C–C single bond takes about 350 kJ mol⁻¹. What do these values suggest about the π bond?
o: It is weaker than the σ bond, about 260 kJ mol⁻¹
It is stronger than the σ bond, about 610 kJ mol⁻¹
It equals the σ bond, about 305 kJ mol⁻¹ each
It is stronger than the σ bond, about 350 kJ mol⁻¹
e: A C=C is one σ plus one π bond, so π ≈ 610 − 350 = 260 kJ mol⁻¹.
260 < 350: side-by-side p overlap is weaker than head-on σ overlap, which is why π bonds are the reactive part of alkenes.
w: Recheck: 610 − 350.
The π bond isn't equal to the σ bond: 610 − 350 = 260 kJ mol⁻¹ for π, less than the 350 for σ.
Weaker, not stronger.

q: Acrolein, CH₂=CH–CHO, has a resonance form in which the C=C and C=O electrons both shift. Besides the carbonyl carbon, which atom carries a partial + charge as a result?
o: The terminal CH₂ carbon (the β-carbon)
The middle CH carbon (the α-carbon)
The carbonyl oxygen atom
The hydrogen on the aldehyde carbon
e: Push the C=O π electrons onto O (O⁻), then move the C=C π electrons toward the carbonyl carbon.
That leaves the end CH₂ carbon with a + charge: ⁺CH₂–CH=CH–O⁻.
So the β-carbon is electrophilic, which is why nucleophiles can add there.
w: α-carbon isn't +.
O is −.
Not this H.

q: Lab techs estimate protein concentration from absorbance at 280 nm. Which structural feature is mainly responsible for this absorbance?
o: Conjugated aromatic rings of Trp and Tyr side chains
The C=O π bonds found in every peptide bond
The sp³ C–H bonds of the Leu, Ile and Val side chains
Hydrogen bonds between backbone N–H and C=O
e: Isolated π bonds (like a peptide C=O) absorb below about 230 nm; sp³ C–H bonds absorb only in the far UV.
The larger conjugated π systems of tryptophan's indole and tyrosine's phenol have smaller HOMO–LUMO gaps and absorb near 280 nm.
w: Isolated peptide C=O π bonds absorb below ~230 nm, not at 280 nm.
sp³ C–H bonds absorb only in the far UV.
Hydrogen bonds don't absorb UV at 280 nm.
t: More conjugation → smaller energy gap → longer wavelength absorbed.

q: Which pair are NOT resonance structures of each other?
o: Acetone and its enol form, prop-1-en-2-ol
The two Kekulé structures of benzene
Acetate drawn with − on either oxygen
Allyl cation drawn with + on either end
e: Resonance structures differ only in where electrons are drawn; every atom stays put.
Going from acetone to its enol moves a hydrogen atom, so they are tautomers: two different real compounds.
w: The two Kekulé structures of benzene differ only in where the π electrons are drawn, so they are resonance structures.
Moving the negative charge between acetate's oxygens shifts only electrons, so these are resonance structures.
Drawing the allyl cation's + on either end carbon moves only π electrons, so these are resonance structures.
t: If an atom moves, it's not resonance.

q: What is the hybridization of the nitrogen in an amide (R–CONH₂)?
o: sp², because its lone pair is in resonance with the C=O
sp³, because it has three σ bonds plus one lone pair
sp, because the C–N bond has partial triple-bond character
sp³d, because N expands its octet to form the C–N π bond
e: The N lone pair delocalizes into the C=O, making the amide group planar.
This planarity is why peptide bonds don't rotate freely.
w: Resonance changes it.
No triple bond.
N can't expand.

q: In methyl vinyl ether, CH₂=CH–O–CH₃, oxygen's lone pair is conjugated with the C=C. Which carbon becomes electron-rich (δ−) as a result?
o: The terminal CH₂ carbon
The CH carbon bonded to O
The methyl carbon on O
None; O only withdraws electrons
e: Draw the resonance form: an O lone pair forms a C=O⁺ π bond, pushing the C=C electrons onto the end carbon: ⁻CH₂–CH=O⁺–CH₃.
So the terminal carbon is δ− (nucleophilic) — the opposite of an α,β-unsaturated carbonyl, where the end carbon is δ+.
w: That's next to O⁺.
The methyl carbon on oxygen isn't part of the conjugated π system, so resonance doesn't put charge on it.
O donates here.
t: Lone-pair donors (O, N) push electron density to the far end of an attached C=C.

q: Which oxygen atom is best described as sp³ hybridized?
o: The oxygen in methanol, CH₃OH
The carbonyl oxygen in acetone
The ring oxygen in furan
An oxygen in carbon dioxide
e: Methanol's O has two single bonds and two lone pairs: four electron groups, sp³ (bent, about 108°).
w: A carbonyl oxygen has three electron groups (one double bond, two lone pairs), so it is sp².
Furan's oxygen puts one lone pair into the aromatic π system, so it is sp².
Each CO₂ oxygen is double-bonded with two lone pairs, so it is sp².

q: Why is cyclopropane far more strained than cyclohexane?
o: Its C–C–C angles are 60°, far from the ideal 109.5°
Its carbons are sp², which forces 120° angles
Its chair form puts every hydrogen in an axial position
Its C–C bonds are π bonds, which are weaker
e: Each carbon in cyclopropane is sp³-like and 'wants' 109.5°.
A triangle forces 60° angles, so the orbitals overlap poorly (bent bonds). This angle strain, plus eclipsed H's, makes cyclopropane reactive. Cyclohexane's chair is nearly strain-free.
w: Cyclopropane's carbons are sp³-like, wanting 109.5°; the strain comes from forcing them into 60° angles.
Cyclopropane is a flat three-membered ring and has no chair form; chairs are a cyclohexane feature.
Cyclopropane's C–C bonds are bent σ bonds formed from sp³-like orbitals, not π bonds.

q: Histidine's imidazole side chain has two nitrogens. Why is only one of them basic?
o: One N's lone pair is in the aromatic π system; the other's is free
One N is permanently protonated, so only the other can take H⁺
One N is sp³ and the other sp², and sp³ lone pairs aren't basic
The two N atoms share one lone pair, so only one can be protonated
e: The pyridine-like N can be protonated (pKa about 6), making histidine useful in enzyme active sites.
w: Neither N is permanently protonated; the ring is mostly neutral at pH 7.4 (pKa ≈ 6).
Both N's are sp² in the aromatic ring; the difference is where the lone pair sits.
Each N has its own lone pair; one is in the aromatic π system, the other is free.

q: What is the hybridization of nitrogen in methylamine (CH₃NH₂), pyridine and acetonitrile (CH₃C≡N), in that order?
o: sp³, sp², sp
sp², sp², sp
sp³, sp³, sp²
sp, sp², sp³
e: Methylamine N: three single bonds + one lone pair = 4 groups → sp³.
Pyridine N: two ring bonds (in the aromatic π system) + a lone pair in the ring plane = 3 groups → sp².
Nitrile N: one triple bond + one lone pair = 2 groups → sp.
w: Methylamine's N has four electron groups, so it is sp³, not sp².
Pyridine's N is part of a planar aromatic ring, so it is sp², not sp³.
This reverses the order; the triple-bonded nitrile N is the sp one.

q: Cycloocta-1,3,5,7-tetraene has 8 π electrons but is NOT strongly destabilized the way cyclobutadiene is. Why?
o: It folds into a tub, so π overlap around the ring breaks
8 electrons fit 4n + 2, so it is actually aromatic
Its carbons are sp³, so it has no π bonds
It is planar, but its large ring has no strain
e: A planar, fully conjugated ring with 8 π electrons (4n, n = 2) would be antiaromatic.
Cyclooctatetraene avoids this by bending into a tub shape: its C=C bonds are no longer conjugated around the ring, so it behaves as an ordinary (nonaromatic) polyene.
w: 8 is 4n.
Cyclooctatetraene's carbons are sp², so it does have π bonds; it avoids antiaromaticity by folding into a tub.
It isn't planar.
t: Antiaromaticity can only happen if the ring stays flat; big rings can pucker to escape it.

q: What is the geometry of the methyl anion, :CH₃⁻?
o: Trigonal pyramidal, like NH₃
Trigonal planar, like BF₃
Tetrahedral, with four bonds
Linear, like CO₂
e: The carbon has three bonds and one lone pair: four electron domains → sp³.
With one domain a lone pair, the shape is trigonal pyramidal; :CH₃⁻ is isoelectronic with NH₃.
w: Has a lone pair.
The methyl anion has three C–H bonds and a lone pair, not four bonds, so its shape is pyramidal.
With four electron domains (three bonds and a lone pair), the carbon is sp³ and pyramidal, not linear.

q: 2-Bromobutane is heated with sodium ethoxide in ethanol. What is the major product?
o: trans-But-2-ene
cis-But-2-ene
But-1-ene
2-Ethoxybutane
e: A strong, unhindered base with a 2° halide and heat favors E2.
Zaitsev: the more substituted alkene (but-2-ene) is favored over but-1-ene.
The trans isomer is favored over cis because its methyls are kept apart.
w: Cis is crowded.
But-1-ene is the less substituted alkene; with ethoxide, Zaitsev's rule favors the more substituted but-2-ene.
Base and heat: E2.

q: Which solvent best favors SN2 reactions?
o: A polar aprotic solvent, like acetone or DMSO
A polar protic solvent, like water or methanol
A nonpolar solvent, like hexane or toluene
A protic acidic solvent, like acetic acid
e: Polar aprotic solvents don't hydrogen bond to the nucleophile, so it stays reactive.
w: Solvates the nucleophile.
Most ionic nucleophiles dissolve poorly in nonpolar solvents like hexane, so SN2 isn't favored there.
Solvates the nucleophile.

q: An SN2 reaction at a chiral carbon gives:
o: Inversion of configuration
Retention of configuration
A racemic mixture
No change
e: Backside attack flips the molecule like an umbrella in the wind.
w: Backside attack inverts.
A racemic mixture comes from SN1 attack on a planar carbocation, not the backside attack of SN2.
Backside attack flips the stereocenter like an umbrella, so the configuration does change.

q: Which species has the same geometry and orbital picture as the methyl cation, CH₃⁺?
o: BH₃: trigonal planar, with an empty p orbital
NH₃, trigonal pyramidal with a lone pair
CH₃⁻, trigonal pyramidal with a lone pair
CH₄: tetrahedral, with four bonds and no empty orbital
e: CH₃⁺ has three bonds, six valence electrons and no lone pair: sp², trigonal planar, empty p orbital.
BH₃ is isoelectronic (three bonds, six electrons), so it has the same shape and an empty p orbital.
w: NH₃ has a lone pair, making it sp³ and pyramidal.
The methyl anion has a lone pair and is pyramidal like NH₃.
CH₄ has four bonds and is sp³ tetrahedral.

q: Which compound reacts fastest by SN1 in aqueous ethanol?
o: 2-Bromo-2-phenylpropane, PhC(CH₃)₂Br
2-Bromo-2-methylpropane, (CH₃)₃CBr
2-Bromopropane, (CH₃)₂CHBr
Bromobenzene, C₆H₅Br
e: SN1 rate tracks the stability of the carbocation formed in the slow step.
PhC(CH₃)₂⁺ is tertiary AND benzylic: the + charge spreads into the ring by resonance, so it forms fastest.
A phenyl cation (from bromobenzene) is extremely unstable, so bromobenzene doesn't react by SN1.
w: (CH₃)₃CBr forms a tertiary cation but lacks benzylic resonance into a ring, so it ionizes more slowly than PhC(CH₃)₂Br.
2-Bromopropane forms only a secondary carbocation, much less stable than a tertiary benzylic one.
Bromobenzene would have to form a phenyl cation, which is extremely unstable, so it doesn't react by SN1.

q: Bromobenzene is stirred with NaOH in water at 25 °C. What happens?
o: No reaction occurs at the ring C–Br bond
SN2 gives phenol, with inversion at C1
SN1 gives phenol via a phenyl cation
E2 gives cyclohexene as the main product
e: SN2 fails: backside attack would require the nucleophile to approach through the ring, and the sp² C–Br bond is strong.
SN1 fails: a phenyl cation is very unstable because its empty orbital lies in the ring plane, so the ring's π system can't stabilize it.
w: SN2 needs backside attack, but the ring blocks approach from behind the C–Br bond, so no phenol forms.
Phenyl cation unstable.
No β-H on ring.
t: Aryl and vinyl halides don't do SN1 or SN2.

q: A carbocation rearranges from secondary to tertiary by a 1,2-hydride shift. Why?
o: The tertiary carbocation is more stable
Secondary cations are actually more stable
Hydrogen atoms repel each other
The product loses a carbon
e: Rearrangements are common in SN1 and E1 reactions.
w: Tertiary is more stable.
Not the reason.
A 1,2-hydride shift only moves a hydrogen, so the cation keeps all of its carbons.

q: In a polar protic solvent such as methanol, which halide ion is the strongest nucleophile?
o: I⁻
F⁻
Cl⁻
Br⁻
e: Protic solvents hydrogen-bond strongly to small, charge-dense anions like F⁻, surrounding and slowing them.
I⁻ is large and polarizable, so it is the least tied up and the most nucleophilic in protic solvents.
w: F⁻ is small and charge-dense, so methanol hydrogen-bonds to it most strongly, making it the weakest nucleophile here.
Cl⁻ is smaller than I⁻ and more tightly solvated by methanol's hydrogen bonds, so it reacts more slowly.
Br⁻ is smaller and less polarizable than I⁻, so methanol solvates it more and it is less nucleophilic.
t: Protic: I⁻ best. Aprotic: F⁻ best. The solvent flips the order.

q:
The table gives the pKa of each ion's conjugate acid. Which ion is the best leaving group?
IonConjugate acid pKa
CF₃COO⁻0.2
CH₃COO⁻4.8
CH₃O⁻15.5
NH₂⁻38
o: CF₃COO⁻
CH₃COO⁻
CH₃O⁻
NH₂⁻
e: Good leaving groups are weak bases, stable on their own.
The lower the conjugate acid's pKa, the weaker the base.
CF₃COOH has the lowest pKa, so CF₃COO⁻ is the weakest base and the best leaving group.
w: Acetate is a reasonable leaving group, but CF₃ groups make trifluoroacetate a weaker base.
Methoxide is a strong base (pKa 15.5), so it leaves poorly.
Amide ion is an extremely strong base (pKa 38) and almost never leaves.

q: An oxidation in organic chemistry usually involves:
o: Gaining bonds to oxygen or losing bonds to hydrogen
Gaining bonds to hydrogen or losing bonds to oxygen
Gaining bonds to carbon or losing bonds to halogen
Adding water across a C=C bond with an acid catalyst
e: Example: alcohol → aldehyde is an oxidation.
w: Gaining bonds to hydrogen or losing bonds to oxygen is reduction, the opposite of oxidation.
Oxidation is defined by bonds to oxygen (or other electronegative atoms) and to hydrogen, not by C–C bond formation.
Adding water across a C=C is hydration, which doesn't change the oxidation level overall.

q: An SN1 reaction has k = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹. What is the initial rate when [R–Cl] = 0.50 M and the nucleophile concentration is 2.0 M?
e: SN1: rate = k[R–Cl]; the nucleophile is not in the rate law.
w: Multiply by 0.50 M.
Nu isn't in it.
Recheck: 2.0e−4 × 0.50.
t: 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ is the trap answer that wrongly multiplies by [Nu] = 2.0 M.

q: For E2 in a cyclohexane chair, the H and leaving group must be anti-periplanar. In the chair, this means both must be:
o: Axial, on adjacent carbons and opposite faces
Equatorial, on adjacent carbons and the same face
Axial, on adjacent carbons and the same face
Equatorial, on adjacent carbons and opposite faces
e: Anti-periplanar means the H–C–C–LG atoms lie in one plane with the H and LG 180° apart.
On adjacent ring carbons, only two axial bonds (one up, one down: trans-diaxial) line up this way.
w: Equatorial bonds point outward from the ring, so an equatorial H and leaving group can't be 180° apart.
Must be opposite.
Equatorial bonds on adjacent carbons are never anti-periplanar; only a trans-diaxial pair lines up at 180°.
t: Ring E2 needs trans-diaxial H and LG.

q:
Using the water-solubility data at 25 °C, which value best estimates the solubility of pentan-1-ol?
AlcoholSolubility (g per 100 mL)
MethanolMiscible
Butan-1-ol7.3
Hexan-1-ol0.59
Octan-1-ol0.05
o: About 2 g per 100 mL
About 7 g per 100 mL
About 0.6 g per 100 mL
About 15 g per 100 mL
e: Each added CH₂ makes the alcohol less water-soluble, because the nonpolar chain grows while there is still just one –OH.
Pentan-1-ol falls between butan-1-ol (7.3) and hexan-1-ol (0.59), so about 2 g per 100 mL fits (measured ≈ 2.2).
w: 7 g matches butan-1-ol; one more CH₂ should lower it.
0.6 g matches hexan-1-ol, which has one more CH₂ than pentan-1-ol.
15 g is above butan-1-ol's value, but solubility falls as the chain gets longer.

q: Glycerol (propane-1,2,3-triol) is used in many medicines and lotions. Why is it so water-soluble?
o: Its three –OH groups form many hydrogen bonds with water
It ionizes in water to give a glycerate anion and H⁺
Its polar C–H bonds interact strongly with water's dipoles
Its three ester groups accept hydrogen bonds from water
e: Small molecules with several –OH groups are highly water-soluble.
w: Glycerol's –OH groups (pKa ~14) don't ionize in water.
C–H bonds are essentially nonpolar; the –OH groups do the work.
Glycerol has no ester groups; it's an alcohol (triglycerides are the esters).

q: Oxidizing ethanol with PCC gives:
o: Ethanal (acetaldehyde)
Ethanoic (acetic) acid
Ethane
Ethene (ethylene)
e: PCC stops at the aldehyde.
w: Over-oxidation; PCC is anhydrous and mild, so it stops at the aldehyde instead of going on to the acid.
Ethane would need full reduction (loss of oxygen); PCC is an oxidant, not a reductant.
Ethene comes from acid-catalyzed dehydration, not oxidation.

q: Ethane-1,2-diol and acetone form a five-membered cyclic acetal. Which diol would form a six-membered cyclic acetal with acetone?
o: Propane-1,3-diol
Propane-1,2-diol
Butane-1,4-diol
Butane-2,3-diol
e: Ring atoms = acetal carbon + 2 oxygens + the carbons between the two –OH groups.
Ethane-1,2-diol: 1 + 2 + 2 = 5. Propane-1,3-diol: 1 + 2 + 3 = 6.
w: The –OH groups of propane-1,2-diol are on adjacent carbons, so it gives a 5-membered ring.
Butane-1,4-diol has four carbons between its –OH groups, giving a 7-membered ring.
Butane-2,3-diol is a vicinal diol, so it gives a 5-membered ring.

q: In the body, ethanol is oxidized first to:
o: Acetaldehyde
Acetic acid directly
Methanol
Acetone
e: Alcohol dehydrogenase: ethanol → acetaldehyde (toxic, causes hangover symptoms).
Aldehyde dehydrogenase then makes acetate.
w: Skips a step; acetate forms only after aldehyde dehydrogenase acts on acetaldehyde.
Methanol has one fewer carbon; metabolism oxidizes ethanol without removing a carbon.
Acetone is a three-carbon ketone (a ketone body); it cannot come from two-carbon ethanol.

q: Which compound has the highest boiling point?
o: Ethane-1,2-diol, HOCH₂CH₂OH (62 g mol⁻¹)
Propan-1-ol, CH₃CH₂CH₂OH (60 g mol⁻¹)
Methoxyethane, CH₃OCH₂CH₃ (60 g mol⁻¹)
Butane, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃ (58 g mol⁻¹), a nonpolar alkane
e: The molar masses are nearly equal, so intermolecular forces decide.
Ethane-1,2-diol has two –OH groups per molecule, so it forms a dense H-bond network (bp 197 °C vs 97 °C for propan-1-ol).
w: Propan-1-ol H-bonds, but with only one –OH it forms fewer H-bonds than the diol.
An ether has no O–H, so it can't H-bond to itself (bp 7 °C).
Butane has only London forces, so it boils lowest (−0.5 °C).

q: Why does the Williamson ether synthesis fail with tertiary alkyl halides?
o: The alkoxide acts as a base, causing E2 elimination instead
The alkoxide is too weak a nucleophile to attack tertiary carbon
Tertiary carbocations are too unstable to form in the solvent
Tertiary ethers are unstable and decompose as soon as they form
e: Alkoxides are strong bases; hindered substrates favor E2.
w: Alkoxides are strong nucleophiles; the problem is steric blocking of backside attack, which lets their basicity win (E2).
Williamson is SN2 and never involves a carbocation; carbocation stability is irrelevant here.
Tertiary ethers (e.g., MTBE) are stable; the reaction fails because elimination outcompetes substitution.

q: Which alcohol is most easily dehydrated by acid?
o: (CH₃)₃COH (tertiary)
CH₃CH₂OH (primary)
CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ (secondary)
CH₃OH
e: Dehydration goes through a carbocation (E1); tertiary cations form most easily.
w: Primary is slowest.
Tertiary is faster.
Can't form a cation.

q: Menthol, a secondary alcohol, is oxidized with chromic acid to menthone. Which change in the IR spectrum confirms the reaction?
o: The broad 3200–3550 cm⁻¹ band vanishes and a strong 1715 cm⁻¹ band appears
A broad 2500–3300 cm⁻¹ band and a band near 1710 cm⁻¹ both appear
Two weak bands near 2720 and 2820 cm⁻¹ appear beside a new strong band near 1725 cm⁻¹
The 3200–3550 cm⁻¹ band grows stronger and nothing appears near 1700 cm⁻¹
e: Oxidizing a secondary alcohol gives a ketone.
So the alcohol O–H stretch (broad, 3200–3550) vanishes and a ketone C=O stretch (~1715) appears.
w: That broad O–H plus C=O pattern is a carboxylic acid, which a secondary alcohol can't form.
The 2720/2820 bands are aldehyde C–H stretches; secondary alcohols give ketones, not aldehydes.
The O–H band should disappear, and a C=O band should appear.

q: (S)-Butan-2-ol is treated with TsCl and pyridine. What is the configuration at the stereocenter of the tosylate that forms?
o: S, because the C–O bond is not broken
R, because the oxygen is attacked from the back
Racemic, because a carbocation forms first
R, because OTs changes the priority order
e: The alcohol's oxygen attacks the sulfur of TsCl; only the O–H bond breaks.
The C–O bond to the stereocenter is untouched, so its arrangement is retained, and O still has top priority, so the label stays S.
Inversion happens only later, if a nucleophile does SN2 on the tosylate.
w: C–O is kept.
Tosylation breaks only the O–H bond, not the C–O bond, so no carbocation forms and the center isn't racemized.
O still ranks first.

q: Which alcohol gives only ONE alkene product when dehydrated with acid (counting cis/trans isomers as different products)?
o: Cyclohexanol
Butan-2-ol
Pentan-2-ol
2-Methylbutan-2-ol
e: Cyclohexanol's carbocation is symmetric: losing H⁺ from either neighbor gives the same cyclohexene.
Butan-2-ol and pentan-2-ol give a 1-ene plus cis- and trans-2-enes.
2-Methylbutan-2-ol gives both 2-methylbut-2-ene and 2-methylbut-1-ene.
w: Gives three products.
Gives three products.
Gives two products.

q: Hydroquinone (benzene-1,4-diol) is gently oxidized. What is the product?
o: 1,4-Benzoquinone
Phenol
Cyclohexane-1,4-diol
Benzoic acid
e: Each –OH loses its H (2 H⁺ + 2 e⁻ in total), and both oxygens become C=O.
The product is a quinone; the change is reversible.
Ubiquinone (coenzyme Q) uses this same quinone ⇌ hydroquinone redox to carry electrons in the ETC.
w: Loses an OH.
Cyclohexane-1,4-diol would require adding hydrogen to the ring, which is a reduction, not an oxidation.
Benzoic acid has a –COOH carbon outside the ring, but gentle oxidation of hydroquinone adds no carbon; its oxygens become C=O.

q: What is the main driving force of the Wittig reaction?
o: Formation of the very strong P=O bond in Ph₃P=O
Formation of a carbocation intermediate on carbon
Release of a gas that bubbles out of solution
Formation of an aromatic ring in the alkene product
e: The ylide carbon attacks the C=O, giving a four-membered ring containing C, C, P and O (an oxaphosphetane).
The ring falls apart to the alkene plus triphenylphosphine oxide; the P=O bond (over 500 kJ mol⁻¹) is so strong that this step is strongly downhill.
w: The Wittig reaction goes through a four-membered oxaphosphetane ring, not a carbocation.
The Wittig reaction releases no gas; its by-product is solid triphenylphosphine oxide.
No aromatic ring forms.

q: Which reagent sequence converts cyclohexanol into 1-methylcyclohexan-1-ol?
o: Chromic acid; then CH₃MgBr; then aqueous acid
CH₃MgBr; then chromic acid; then aqueous acid
Chromic acid; then NaBH₄; then aqueous acid
PCC; then CH₃OH with an acid catalyst
e: Oxidizing the secondary alcohol gives the ketone cyclohexanone.
CH₃MgBr adds a methyl to the carbonyl carbon; acidic workup gives the tertiary alcohol 1-methylcyclohexan-1-ol.
w: The Grignard reagent would be destroyed by the alcohol's O–H before any ketone is present.
NaBH₄ just reduces cyclohexanone back to cyclohexanol, adding no carbon.
Methanol and acid would give a hemiacetal or acetal, not a new C–C bond.

q: Why are aldehydes easily oxidized to carboxylic acids, while ketones resist oxidation?
o: An aldehyde has an H on its carbonyl carbon
An aldehyde has a lone pair on its carbonyl carbon
Ketones have no α-hydrogens
A ketone's oxygen has a full positive charge
e: Oxidizing R–CHO to R–COOH replaces the carbonyl C–H with C–OH.
A ketone's carbonyl carbon has two C–C bonds; oxidizing it would require breaking a C–C bond.
w: No lone pair there.
Ketones have them.
No full charge.

q: 0.050 mol of propanal reacts completely with excess Tollens' reagent, [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺. What mass of silver is deposited? (Ag = 108 g mol⁻¹)
e: RCHO → RCOO⁻ is a 2-electron oxidation, and each Ag⁺ accepts 1 electron, so 2 Ag form per aldehyde.
w: Use 2 Ag per CHO.
Recheck: 0.10 × 108.
Off by 4.

q: Pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B₆) forms an imine with amino acids during transamination. Which functional group on PLP makes this possible?
o: An aldehyde
A ketone
A carboxylic acid
An ether
e: The aldehyde reacts with the amino acid's amine to form a Schiff base.
w: PLP has an aldehyde (C4′ formyl), not a ketone.
Carboxylic acids form amides, not imines, and PLP's key group is an aldehyde.
Ethers are unreactive and can't form imines.

q: When a primary amine reacts with a ketone to form an imine, which intermediate forms just before water is lost?
o: A carbinolamine (C bearing both –OH and –NHR)
An enol (C=C bearing an –OH)
An acetal (C bearing two –OR groups and no N)
An enolate (C=C bearing an –O⁻)
e: The amine adds to the C=O carbon, and proton transfers give a carbinolamine (hemiaminal).
Acid protonates its –OH, water leaves, and loss of N–H gives the C=N bond.
w: Not an enol.
An acetal needs two –OR groups on one carbon, but here the amine nitrogen adds, giving C bearing –OH and –NHR.
Not an enolate.

q: An aldehyde is converted to an alkene using a phosphorus ylide. This reaction is the:
o: Wittig reaction
Aldol reaction
Grignard reaction
Diels–Alder reaction
e: The C=O becomes a C=C.
w: The aldol reaction joins two carbonyls via an enolate to give a β-hydroxy carbonyl, not an alkene from an ylide.
Grignard reactions add RMgX to C=O to form alcohols; no phosphorus ylide.
Diels–Alder is a diene + dienophile cycloaddition forming a ring, not C=O to C=C conversion.

q: Acetaldehyde is treated with excess methanol and a trace of acid. What is the final product?
o: CH₃CH(OCH₃)₂
CH₃CH(OH)OCH₃
CH₃CH₂OCH₃
CH₃COOCH₃
e: One methanol adds to give the hemiacetal, CH₃CH(OH)OCH₃.
With excess alcohol and acid, the –OH is replaced by a second –OCH₃ (water leaves), giving the acetal 1,1-dimethoxyethane.
w: That's the hemiacetal.
Not an ether.
Not an ester.

q: Why does triethylamine, (CH₃CH₂)₃N, form neither an imine nor an enamine with acetone?
o: Its nitrogen has no H to lose after adding
It is too weakly basic to attack any C=O
It is fully protonated at every pH
Its nitrogen has no lone pair to donate
e: Imines need an N with two H's (1° amine); enamines need an N with one H (2° amine).
After a 3° amine adds, the nitrogen is positive with no H to remove, so no stable neutral product forms and the addition reverses.
w: It's basic enough.
Not at all pH.
It has a lone pair.

q: The imine (CH₃)₂C=N–CH₂CH₃ is hydrolyzed in aqueous acid. Which products form?
o: Acetone and ethylamine
Ethanal and propan-2-amine
Acetone and ethanol
N-Ethylpropanamide
e: Hydrolysis reverses imine formation: water adds across C=N, and the C–N bond breaks.
The carbon side becomes a C=O: (CH₃)₂C=O, acetone.
The nitrogen side becomes the amine: H₂N–CH₂CH₃, ethylamine.
w: Hydrolysis breaks the C=N bond, so the carbon side becomes acetone and the N side ethylamine, not ethanal and propan-2-amine.
N side is an amine.
Not an amide.

q: 2,4-Dinitrophenylhydrazine (2,4-DNP) is added to each compound. Which one gives NO colored precipitate?
o: Ethyl acetate
Cyclohexanone
Benzaldehyde
Acetone
e: 2,4-DNP adds to the C=O of aldehydes and ketones and loses water to form a colored hydrazone.
An ester's C=O is much less electrophilic (lone-pair donation from the –OR oxygen), so it doesn't form a hydrazone.
w: Cyclohexanone is a ketone and gives an orange hydrazone.
Benzaldehyde is an aldehyde and gives a hydrazone.
Acetone is a ketone and gives a hydrazone.

q: Glucose cyclizes when its C5 –OH attacks its C1 aldehyde. What functional group forms?
o: A hemiacetal
An acetal
A ketone
An ester
e: One –OH and one –OR on the same carbon: a hemiacetal.
w: An acetal needs two –OR groups on one carbon; intramolecular cyclization gives one –OH and one –OR.
C5–OH attacking C1 does not create a ketone; the C1 carbonyl is consumed.
An ester needs an acyl carbon; glucose's C1 is an aldehyde, so cyclization yields a hemiacetal.

q: Racemization at an α-carbon stereocenter can happen in acid or base. Why?
o: Forming the planar enol or enolate erases the stereochemistry
Forming a planar carbocation at the α-carbon erases it
Repeated SN2 attack by water inverts the α-carbon each time
Reduction of the carbonyl makes the α-carbon achiral
e: Re-protonation can occur on either face.
w: α-Carbons of carbonyls do not form carbocations under these conditions; the planar intermediate is the enol/enolate.
Water does not do SN2 at the α-carbon here; racemization goes through the enol.
No reduction occurs; acid or base only catalyzes tautomerization.

q: Ethyl acetate, CH₃COOCH₂CH₃, is treated with LDA at −78 °C. Which hydrogen is removed?
o: A hydrogen on the CH₃ attached to the C=O
A hydrogen on the O–CH₂ group
A hydrogen on the terminal CH₃ of the ethyl group
The carbonyl carbon's hydrogen
e: LDA removes the most acidic C–H: one on the α-carbon (bonded to the C=O carbon).
Here that is the acetyl CH₃; the resulting enolate is resonance-stabilized onto the carbonyl oxygen (pKa ≈ 25).
w: The O–CH₂ carbon is bonded to oxygen, not to the carbonyl carbon, so its anion isn't resonance-stabilized.
The terminal CH₃ is far from the C=O, so its H's are not acidic.
An ester's carbonyl carbon has no hydrogen.

q: Pentane-2,4-dione (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 9) is mixed with sodium ethoxide (ethanol pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 16). About what is the equilibrium constant for the proton transfer?
o: About 10<sup>7</sup>
About 10<sup>−7</sup>
About 10<sup>25</sup>
About 7
e: K = 10<sup>(pK<sub>a</sub> of product acid − pK<sub>a</sub> of reactant acid)</sup> = 10<sup>(16 − 9)</sup> = 10<sup>7</sup>.
The equilibrium lies far toward the enolate and ethanol, so ethoxide deprotonates the dione essentially completely.
w: 10⁻⁷ flips the exponent; the stronger acid (dione, pKa 9) is on the left, so K = 10^(16 − 9) = 10⁷.
Recheck: 16 − 9.
Exponent, not 7.
t: Proton transfer favors the side with the weaker acid (the higher pK<sub>a</sub>).

q:
Use the average bond enthalpies (kJ mol⁻¹) to estimate ΔH for acetone (keto) → prop-1-en-2-ol (enol).
BondEnthalpy
C=O745
C–C347
C–H413
C=C614
C–O358
O–H467
o: About +66 kJ mol⁻¹
About −66 kJ mol⁻¹
About +131 kJ mol⁻¹
About +77 kJ mol⁻¹
e: Keto → enol breaks C=O, one C–C and one C–H, and forms C=C, C–O and O–H.
ΔH ≈ 1505 − 1439 = +66 kJ mol⁻¹, so the keto form is favored.
w: −66 subtracts in the wrong order (formed − broken).
+131 compares only C=O with C=C (745 − 614) and ignores the other bond changes.
+77 counts only C=O and C–H broken and C=C and O–H formed, leaving out the C–C bond broken and the C–O bond formed.
t: The strong C=O bond is why simple ketones are almost entirely keto.

q: Acetoacetic acid (a ketone body) spontaneously decarboxylates to form:
o: Acetone
Acetic acid
Ethanol
β-Hydroxybutyrate
e: CH₃COCH₂COOH → CH₃COCH₃ + CO₂
w: Acetic acid has two carbons and a COOH; losing CO₂ removes the acid group, leaving acetone.
Ethanol would require reduction and C–C cleavage; decarboxylation leaves a ketone.
β-Hydroxybutyrate forms by enzymatic reduction of acetoacetate, not by decarboxylation.

q: Acetone is heated with NaOH so that the aldol product dehydrates. What is the main product?
o: 4-Methylpent-3-en-2-one
4-Hydroxy-4-methylpentan-2-one
Hex-3-en-2-one
2-Methylpent-2-enal
e: The acetone enolate (CH₂⁻) attacks another acetone: (CH₃)₂C(OH)–CH₂–CO–CH₃.
Heat removes water, giving a C=C conjugated with the C=O: (CH₃)₂C=CH–CO–CH₃.
4-Hydroxy-4-methylpentan-2-one is the addition product before dehydration.
w: 4-Hydroxy-4-methylpentan-2-one is the aldol addition product, before heat removes water to form the C=C.
Hex-3-en-2-one is an unbranched chain, but joining two acetones gives a branched (CH₃)₂C=CH–CO–CH₃ skeleton.
Not an aldehyde.

q: The Claisen condensation joins two esters to form a:
o: β-Keto ester
β-Hydroxy aldehyde
Diol
Carboxylic acid
e: It's the ester version of the aldol reaction.
w: β-Hydroxy aldehydes come from aldol reactions of aldehydes; esters lose alkoxide to give a β-keto ester.
Claisen condensation forms a C–C bond and keeps a carbonyl; it does not reduce to a diol.
The product retains an ester and a new ketone; no free carboxylic acid forms.

q: Fatty acid synthase builds fatty acids by joining acetyl and malonyl units with loss of CO₂. Which pair of reactions does this combine?
o: Decarboxylation and Claisen-type condensation
Carboxylation and Claisen-type condensation
Decarboxylation and Wittig-type olefination
Hydrolysis and Fischer-type esterification
e: Decarboxylating malonyl drives the C–C bond-forming condensation.
w: Malonyl loses CO₂ during the condensation; that's decarboxylation, not carboxylation.
Wittig reactions use phosphorus ylides to make alkenes, not C–C bond formation in fatty acid synthesis.
No hydrolysis or esterification drives chain growth; C–C bonds form by condensation.

q: Propanal is treated with dilute NaOH at low temperature (no dehydration). What is the aldol addition product?
o: 3-Hydroxy-2-methylpentanal
3-Hydroxyhexanal
2-Hydroxy-3-methylpentanal
2-Methylpent-2-enal
e: The enolate forms at C2 of propanal (the CH₂ next to C=O).
C2 attacks C1 of a second propanal: CH₃CH₂–CH(OH)–CH(CH₃)–CHO.
Longest chain with CHO: 5 carbons, OH on C3, methyl on C2.
w: Branch at C2.
OH on C3.
2-Methylpent-2-enal is the dehydrated condensation product, but low temperature stops the reaction before water is lost.
t: The α-carbon becomes the branch point, so self-aldols of aldehydes other than acetaldehyde always give a branch at C2.

q: In the last step of each β-oxidation cycle, thiolase uses CoA–SH to split a 3-ketoacyl-CoA into acetyl-CoA and an acyl-CoA two carbons shorter. This cleavage is the reverse of which reaction?
o: A Claisen condensation
An aldol condensation
A Michael addition
A Fischer esterification
e: A Claisen condensation joins an ester (or thioester) enolate to another (thio)ester, giving a β-keto (thio)ester.

Thiolase does the reverse. In the net reaction a thiolate (first the enzyme's cysteine, then CoA–SH) attacks the ketone C=O of the β-keto thioester, and the enolate of acetyl-CoA leaves (a retro-Claisen).
In ketone-body synthesis the same chemistry runs forward, joining two acetyl-CoA into acetoacetyl-CoA.
w: Aldol makes β-hydroxy carbonyls from aldehyde/ketone enolates, not β-keto thioesters.
Michael addition is conjugate addition to α,β-unsaturated carbonyls.
Fischer esterification forms esters from acids and alcohols; no C–C bond is involved.

q: Why can a ketone's stereocenter at the α-carbon be lost over time in a basic drug formulation?
o: Enolate formation lets the α-stereocenter racemize
Base hydrolyzes the ketone into a carboxylate salt
Hydroxide attacks the α-carbon by SN2, inverting it
Base reduces the ketone to an achiral alcohol
e: Formulations may be buffered to slow this process.
w: Ketones aren't hydrolyzed to carboxylates by base; there's no leaving group.
SN2 needs a leaving group at the α-carbon; racemization goes through a planar enolate.
Base is not a reducing agent; reduction would need a hydride source.

q: In a Claisen condensation of ethyl acetate, why is sodium ethoxide used instead of sodium hydroxide?
o: NaOH would hydrolyze the ester to a carboxylate
NaOH is too weak a base to form any enolate at all
Ethoxide is a stronger base than LDA
Ethoxide reacts with the ester irreversibly
e: Hydroxide attacks the ester C=O, giving acetate (saponification), which can't do a Claisen.
Ethoxide can also attack the ester, but that only swaps –OEt for –OEt, so nothing is lost.
Rule: match the alkoxide base to the ester's alkoxy group.
w: It's strong enough.
Not stronger than LDA.
Ethoxide's attack on an ethyl ester is reversible and only swaps –OEt for –OEt, so nothing is lost.

q: 4-Hydroxybutanoic acid forms a lactone easily when warmed with acid, but 3-hydroxypropanoic acid does not. Why?
o: Its lactone would be a strained four-membered ring
It has no –OH group to attack the carboxyl carbon
Its –OH is too acidic to act as a nucleophile
Its lactone would be a strained three-membered ring
e: Count ring atoms: the –OH oxygen, the carbons in between, and the carboxyl carbon.
4-Hydroxybutanoic acid gives a five-membered ring (γ-butyrolactone), which is almost strain-free.
3-Hydroxypropanoic acid would give a four-membered β-lactone, which is highly strained, so it doesn't form easily.
w: It has an –OH.
–OH can attack.
Ring is four atoms.

q: Acetic acid + ethanol (with H₂SO₄) gives which ester?
o: Ethyl acetate (ethyl ethanoate)
Methyl acetate (methyl ethanoate)
Ethyl formate (ethyl methanoate)
Methyl propanoate (methyl propionate)
e: Alkyl group from the alcohol (ethyl) + acid part (acetate).
w: Methyl acetate would require methanol; ethanol supplies an ethyl group.
Ethyl formate would require formic acid; acetic acid supplies the acetate part.
Methyl propanoate would need methanol and propanoic acid; both parts are wrong.

q: Benzoic acid is treated with SOCl₂, and the product is then added to excess NH₃. What is the final product?
o: Benzamide (C₆H₅CONH₂)
Benzoyl chloride (C₆H₅COCl)
Ammonium benzoate (C₆H₅COO⁻ NH₄⁺)
Aniline (C₆H₅NH₂)
e: SOCl₂ converts –COOH into the very reactive acid chloride, C₆H₅COCl.
NH₃ attacks the acid chloride C=O and Cl⁻ leaves, giving the amide (extra NH₃ absorbs the HCl).
Mixing benzoic acid with NH₃ directly would only give the ammonium salt.
w: Benzoyl chloride is the intermediate formed by SOCl₂; excess NH₃ then converts it to benzamide.
That's direct mixing.
Aniline would require removing the carbonyl carbon entirely, but NH₃ substitutes at the C=O, keeping it.

q: Many drugs that contain a carboxylic acid are given as ethyl ester prodrugs (for example, the ACE inhibitor enalapril). How does this most likely improve oral absorption?
o: Masking one –COOH makes it less charged; esterases free the acid
The ester is more ionized at pH 7.4, so it dissolves better in the gut
Esters bind the drug target more strongly than acids
The ester cannot be hydrolyzed, so it lasts longer
e: At intestinal and blood pH, a –COOH (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 4) is mostly ionized and crosses lipid membranes poorly.
Esterifying the –COOH removes one negative charge, so the molecule is less polar and more lipophilic.
After absorption, esterase enzymes hydrolyze it back to the active carboxylic acid.
w: Esters are neutral, not ionized; that's why they cross membranes.
The ester is an inactive prodrug; the acid binds the target.
Esterases do hydrolyze it; that's how the active drug is freed.

q: Freezing-point depression in benzene gives an apparent molar mass of about 120 g mol⁻¹ for acetic acid (true value 60 g mol⁻¹). What explains this?
o: Acetic acid forms hydrogen-bonded dimers in benzene
Acetic acid ionizes completely in benzene
Benzene reacts with acetic acid to form an ester
Acetic acid's molar mass doubles when it freezes
e: Colligative properties count particles.
In a nonpolar solvent, two acid molecules pair up through two O–H···O=C hydrogen bonds.
Half as many particles makes the apparent molar mass about 2 × 60 = 120 g mol⁻¹.
w: Complete ionization would increase the number of particles and lower the apparent molar mass, not double it.
Benzene doesn't react with acetic acid, and forming an ester would require an alcohol.
Freezing doesn't change a molecule's molar mass; the doubling comes from two acid molecules pairing up.

q: A student tries to make terephthalic acid (benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid) by treating 4-bromobenzoic acid with Mg in ether, then CO₂, then H₃O⁺. Mostly benzoic acid is recovered. What went wrong?
o: Each Grignard formed was protonated by a –COOH group
CO₂ added twice to the same Grignard carbon atom
The Grignard reagent attacked the ether solvent instead
The ring bromine was replaced by an –OH group in workup
e: An aryl Grignard carbon is extremely basic (its conjugate acid, benzene, has pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 43).
As soon as Ar–MgBr forms, it removes an acidic –COOH proton (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 4), turning the C–Mg carbon into C–H. After workup, that molecule is benzoic acid.
Grignard reagents can't be made or used in the presence of O–H groups such as acids, alcohols or water.
w: CO₂ adds once to a Grignard carbon to give a carboxylate.
Ether is the usual Grignard solvent; it's not attacked.
Workup doesn't replace bromine with –OH.

q: A carboxylic acid and a primary amine are mixed at room temperature. What mainly forms?
o: An ammonium carboxylate salt
An amide, with loss of water
An ester, with loss of ammonia
An imine, with loss of water
e: The fastest reaction is acid–base: RCOOH + R′NH₂ → RCOO⁻ ⁺H₃NR′.
The carboxylate is a poor electrophile, so amide formation requires strong heating or an activating agent (e.g., converting to an acid chloride, or DCC).
w: Amide formation from an acid and amine requires strong heating or an activating agent, not room temperature.
An ester requires an alcohol, which isn't present; an amine and acid just form a salt.
Imines form from aldehydes or ketones, not carboxylic acids, so no imine appears here.
t: Acid + amine at room temperature = salt, not amide.

q: How does distance affect the acid-strengthening effect of a chlorine substituent?
o: The closer the Cl is to the carboxyl group, the stronger the effect
The farther the Cl is from the carboxyl group, the stronger the effect
The effect is the same at every position along the carbon chain
A nearby Cl weakens the acid, while a distant Cl strengthens it
e: The inductive effect falls off quickly with distance.
w: Reversed; the inductive effect weakens rapidly with each intervening bond.
Inductive effects are distance-dependent, falling off sharply along the chain.
Cl is electron-withdrawing at any position; nearby Cl strengthens the acid most.

q: Formic acid (HCOOH, pK<sub>a</sub> 3.75) is a stronger acid than acetic acid (CH₃COOH, pK<sub>a</sub> 4.76). Why?
o: The CH₃ group donates electron density, destabilizing acetate
Formic acid has more resonance forms in its conjugate base than acetic acid
The CH₃ group withdraws electron density from the O–H
Formate is stabilized by hydrogen bonding to its C–H
e: Alkyl groups are weakly electron-donating.
Pushing electron density toward an already-negative carboxylate destabilizes it, so acetic acid ionizes less.
w: Formate and acetate each have the same two equivalent resonance forms, so resonance can't explain the difference.
The CH₃ group donates electron density, not withdraws it; that donation destabilizes acetate.
A C–H bond doesn't hydrogen bond to stabilize formate; acetate is weaker because CH₃ donates electron density.

q: Which haloacetic acid is the strongest acid?
o: FCH₂COOH
ClCH₂COOH
BrCH₂COOH
ICH₂COOH
e: All four have one halogen on the α-carbon, so the difference is electronegativity.
F is the most electronegative, so it withdraws the most electron density and best stabilizes the carboxylate.
w: Chlorine is less electronegative than fluorine, so it stabilizes the carboxylate less and ClCH₂COOH is weaker.
Bromine is less electronegative than fluorine, so it withdraws less electron density and BrCH₂COOH is weaker.
Iodine is the least electronegative halogen here, so ICH₂COOH is the weakest of these acids.

q: Acetic acid reacts with ethanol whose oxygen is labeled with ¹⁸O, using an acid catalyst. Where does the ¹⁸O end up?
o: In the ester, as the O bonded to the ethyl group
In the water by-product
In the ester's C=O oxygen
Split evenly between the ester's two oxygens and the water
e: The alcohol's oxygen attacks the protonated acid's carbonyl carbon and stays bonded to ethyl.
The water that leaves comes from the acid's original –OH.
So the label appears as CH₃CO–¹⁸O–CH₂CH₃.
w: Acid loses OH.
Not the C=O.
The labeled alcohol oxygen stays bonded to ethyl throughout, so the ¹⁸O isn't scrambled among the oxygens.
t: In Fischer esterification, the acid loses OH and the alcohol loses H.

q: Which sequence converts 1-bromobutane into pentanoic acid?
o: NaCN in DMSO, then H₃O⁺ with heat
Mg in ether, then H₂C=O, then H₃O⁺
NaOH(aq), then hot KMnO₄, then H₃O⁺
Mg in ether, then H₂O as workup
e: Pentanoic acid (C₅) has one carbon more than 1-bromobutane (C₄), so the new COOH carbon must be added.
CN⁻ displaces Br⁻ (SN2) to give CH₃(CH₂)₃CN; hot aqueous acid then hydrolyzes C≡N to COOH: CH₃(CH₂)₃COOH.
Mg/H₂C=O gives pentan-1-ol (an alcohol), NaOH then KMnO₄ gives butanoic acid (no added carbon), and Mg then H₂O gives butane.
w: Gives an alcohol.
No added carbon.
Making the Grignard reagent and then adding water just protonates it, giving butane with no new carbon.

q: A kinase phosphorylates a serine side chain (–CH₂OH → –CH₂OPO₃H₂, whose second pK<sub>a</sub> is about 6). At pH 7.4, how does this change the charge at that site?
o: From 0 to about −2
From 0 to about −1
From 0 to about +1
From −1 to about −3
e: The serine –OH is neutral at pH 7.4.
A phosphate monoester has two acidic O–H groups: pK<sub>a1</sub> ≈ 1–2 (fully ionized) and pK<sub>a2</sub> ≈ 6. At pH 7.4, about 1.4 units above pK<sub>a2</sub>, about 96% is the dianion.
w: Two P–OH ionize.
Adding a phosphate adds ionizable acidic O–H groups, which make the site negative, not positive.
Serine starts neutral.
t: Adding a phosphate adds roughly two negative charges, which is why phosphorylation can switch protein shape so strongly.

q: Amphetamine is a basic drug. Making the urine more acidic speeds up its excretion. Why?
o: More drug is protonated (charged) in acidic urine, so less is reabsorbed
More drug is neutral in acidic urine, so it is filtered out by the kidney faster
More drug is deprotonated in acidic urine, so less is reabsorbed
Acidic urine hydrolyzes the amine into easily excreted fragments
e: Charged molecules are 'trapped' in urine (ion trapping).
w: Acidic urine protonates bases, making them charged, not neutral.
Acidic conditions protonate, not deprotonate, a base.
Acidic urine doesn't break down amines; the effect is ion trapping.

q: At pH 7.4, a typical primary amine (conjugate acid pKa ≈ 10.6) exists mainly as:
o: The protonated ammonium ion (R–NH₃⁺)
The neutral free amine (R–NH₂)
The deprotonated amide anion (R–NH⁻)
A roughly 50:50 mix of R–NH₂ and R–NH₃⁺
e: pH below pKa → protonated.
w: pH 7.4 is ~3 units below the pKa, so about 99.9% is protonated, not neutral.
Forming R–NH⁻ requires pH far above ~35; it doesn't exist in water.
A 50:50 mix occurs only at pH = pKa (10.6), not 7.4.

q: How many water molecules are released when 4 amino acids join to form a tetrapeptide?
e: Each peptide bond releases one water (condensation).
w: Four amino acids form three peptide bonds, releasing three waters, not four.
Two waters would correspond to a tripeptide.
One water forms a single bond, i.e., a dipeptide.

q: In terpene biosynthesis, dimethylallyl diphosphate, (CH₃)₂C=CHCH₂–OPP, loses its diphosphate group to form an allylic carbocation. Why is diphosphate such a good leaving group here?
o: As an anion it is a weak base, stabilized by resonance and Mg²⁺
It is a strong base, so it pulls away from carbon with great force
It is neutral when it leaves, so no charge has to be stabilized
It forms a C=O bond as it leaves, releasing a great deal of energy
e: Good leaving groups are weak bases. Diphosphate's negative charges are spread over several oxygens by resonance.
In enzymes, bound Mg²⁺ ions further neutralize that charge. The allylic cation left behind is also resonance-stabilized.
w: Weak bases leave well.
Diphosphate leaves as a negatively charged anion, not a neutral species; resonance and Mg²⁺ stabilize that charge.
No C=O forms.

q: Acetylating aniline gives acetanilide, C₆H₅NHCOCH₃. How does the basicity of its nitrogen compare with that of aniline?
o: Much less basic, since the lone pair is also shared with C=O
Much more basic, since the acetyl group donates electrons
About the same, since the N still has a lone pair
More basic, since the N now has only one H attached
e: In acetanilide, the N lone pair is delocalized into the carbonyl (amide resonance) as well as the ring.
Amide nitrogens are essentially non-basic, so acetylation is a way to 'tame' a reactive amine.
w: The acetyl group withdraws electron density by pulling the nitrogen lone pair into its C=O, making the N less basic.
Lone pair is shared.
Not more basic.

q: Why is 2-bromo-2-methylpropane a poor choice for making tert-butylamine by the Gabriel synthesis?
o: Tertiary halides can't undergo SN2, so elimination dominates
Tertiary halides are too unreactive to give any product
The amine product would be alkylated two more times by the halide
Tertiary carbocations cannot form, so no reaction occurs
e: The Gabriel synthesis needs SN2 attack by the bulky phthalimide anion.
A tertiary carbon is too hindered for SN2; the basic anion removes a β-H instead (E2), giving 2-methylpropene.
w: It reacts by E2.
Phthalimide alkylates once.
The Gabriel synthesis is an SN2 process, not SN1; the problem is that the hindered tertiary carbon undergoes E2.
t: SN2-based amine syntheses (Gabriel, azide) work best on methyl and primary halides.

q: Strong acids protonate amides on the carbonyl oxygen rather than on nitrogen. Why?
o: O-protonation keeps the resonance, spreading + over O, C and N
Oxygen is less electronegative than nitrogen, so it is more basic
Nitrogen in an amide has no lone pair left to share at all
Protonating oxygen breaks the C–N bond, giving a stable product
e: Protonating N would take its lone pair out of resonance and leave the + charge stuck on N.
Protonating O gives a cation where the N lone pair still donates: [C=OH⁺ ↔ C(OH)=N⁺], so the charge is delocalized and the ion is more stable.
w: O is more electronegative.
It has one; it's delocalized.
No bond breaks.
t: Amides protonate on O, not N; the same resonance that makes them non-basic decides where H⁺ goes.

q: The second pK<sub>a</sub> of phosphoric acid (H₂PO₄⁻ ⇌ HPO₄²⁻ + H⁺) is about 7.2. In a phosphate buffer at pH 6.2, what is the ratio [HPO₄²⁻] : [H₂PO₄⁻]?
e: log([HPO₄²⁻]/[H₂PO₄⁻]) = pH − pK<sub>a</sub> = 6.2 − 7.2 = −1
Ratio = 10⁻¹, or 1 : 10, so the more protonated H₂PO₄⁻ dominates.
w: This reverses the ratio: at a pH one unit below the pKa, the protonated H₂PO₄⁻ dominates, giving 1 : 10.
That's at the pKa.
That's 2 pH units.

q: ATP stores energy in its:
o: Phosphoanhydride bonds
Phosphodiester bonds
Ester bonds only
Glycosidic bonds
e: Two phosphoanhydride bonds link its three phosphates.
w: Phosphodiester bonds link nucleotides in DNA/RNA; ATP's energy is in the anhydrides between phosphates.
ATP has a phosphoester bond to ribose, but the high-energy bonds are phosphoanhydrides.
The glycosidic bond attaches adenine to ribose; it isn't the energy-storing bond.

q: N-Methylacetamide (73 g mol⁻¹, bp 206 °C) boils much higher than N,N-dimethylacetamide (87 g mol⁻¹, bp 165 °C), even though it is lighter. Why?
o: It has an N–H that H-bonds to neighboring C=O groups
As a tertiary amide, it has stronger dipole–dipole forces
Its nitrogen is more basic, so the pure liquid is partly ionized into ammonium salts
Its smaller size gives it stronger London dispersion forces
e: N-Methylacetamide (CH₃CONHCH₃) has one N–H; N,N-dimethylacetamide has none.
The N–H···O=C hydrogen bonds hold N-methylacetamide's molecules together more strongly.
w: N-Methylacetamide is the secondary amide; the tertiary one is N,N-dimethylacetamide.
Amide nitrogens are barely basic, so neither liquid is significantly ionized.
Smaller molecules have weaker London forces, not stronger.

q: What is the main reason DNA's phosphate backbone resists hydrolysis much better than RNA's?
o: DNA lacks the 2′-OH that can attack the neighboring phosphate
DNA's 2′-OH hydrogen bonds to and shields the neighboring phosphate
DNA's thymine methyl groups sterically shield each phosphate
DNA has fewer phosphate groups per nucleotide than RNA has
e: RNA's 2′-OH acts as an internal nucleophile, cleaving the backbone.
w: DNA has no 2′-OH at all (it's deoxyribose); the absence is what matters.
Thymine methyl groups don't shield the backbone; the missing 2′-OH does.
Both have one phosphate per nucleotide in the backbone.

q: β-Carotene, with 11 conjugated C=C bonds, looks orange. In which part of the visible spectrum does it absorb most strongly?
o: Blue, around 450 nm
Orange, around 600 nm
Red, around 700 nm
Ultraviolet, around 200 nm
e: The color we see is the light that is NOT absorbed (the complementary color).
Orange appears when blue (about 450–480 nm) is absorbed. Long conjugation lowers the π → π* energy gap enough to absorb visible light.
w: That's what we see.
Absorbing red light near 700 nm would make the compound look green-blue, not orange.
Absorption near 200 nm is in the ultraviolet, which can't produce a visible color like orange.
t: Seen color is the complement of the absorbed color: absorbs blue → looks orange.

q: Which ¹³C NMR feature distinguishes a ketone carbonyl carbon?
o: A signal near 200 ppm
A signal near 20 ppm
No signal
A signal near 70 ppm
e: Carbonyl carbons are strongly deshielded (about 160–220 ppm).
w: A signal near 20 ppm is typical of alkyl (sp³) carbons, far less deshielded than a carbonyl carbon.
It has a signal.
Near 70 ppm is typical of a carbon single-bonded to oxygen (C–O), not a C=O carbon.

q: How many degrees of unsaturation (rings + π bonds) does C₆H₁₀O have?
e: Oxygen doesn't change the count, so ignore it.
Cyclohexanone (1 ring + 1 C=O) is one example.
w: Recheck the formula.
Recheck the formula.

q: By the n + 1 rule, a hydrogen with 2 equivalent neighboring hydrogens appears as a:
o: Triplet
Doublet
Quartet
Singlet
e: n + 1 = 2 + 1 = 3 peaks.
w: That's 1 neighbor.
That's 3 neighbors.
That's 0 neighbors.

q: A compound C₃H₆O shows a ¹H NMR triplet (3 H, ~1.1 ppm), a multiplet (2 H, ~2.4 ppm) and a triplet (1 H, ~9.8 ppm). Which structure fits best?
o: Propanal (CH₃CH₂CHO)
Acetone (CH₃COCH₃)
Propan-2-ol (isopropanol)
Prop-2-en-1-ol
e: The ~9.8 ppm signal is an aldehyde H.
It is split by the neighboring CH₂ (small coupling).
w: No aldehyde H.
Has an OH.
Has vinyl H's.

q: Which compound's C=O stretch appears at the highest wavenumber?
o: Acetyl chloride (CH₃COCl)
Acetone (CH₃COCH₃)
Acetamide (CH₃CONH₂)
Methyl acetate (CH₃COOCH₃)
e: Cl withdraws electrons inductively and donates little by resonance, so the C=O stays short and stiff (about 1800 cm⁻¹).

Ester (about 1740) > ketone (about 1715): the ester oxygen withdraws electrons inductively more than it donates by resonance. Amide (about 1650–1690 cm⁻¹) is lowest because nitrogen's strong resonance donation gives the C=O the most single-bond character.
w: Acetone's C=O (about 1715 cm⁻¹) lacks the strong inductive withdrawal of Cl, so it absorbs lower.
Acetamide's nitrogen donates strongly by resonance, weakening the C=O and giving the lowest wavenumber here.
Methyl acetate's ester C=O absorbs near 1740 cm⁻¹, lower than acetyl chloride's near 1800 cm⁻¹.
t: Acid chloride (~1800) > ester (~1740) > ketone (~1715) > amide (~1650–1690): inductive withdrawal raises the C=O frequency, and resonance donation (strongest from N) lowers it.

q: A strong IR absorption appears at 1700 cm⁻¹. What wavelength of light does this correspond to?
o: About 5.9 μm
About 1.7 μm
About 590 nm
About 59 μm
e: Wavenumber is 1/λ, so λ = 1 ÷ 1700 cm⁻¹ = 5.88 × 10⁻⁴ cm.
5.88 × 10⁻⁴ cm × 10⁴ μm cm⁻¹ ≈ 5.9 μm, in the infrared.
w: 1.7 μm reads the wavenumber's digits as a wavelength instead of taking the reciprocal.
590 nm is visible light; the cm-to-nm conversion is off by a factor of 10.
59 μm is off by a factor of 10 in the cm-to-μm conversion.

q: Amide C=O stretches (about 1650–1690 cm⁻¹) appear at lower wavenumbers than ketone C=O stretches (about 1715 cm⁻¹). Why?
o: N lone-pair resonance gives the C=O partial single-bond character
Amides are heavier, so all of their bonds vibrate more slowly
Hydrogen bonding is impossible in amides, weakening the C=O
The nitrogen withdraws electrons, strengthening the C=O bond
e: Stretching frequency rises with bond strength (a stiffer 'spring').
N donates its lone pair into the carbonyl (N–C=O ↔ N⁺=C–O⁻), so the C=O bond is weaker than a ketone's and absorbs at a lower wavenumber.
w: The C=O stretch depends on the C=O bond strength, not the molecule's total mass; amide resonance weakens it.
They can H-bond.
Nitrogen donates its lone pair into the carbonyl, which weakens the C=O rather than strengthening it.

q: Each carbon atom has about a 1.1% chance of being ¹³C. A hydrocarbon's mass spectrum shows an M + 1 peak that is 6.6% as tall as its M⁺ peak. About how many carbon atoms does it contain?
e: Each carbon adds about 1.1% to the M + 1 / M ratio.
Number of C ≈ 6.6 ÷ 1.1 = 6 (for example, C₆H₁₄ or C₆H₁₂).
w: Recheck: 6.6 ÷ 1.1.
Off by about 2.
Three carbons would require each carbon to add 2.2%, double the actual 1.1%; 6.6 ÷ 1.1 gives 6.

q: A patient in diabetic ketoacidosis has a fruity odor on the breath. GC–MS of a breath sample shows a compound with M⁺ at m/z 58 and a base peak at m/z 43. Which compound fits?
o: Acetone, CH₃COCH₃
Ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH
Acetic acid, CH₃COOH
Acetaldehyde, CH₃CHO
e: Acetone, C₃H₆O: 3(12) + 6(1) + 16 = 58 ✓ (ethanol = 46, acetic acid = 60, acetaldehyde = 44).
Losing ·CH₃ (15) gives the stable acylium ion CH₃C≡O⁺ at m/z 43.
Acetone forms when the ketone body acetoacetate loses CO₂.
w: Ethanol has M⁺ at 46, not 58.
Acetic acid has M⁺ at 60, not 58.
Acetaldehyde has M⁺ at 44, not 58.

q: The mass spectra of many alcohols show a peak 18 units below the molecular ion (M − 18). What neutral loss does this represent?
o: A water molecule
An ammonia molecule
A hydroxyl radical
A methane molecule
e: Water, H₂O, has mass 2(1) + 16 = 18.
Alcohol radical cations often lose H₂O (dehydration), giving an M − 18 peak. Loss of ·OH or NH₃ would give M − 17; loss of CH₄ gives M − 16.
w: That's M − 17.
That's M − 17.
That's M − 16.

q: Aromatic ring hydrogens appear near:
o: 0.9 ppm
2 ppm
e: The ring current deshields them.
w: 0.9 ppm is typical of alkyl CH₃ protons, which lack the ring-current deshielding of aromatic H.
That's α to C=O.
10–12 ppm is the range for a carboxylic acid O–H, which is more deshielded than aromatic H.

q: Nicotine (shown) has two nitrogen atoms. When nicotine picks up one proton in water, which nitrogen is protonated?
o: The sp³ nitrogen in the five-membered ring
The sp² nitrogen in the six-membered aromatic ring
Neither; nicotine's nitrogens are not basic
Both equally, since they have the same pK<sub>a</sub>
e: The five-membered ring N is a tertiary alkylamine (sp³), conjugate-acid pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 8.
The pyridine-type N is sp² (more s character), pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 3, so it is much less basic. The first proton goes to the sp³ N.
w: sp² is less basic.
Nicotine's sp³ ring nitrogen is a tertiary alkylamine (conjugate-acid pKa ≈ 8), so nicotine is basic and does pick up a proton.
pK_a values differ.
t: Most basic N = the sp³ N whose lone pair is not tied up in resonance or an aromatic ring.

q: The table shows a compound's solubility in four solvents, cold and at the boiling point. Which solvent is best for recrystallizing it?
o: Toluene
Ethanol
Water
Hexane
e: A good solvent dissolves a lot hot and very little cold.
Toluene: 15 g hot vs 0.4 g cold, so most of it crystallizes on cooling. Ethanol keeps too much dissolved cold (18 g); water and hexane barely dissolve it even hot.
w: Too soluble cold.
The compound barely dissolves in water even when hot, so water can't dissolve enough to recrystallize it.
The compound barely dissolves in hexane even when hot, so hexane can't dissolve enough to recrystallize it.

q: The β-hydroxy ketone shown was made by an aldol addition. Which starting material(s) were used?
o: Two molecules of acetone
Acetone and acetaldehyde
Butan-2-one and formaldehyde
Two molecules of propanal
e: Break the bond between the α-carbon and the carbon bearing the –OH (the β-carbon).
CH₃CO–CH₂ | C(OH)(CH₃)₂: the left piece is acetone's enolate, and the right piece is an acetone C=O.
So two acetones combine to give 4-hydroxy-4-methylpentan-2-one.
w: Mixed aldol differs.
Butan-2-one and formaldehyde would give a primary –CH₂OH, but the product's –OH is on a carbon with two methyls.
Two propanals would give an aldehyde product, but the compound shown is a β-hydroxy ketone.
