Esterifying that OH removes the only polar group, so cholesteryl ester joins TAG in the nonpolar core.
w: It loses polarity.
Cholesteryl ester is neutral, with no new charge; esterifying the 3-OH just makes it more hydrophobic.
No longer amphipathic.

q: Pancreatic lipase removes the fatty acids at glycerol carbons 1 and 3 of a dietary triacylglycerol. What is left for absorption with the free fatty acids?
o: 2-Monoacylglycerol
Free glycerol
1,2-Diacylglycerol
Lysophosphatidic acid
e: Removing the C1 and C3 fatty acids leaves one fatty acid on C2: 2-monoacylglycerol.
Intestinal cells absorb 2-MAG and fatty acids from micelles and rebuild TAG inside the cell.
w: C2 keeps its acid.
Only C1 and C3 cut.
Lysophosphatidic acid is a phospholipid, but a triacylglycerol has no phosphate, so the leftover is 2-monoacylglycerol.

q: A mouse lacking lipin, the phosphatase that removes the phosphate from phosphatidic acid, makes little triacylglycerol. Why?
o: Phosphatidic acid must become diacylglycerol before the third acylation
Phosphatidic acid is the final product of triacylglycerol breakdown
Lipin is the enzyme that adds the first fatty acid to glycerol-3-phosphate
Without lipin, phosphatidic acid is converted into cholesterol instead
e: Phosphatidic acid is glycerol-3-phosphate with fatty acids on C1 and C2: the simplest glycerophospholipid.
Removing its phosphate gives diacylglycerol, whose free C3 –OH accepts the third fatty acid to make triacylglycerol.
w: Phosphatidic acid is an intermediate in synthesis, not a breakdown product.
Acyltransferases add the first fatty acids; lipin acts later, on phosphatidic acid.
Phosphatidic acid is not a cholesterol precursor; cholesterol comes from acetyl-CoA through mevalonate.

q: Vitamin A is needed for vision because it is converted to:
o: Retinal, the light-absorbing part of rhodopsin
Calcitriol, which regulates calcium absorption
Retinoic acid, which binds opsin to absorb light
A cofactor for carboxylating clotting proteins
e: Light changes 11-cis-retinal to all-trans-retinal, triggering the visual signal.
Deficiency causes night blindness.
w: That's vitamin D.
Retinal, not retinoic acid, absorbs light.
That's vitamin K.

q: Vitamin E's main role in the body is as:
o: An antioxidant protecting membrane lipids
A cofactor for carboxylating clotting factors
A hormone that regulates calcium absorption
The light-absorbing chromophore in rhodopsin
e: Vitamin E (tocopherol) neutralizes free radicals in membranes, protecting unsaturated fatty acids from oxidation.
w: That's vitamin K.
That's vitamin D.
That's vitamin A.

q: Phospholipids are spread on the surface of water in a trough, where they form a single layer (monolayer). How are they oriented?
o: Polar heads in the water, nonpolar tails pointing up into the air
Nonpolar tails in the water, polar heads pointing up into the air
Lying flat on the surface, with heads and tails both touching water
Randomly oriented, since a monolayer has no inside or outside
e: Phospholipids are amphipathic: they have a polar head and nonpolar tails.
At an air–water interface, heads stay in contact with water and tails point into the nonpolar air, which keeps them out of water.
w: Placing tails in water is unfavorable because of the hydrophobic effect.
Lying flat would expose the tails to water.
The amphipathic structure gives a consistent orientation.

q: Vitamin D₃ made in the skin must be hydroxylated twice to become active. In a patient with severe liver failure but normal kidneys, which form is most directly reduced?
o: 25-Hydroxyvitamin D, since the liver adds the 25-OH
7-Dehydrocholesterol, since the liver converts it in skin
Parathyroid hormone, since the liver activates it
Vitamin D₃, since the liver absorbs UV light for the skin
e: The skin converts 7-dehydrocholesterol to vitamin D₃ using UVB; the liver's 25-hydroxylase then makes 25-hydroxyvitamin D, the main circulating form.
The kidney's 1α-hydroxylase finishes the job (calcitriol), so with liver failure the supply of 25-OH-D to the kidney falls first.
w: Made in skin.
Parathyroid hormone is a peptide hormone from the parathyroid glands; it isn't activated by the liver.
Liver doesn't absorb UV.
t: Skin → liver (25) → kidney (1).

q: Two oils are saponified. Oil A uses more KOH per gram than oil B. What does this best indicate?
o: Oil A's fatty acids are shorter on average
Oil A's fatty acids are longer on average
Oil A's fatty acids have more double bonds
Oil A contains much more free cholesterol
e: Each TAG uses 3 KOH regardless of chain length.
Shorter chains mean a smaller molar mass, so more TAG molecules (and more ester bonds) per gram, which uses more KOH.
w: Longer means fewer per gram.
Double bonds don't use KOH.
Cholesterol isn't saponified.
t: More base per gram = more ester bonds per gram = shorter chains.

q: Linoleic acid is written 18:2. What does this notation mean?
o: 18 carbons and 2 double bonds
18 double bonds and 2 carbons
18 hydrogens and 2 oxygens
18 carbons and 2 ester bonds
e: Fatty acid shorthand: number of carbons : number of C=C double bonds.
w: This swaps the numbers.
Not H and O.
Not ester bonds.

q: Sphingomyelin is unusual among membrane lipids because it is:
o: Both a sphingolipid and a phospholipid
Both a steroid and a phospholipid
A glycolipid with no phosphate group at all
A glycerolipid with no fatty acid
e: Sphingomyelin is built on sphingosine (so it is a sphingolipid).
Its head group is phosphocholine, so it is also a phospholipid. It is abundant in the myelin sheath.
w: Not a steroid.
It has phosphate.
Built on sphingosine.
t: Sphingo- means sphingosine backbone; -myelin hints at where it is concentrated.

q: A snack contains 10 g fat, 20 g carbohydrate and 10 g protein. Using 9, 4 and 4 kcal g⁻¹, about how much energy does it provide?
o: 210 kcal
170 kcal
360 kcal
120 kcal
e: Fat: 10 × 9 = 90 kcal. Carbohydrate: 20 × 4 = 80 kcal. Protein: 10 × 4 = 40 kcal.
w: Fat is 9 kcal/g.
Only fat is 9.
Recheck the sum.

q: A person uses about 8,000 kJ of free energy as ATP each day. If each mole of ATP hydrolyzed in cells releases about 50 kJ and ATP's molar mass is about 500 g mol⁻¹, about how much ATP is recycled per day?
o: About 80 kg
About 80 g
About 8 kg
About 800 kg
e: Moles of ATP = 8000 kJ ÷ 50 kJ mol⁻¹ = 160 mol.
Mass = 160 mol × 0.5 kg mol⁻¹ = 80 kg.
The body holds only a small ATP pool at any moment, so each ATP is regenerated hundreds of times a day.
w: Recheck the units.
Off by 10.
Off by 10.

q: Why does the actual ΔG of a reaction in a cell often differ from its ΔG°′?
o: Real cellular concentrations differ from standard conditions
Enzymes in the cell change the reaction's free energy change
Cells are much colder than the standard temperature of 25 °C
ΔG°′ applies only to gas-phase reactions, not to solutions
e: ΔG = ΔG°′ + RT ln Q.
Cells keep products low or reactants high, shifting ΔG.
w: Enzymes don't change ΔG.
Cells are warmer than 25 °C.
ΔG°′ applies to solutions.

q: In a patient with insulin resistance, a brisk 30-minute walk lowers blood glucose even though insulin signaling in muscle is impaired. What best explains this?
o: Rising AMP activates AMPK, which moves GLUT4 to the membrane without insulin
Exercise raises glucagon, which makes skeletal muscle take up glucose
Exercise releases insulin that is stored inside the muscle fibers
Contraction makes the liver convert blood glucose into glycogen
e: Contracting muscle uses ATP, so AMP rises and activates AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK).
AMPK (along with Ca²⁺ signals) moves GLUT4 to the muscle surface through a pathway independent of the insulin receptor.
This is one reason exercise helps control blood glucose in type 2 diabetes.
w: Glucagon raises blood glucose; it doesn't drive muscle uptake.
Muscle doesn't store insulin; insulin comes from pancreatic β cells.
Exercise pulls glucose into muscle; the liver releases glucose during exercise.

q: Glucagon is injected into two patients with hypoglycemia. Patient A has fasted overnight; patient B has had no food for three days and has been drinking heavily. Only A's glucose rises quickly. Why?
o: B's liver glycogen, glucagon's fast source, is used up
Glucagon acts only on muscle glycogen, which B has already used up
B lacks glucagon receptors in the liver
Alcohol speeds glucagon's breakdown in the blood
e: Glucagon raises blood glucose by stimulating liver glycogenolysis (fast) and gluconeogenesis (slower).
After days without food, liver glycogen is gone; heavy drinking also slows gluconeogenesis, so glucagon has little quick effect.
w: Muscle lacks glucagon receptors and can't release free glucose.
Starvation doesn't remove liver glucagon receptors.
The issue is the liver's empty glycogen store, not glucagon breakdown.

q: During a long fast, the body's fuel sources change over time. Which order is correct?
o: Liver glycogen → gluconeogenesis rises → ketone bodies become major fuel
Ketone bodies → liver glycogen is used → gluconeogenesis rises
Muscle protein → liver glycogen → fat stores become major fuel
Liver glycogen → ketone bodies become major fuel → gluconeogenesis rises
e: Liver glycogen lasts roughly a day.
Gluconeogenesis rises (from amino acids, lactate, glycerol).
After several days, ketone bodies from fat become a major fuel, sparing protein.
w: Ketones come last.
Glycogen comes first.
Gluconeogenesis rises before ketones.

q: Many biosynthetic reactions split ATP into AMP + PPi, after which pyrophosphatase rapidly hydrolyzes PPi to 2 Pi. What is the purpose of the second step?
o: Removing PPi makes the overall reaction strongly favorable and essentially irreversible
PPi hydrolysis regenerates the ATP that the first step used, so no energy is spent
PPi is toxic to the enzyme, which would be inhibited permanently if PPi remained
Pyrophosphatase transfers the phosphate onto the product to form the final compound
e: PPi hydrolysis has ΔG°′ ≈ −19 kJ mol⁻¹, and keeping [PPi] very low pulls the first reaction forward.
Examples include fatty acid activation, UDP-glucose formation and DNA synthesis; such steps cost 2 ATP equivalents.
w: PPi hydrolysis releases energy as heat-driving force; it doesn't regenerate ATP.
PPi is removed to pull equilibrium, not mainly to prevent enzyme poisoning.
Pyrophosphatase hydrolyzes PPi to free Pi; it doesn't transfer phosphate to products.
t: PPi → 2 Pi is the cell's ratchet: it makes activation steps one-way.

q: In a cell at 37 °C (RT ≈ 2.6 kJ mol⁻¹), a reaction has K′<sub>eq</sub> = 1000 and mass-action ratio Q = 10. What is ΔG? (ln 0.01 ≈ −4.6)
o: About −12 kJ mol⁻¹
About +12 kJ mol⁻¹
About −5 kJ mol⁻¹
About −24 kJ mol⁻¹
e: = 2.6 × (−4.6) ≈ −12 kJ mol⁻¹. Q < K, so the reaction proceeds forward.
w: Q is below K, so ΔG is negative.
Use ln, not log₁₀.
Recheck: 2.6 × −4.6.
t: Using log₁₀ instead of ln gives the −5 trap (2.6 × −2).

q: Phosphoglucose isomerase converts glucose-6-phosphate to fructose-6-phosphate with ΔG°′ = +1.7 kJ mol⁻¹. Using ΔG°′ = −RT ln K′<sub>eq</sub> (RT ≈ 2.5 kJ mol⁻¹, e<sup>−0.7</sup> ≈ 0.5), what is K′<sub>eq</sub> for this step?
o: About 0.5
About 2
About 0.05
About 5
e: K′<sub>eq</sub> = e<sup>−0.7</sup> ≈ 0.5: at equilibrium, fructose-6-phosphate is about half as abundant as glucose-6-phosphate. A small positive ΔG°′ means K′<sub>eq</sub> slightly below 1.
w: Sign error; a positive ΔG°′ gives K′eq below 1, so e⁻⁰·⁷, not e⁰·⁷.
Too small; −1.7/2.5 = −0.7 gives about 0.5, not a factor-of-ten smaller value.
Sign error and wrong magnitude; positive ΔG°′ means K′eq just under 1.

q: In a cell at 37 °C (RT ≈ 2.6 kJ mol⁻¹), [ATP] = 5 mM, [ADP] = 0.5 mM and [Pi] = 5 mM. Given ΔG°′ = −30.5 kJ mol⁻¹ for ATP hydrolysis and ln(5 × 10⁻⁴) ≈ −7.6, what is the actual ΔG?
o: About −50 kJ mol⁻¹
About −30.5 kJ mol⁻¹
About −11 kJ mol⁻¹
About −70 kJ mol⁻¹
e: ΔG = −30.5 + 2.6 × (−7.6) ≈ −30.5 − 19.8 ≈ −50 kJ mol⁻¹. Keeping ATP far above ADP makes hydrolysis much more favorable than under standard conditions.
w: That's ΔG°′; it ignores the RT ln Q term from cellular concentrations.
Sign error on RT ln Q; Q < 1 makes ΔG more negative, not less.
Overcounted the concentration term; 2.6 × (−7.6) ≈ −20, giving −50.
t: Cells keep ATP far from equilibrium, so its real ΔG (about −50) beats the textbook −30.5.

q: A reaction A → B + H⁺ has ΔG° = −10 kJ mol⁻¹ under chemical standard conditions (1 M H⁺, 25 °C). Using RT ≈ 2.48 kJ mol⁻¹ and ln(10⁻⁷) ≈ −16.1, what is ΔG°′ at pH 7?
o: About −50 kJ mol⁻¹
About +30 kJ mol⁻¹
About −10 kJ mol⁻¹
About −27 kJ mol⁻¹
e: ΔG°′ uses [H⁺] = 10⁻⁷ M instead of 1 M; all other species stay at 1 M.
Making a product (H⁺) far scarcer pulls the reaction forward.
w: +30 kJ mol⁻¹ has the sign of the correction reversed; low [H⁺] favors making H⁺.
−10 kJ mol⁻¹ ignores the change in the standard [H⁺].
−27 kJ mol⁻¹ uses log₁₀(10⁻⁷) = −7 instead of the natural log.

q: Complete oxidation of palmitate is C₁₆H₃₂O₂ + 23 O₂ → 16 CO₂ + 16 H₂O. About how much 'metabolic water' (18 g mol⁻¹) is made when 256 g (1 mol) of palmitate is oxidized?
o: About 288 g
About 576 g
About 256 g
About 144 g
e: 1 mol of palmitate gives 16 mol H₂O.
16 × 18 g mol⁻¹ = 288 g of water, more than the mass of the fat burned.
w: 576 g counts 32 waters, one per H atom; each water holds two H.
256 g assumes the water equals the mass of fat burned.
144 g counts 8 waters, as if from 8 acetyl-CoA.

q: The four tripeptides in the table are spotted at the center of a paper strip in a buffer at pH 6.0, and a voltage is applied. Which moves fastest toward the anode (+)?
o: W
X
Y
Z
e: Every peptide has a free N-terminus (+1) and C-terminus (−1) at pH 6, so the side chains decide the net charge.
W: Asp and Glu side chains are both −1, so net −2, the most negative. X is +1 (Lys), Y is 0, and Z is about +½ (His, pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 6).
w: X carries a Lys side chain, so its net charge is +1 at pH 6 and it moves toward the cathode, not the anode.
Y has a net charge of 0 at pH 6, so it barely moves in either direction.
Z's His side chain (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 6) is about half protonated, giving a net charge near +½, so it drifts toward the cathode.
t: Anode = positive electrode, which attracts negative species. 'An ox' (anode = oxidation) pulls anions.

q: Glycine (pK<sub>a</sub> 2.3 for –COOH and 9.6 for –NH₃⁺) is drawn in the form shown. In which solution is this the main form?
o: pH 1, where its net charge is +1
pH 6, where its net charge is 0
pH 12, where its net charge is −1
pH 6, where its net charge is +1
e: The drawn form has –NH₃⁺ and an un-ionized –COOH, so its net charge is +1.
Both groups are protonated only when pH is below 2.3, so pH 1 fits.
w: That's the zwitterion.
At pH 12 both groups are deprotonated (–NH₂ and –COO⁻), which is a different form from the +1 structure drawn.
Net charge isn't +1 at pH 6.

q: Using the Lineweaver–Burk plot shown, what are the enzyme's V<sub>max</sub> and K<sub>m</sub>?
o: V<sub>max</sub> = 20 µM s⁻¹; K<sub>m</sub> = 4 mM
V<sub>max</sub> = 0.05 µM s⁻¹; K<sub>m</sub> = 0.25 mM
V<sub>max</sub> = 20 µM s⁻¹; K<sub>m</sub> = 0.25 mM
V<sub>max</sub> = 0.05 µM s⁻¹; K<sub>m</sub> = 4 mM
e: The y-intercept is 1/V<sub>max</sub> = 0.05 s µM⁻¹, so V<sub>max</sub> = 1 ÷ 0.05 = 20 µM s⁻¹.
The x-intercept is −1/K<sub>m</sub> = −0.25 mM⁻¹, so K<sub>m</sub> = 1 ÷ 0.25 = 4 mM.
w: Both values are the intercept readings left uninverted; V<sub>max</sub> = 1/0.05 = 20 µM s⁻¹ and K<sub>m</sub> = 1/0.25 = 4 mM.
V<sub>max</sub> is right, but 0.25 mM⁻¹ is the x-intercept magnitude, 1/K<sub>m</sub>; inverting it gives K<sub>m</sub> = 4 mM.
K<sub>m</sub> is right, but 0.05 is the y-intercept, 1/V<sub>max</sub>; inverting it gives V<sub>max</sub> = 20 µM s⁻¹.
t: Every intercept on a double-reciprocal plot is a reciprocal. Flip it before you report it.

q: A young adult has muscle pain and dark urine (myoglobin) after long exercise or fasting. Tests of fatty acid oxidation are shown. Octanoate enters mitochondria without carnitine. Which step is most likely defective?
o: Carnitine palmitoyltransferase II, on the matrix side
Carnitine palmitoyltransferase I, on the outer membrane
Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase in the matrix
Thiolase, the final step of every β-oxidation round
e: Octanoate oxidation is normal (98%), so β-oxidation enzymes inside the matrix, including those for medium chains, work.
Palmitoylcarnitine bypasses CPT-I, yet its oxidation is still low (12%), so the block is at CPT-II, which converts acylcarnitine back to acyl-CoA in the matrix.
w: Palmitoylcarnitine bypasses CPT-I but is still poorly oxidized.
Octanoate oxidation is normal, so medium-chain enzymes work.
Normal octanoate oxidation shows thiolase works.

q: A hurricane kills most of an island's lizards at random, and the few survivors carry only a small fraction of the original alleles. This is an example of:
o: A bottleneck effect
A founder effect
Gene flow
Directional selection
e: A bottleneck is a sharp drop in population size that randomly removes alleles.
The founder effect is similar, but happens when a small group leaves to start a new population.
w: Small group leaves.
Gene flow moves alleles between populations by migration, whereas a hurricane randomly killing most lizards is a bottleneck.
Directional selection favors one extreme phenotype by fitness; random hurricane deaths reduce alleles by chance, a bottleneck.

q: Which observation describes a postzygotic barrier between two frog species?
o: Hybrid tadpoles hatch but die before becoming adults
The two species call at different frequencies and ignore each other
One species breeds in spring and the other in summer
Sperm of one species can't bind eggs of the other
e: Postzygotic barriers act after a hybrid zygote has formed.
Hybrid inviability, where hybrids die before adulthood, is one example.
The other options prevent the zygote from forming at all.
w: Different calls are behavioral isolation, which acts before mating.
Different breeding seasons are temporal isolation, which acts before mating.
Failure of sperm to bind eggs is gametic isolation, before a zygote forms.

q: Two isolated villages of equal size merge. Everyone in village 1 was AA, and everyone in village 2 was aa. If people in the merged town mate at random, what fraction of the children in the first new generation are expected to be Aa?
e: The merged population has p = q = 0.5 (equal numbers of AA and aa adults).
One generation of random mating restores Hardy–Weinberg proportions: 2pq = 2 × 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.5.
1.0 would only be true if every couple had one partner from each village.
w: Random mating would produce Aa from AA × aa couples.
0.25 is p² or q², not 2pq.
1.0 only if every couple paired across villages.
t: Random mating restores Hardy–Weinberg genotype proportions in one generation (for an autosomal gene).

q: One gene affecting many different traits (like the gene in Marfan syndrome) is called:
o: Pleiotropy
Polygenic inheritance
Epistasis
Linkage
e: Pleiotropy: one gene, many effects.
Polygenic: many genes, one trait.
w: Many genes, one trait.
Epistasis is one gene masking or modifying another gene's effect, not one gene affecting many traits.
Genes inherited together.

q: Antibiotic use in a hospital kills most bacteria, but resistant strains survive and spread. What type of selection is this?
o: Directional selection
Stabilizing selection
Disruptive selection
Sexual selection
e: The population's traits shift toward one extreme: resistance.
w: Stabilizing selection favors the middle, not one extreme.
Disruptive selection favors both extremes.
Sexual selection is based on mate choice.

q: In a population, AA and Aa individuals leave an average of 2.0 surviving offspring each, while aa individuals leave 1.0. What is the relative fitness of aa?
e: Relative fitness compares each genotype with the best one.
The best genotypes leave 2.0 offspring, so they have fitness 1.0.
w: 1.0 is the raw offspring count for aa, not its fitness relative to the best.
2.0 is the raw count for AA and Aa.
0.2 divides by the total for all three genotypes (5.0) instead of by the best.

q: A child has type O blood, and the mother has type A blood. Which man could NOT be the biological father?
o: A man with type AB blood
A man with type O blood
A man with type A blood
A man with type B blood
e: Type O means the child is ii, so each parent must have given an i allele (the mother must be Iᴬi).
Men with type A (Iᴬi) or type B (Iᴮi) can carry i, and type O men are ii; a type AB man (IᴬIᴮ) has no i to pass on.
w: A type O father (ii) can pass i.
A type A father could be Iᴬi and pass i.
A type B father could be Iᴮi and pass i.
t: Blood typing can exclude a possible father but can never prove that a man is the father.

q: Fish living in dark caves have small eyes that can't see, while their surface-dwelling relatives have normal eyes. Which explanation fits evolutionary theory best?
o: Relaxed selection on eyes in darkness, leaving reduced remnants
The fish stopped using their eyes, so their offspring inherited smaller eyes
The eyes are newly evolving and will one day become functional
Darkness causes mutations that shrink the eyes
e: Vestigial structures are reduced remnants of structures that worked in ancestors.
In darkness, eyes give no benefit, so mutations that reduce them aren't removed, and saving resources may even be favored.
The small eyes remain as evidence of sighted ancestors.
w: Effects of disuse during one life aren't inherited.
The fish descend from sighted ancestors; their eyes were reduced, not newly forming.
Darkness doesn't cause mutations; mutations arise randomly.

q: Two genes located close together on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together. This is:
o: Linkage
Independent assortment
Nondisjunction
Crossing over
e: Close genes are rarely separated by crossing over, so they don't assort independently.
w: That's unlinked genes.
That's failed separation.
That separates them.

q: Siamese cats have dark fur on their ears, paws and tail but light fur on the body. A patch of body fur shaved and kept cold grows back dark. What does this show?
o: Phenotype depends on genotype and environment
The cold caused a mutation in the fur genes
Different body parts have different genotypes for fur color
Dark fur is dominant over light fur
e: All the cat's cells carry the same genotype.
The pigment enzyme is temperature-sensitive and works only in cooler skin.
So the same genotype gives different phenotypes in different conditions.
w: Cold changes how the enzyme works, not the DNA sequence.
Body cells all carry the same genotype.
Dominance describes interaction of alleles, not the effect of temperature.

q: In mice, the yellow coat allele (Aʸ) is dominant for color but lethal before birth when homozygous. Two yellow mice (Aʸa × Aʸa) are crossed. What ratio is expected among the surviving offspring?
o: 2 yellow : 1 non-yellow
3 yellow : 1 non-yellow
1 yellow : 2 non-yellow
1 yellow : 1 non-yellow
e: Expected genotypes at conception: ¼ AʸAʸ : ½ Aʸa : ¼ aa.
The AʸAʸ embryos die, leaving Aʸa (yellow) and aa (non-yellow) in a 2 : 1 ratio.
w: 3 : 1 is the ratio at conception, before the AʸAʸ embryos die; removing them leaves 2 yellow : 1 non-yellow.
This reverses the ratio: surviving Aʸa yellow mice outnumber aa non-yellow mice two to one.
1 : 1 is the ratio from crossing Aʸa with aa; this Aʸa × Aʸa cross gives 2 : 1 after lethal losses.
t: A 2 : 1 ratio from a monohybrid cross is a red flag for a recessive lethal allele.

q: The founder effect happens when:
o: A small group starts a new population with different allele frequencies
A disaster suddenly shrinks a large population to a few survivors
Many migrants move in and add new alleles to an existing population
Selection favors heterozygotes, keeping both alleles common
e: It's a type of genetic drift, often seen in isolated communities.
w: That's a bottleneck.
That's gene flow.
That's balancing selection.

q: An F⁺ E. coli cell conjugates with an F⁻ cell. What is usually true afterward?
o: Both cells are now F⁺
Both cells are now F⁻
The F⁺ cell becomes F⁻
The F⁻ cell gains the donor's chromosome
e: The donor copies one strand of its F plasmid and passes it through the pilus.
Each cell then makes the complementary strand, so both end up with a complete F plasmid and both are F⁺.
w: The F plasmid is copied, not lost; both cells end up F⁺.
The donor keeps its F plasmid by replicating it during transfer.
Transfer of chromosome happens with Hfr cells, not ordinary F⁺ donors.
t: Conjugation copies the plasmid; the donor doesn't give it away.

q: A cytosolic protein has an Asn–X–Ser sequence that could, in principle, receive an N-linked sugar chain, but it has no ER signal sequence. Will it be N-glycosylated?
o: No; it never enters the ER lumen where this starts
Yes; N-glycosylation begins on free cytosolic ribosomes
Yes; the Golgi will add the sugar chain later
No; N-linked sugars attach only to serine
e: N-linked glycosylation begins in the rough ER lumen as the protein is made.
Only proteins with an ER signal sequence are threaded into the ER.
A protein made and kept in the cytosol never meets the enzyme, so it gets no N-linked chain.
w: Free cytosolic ribosomes release proteins into the cytosol, where N-glycosylation doesn't occur.
Without an ER signal, the protein never reaches the Golgi either.
N-linked sugars attach to asparagine; O-linked sugars go on serine or threonine.
t: The 'N' in N-linked is the asparagine side-chain nitrogen.

q: Intestinal cells are treated with a drug that depolymerizes actin filaments. Which effect on nutrient absorption is most likely?
o: Microvilli collapse, shrinking the absorbing surface
Villi lose their blood capillaries
Cilia stop beating and food stops moving along the gut
Tight junctions open and the cells divide faster
e: Each microvillus is held up by a core bundle of actin filaments.
Without that core, microvilli shorten and collapse.
The brush border's surface area falls, so less is absorbed.
w: Villi are tissue folds with blood vessels; their capillaries don't depend on the cells' actin cores.
Intestinal cells have microvilli, not motile cilia; food is moved by smooth muscle.
Depolymerizing actin may loosen junctions, but it would not make cells divide faster.

q: A Gram stain of pus from a skin abscess shows purple, round cells in grape-like clusters. Which description fits these bacteria?
o: Gram-positive cocci
Gram-negative cocci
Gram-positive bacilli
Gram-negative spirilla
e: Purple after Gram staining means a thick peptidoglycan wall held the crystal violet: Gram-positive.
Round cells are cocci; rods would be bacilli and spirals spirilla.
So these are Gram-positive cocci (clusters suggest Staphylococcus).
w: Gram-negative cells lose the purple dye and appear pink.
Bacilli are rod-shaped, but these cells are round.
Spirilla are spiral, and Gram-negative cells would stain pink.

q: HIV genomes pick up mutations far faster than human DNA does, so drug-resistant strains appear quickly in a patient taking a single drug. Which property of HIV's reverse transcriptase mainly explains this?
o: It copies RNA into DNA with no proofreading
It copies host DNA into viral RNA
It inserts the viral DNA at random sites in the host genome
It degrades the host's DNA repair enzymes
e: Reverse transcriptase builds DNA from the viral RNA template.
Unlike human replicative DNA polymerases, it has no 3′→5′ exonuclease to fix its errors.
Its uncorrected mistakes create many variants, and the drug selects those that resist it.
w: The enzyme runs the other way: it makes DNA from the viral RNA, not RNA from host DNA.
Integration is done by a different enzyme, integrase, and the integration site doesn't change the viral sequence.
Reverse transcriptase doesn't attack host repair enzymes; its errors arise because it lacks its own proofreading.
t: Error-prone copying plus a drug that selects the survivors explains why HIV is treated with drug combinations.

q: Researchers treat dividing animal cells with cytochalasin D, which blocks actin polymerization. Mitosis itself proceeds normally. After one division cycle, what will the cells most likely look like?
o: Single cells that each contain two nuclei
Pairs of daughter cells with no nuclei
Cells arrested with chromosomes at metaphase
Cells whose chromosomes never condensed
e: Chromosome separation depends on microtubules, so mitosis can finish and two nuclei re-form.
Cytokinesis needs an actin–myosin contractile ring to pinch the cell in two. Without actin filaments, the furrow fails, leaving one cell with two nuclei.
w: Nuclei form normally; only cytokinesis fails.
Mitosis proceeds normally, so cells aren't stuck in metaphase.
Chromosome condensation doesn't depend on actin.
t: Microtubule poisons stop mitosis; actin poisons stop cytokinesis.

q: Antibiotic resistance is rising. Why does finishing a full course of antibiotics, rather than stopping early, help limit resistance?
o: It kills the less-susceptible survivors that would otherwise multiply
It prevents the antibiotic from inducing new resistance mutations
It boosts the patient's immune cells so they clear the bacteria
It lets the drug kill bacteria that are already fully resistant
e: Stopping early can leave the toughest bacteria alive.
They then multiply, shifting the population toward resistance: natural selection in action.
w: Antibiotics select for resistance; they do not induce mutations by being stopped.
The antibiotic kills bacteria directly; it does not boost immune cells.
Fully resistant bacteria survive regardless of course length.

q: Penicillin works well against many Gram-positive bacteria but poorly against many Gram-negative ones. Which feature of Gram-negative bacteria most limits its effect?
o: An outer membrane that blocks access to the cell wall
A thicker peptidoglycan layer that soaks up the drug
A complete lack of peptidoglycan in the cell wall
70S ribosomes that resist the drug's binding
e: Penicillin targets enzymes that build peptidoglycan.
Gram-negative bacteria have only a thin peptidoglycan layer, but it lies under an outer membrane (with LPS) that keeps many drugs out.
w: Gram-negatives have a thin wall.
They have peptidoglycan.
Penicillin targets the wall.
t: Gram-negative = thin wall + extra outer membrane. Gram-positive = thick wall, no outer membrane.

q: In a tube of thioglycolate broth, O₂ is highest at the top and falls to almost zero at the bottom. A bacterium grows only in a band at the very bottom. It is most likely:
o: An obligate anaerobe
An obligate aerobe
A facultative anaerobe
An aerotolerant anaerobe
e: Obligate aerobes grow only at the top; facultative anaerobes grow throughout but best near the top.
Aerotolerant anaerobes ignore O₂ and grow evenly.
Growth only where O₂ is absent means O₂ is toxic to the cell: an obligate anaerobe.
w: Grows at top.
A facultative anaerobe grows throughout the tube, densest near the O₂-rich top, not only in a band at the bottom.
An aerotolerant anaerobe ignores O₂ and grows evenly through the tube, not only at the oxygen-free bottom.

q: A virus that inserts its genome into the host chromosome and stays dormant is in which cycle?
o: Lysogenic cycle
Lytic cycle
Krebs cycle
Cell cycle
e: In the lysogenic cycle, the viral DNA (prophage) is copied along with the host's DNA.
Stress can switch it to the lytic cycle, which kills the cell.
w: That kills the cell.
The Krebs cycle is a metabolic pathway in the mitochondria, not a stage of a virus's life cycle.
That's cell division.

q: Gram-positive bacteria treated with lysozyme, which digests peptidoglycan, survive in 0.5 M sucrose but burst when moved into pure water. What explains this?
o: Without a wall, water rushes in and bursts it
Sucrose quickly rebuilds the digested cell wall
Lysozyme only becomes active in pure water
Sucrose feeds the cells so they keep dividing
e: Bacterial cytoplasm is hypertonic to most surroundings; the rigid wall normally resists swelling.
Wall-less cells (protoplasts) survive only in an isotonic medium such as 0.5 M sucrose. In water, osmosis bursts them.
w: Sucrose doesn't rebuild peptidoglycan; it just balances osmotic pressure.
Lysozyme had already digested the wall in sucrose; bursting is from osmosis.
Sucrose acts as an osmotic stabilizer, not as food driving division.

q: Mycoplasma pneumoniae, a cause of 'walking pneumonia', has no cell wall. Which antibiotic would be useless against it?
o: Penicillin, which blocks wall synthesis
Tetracycline, which blocks its 30S subunit
Azithromycin, which blocks its 50S subunit
Ciprofloxacin, which blocks its DNA gyrase
e: β-lactams like penicillin work by blocking peptidoglycan cross-linking.
With no wall, Mycoplasma has no target for penicillin; drugs that hit its ribosomes or DNA gyrase still work.
w: Tetracycline targets the ribosome, which Mycoplasma still has.
Macrolides target the 50S subunit, which Mycoplasma still has.
Fluoroquinolones target DNA gyrase, which Mycoplasma still has.
t: No wall, no target: β-lactams can't touch wall-less bacteria.

q: In an anovulatory cycle, the follicle never gets an LH surge and no ovulation occurs. What is expected during the second half of that cycle?
o: Progesterone stays low, because no corpus luteum forms
Progesterone rises, because the follicle keeps growing
hCG rises to keep the unruptured follicle alive
Estrogen falls to zero, so no bleeding ever occurs
e: The corpus luteum forms from the follicle only after ovulation.
Without it there is no luteal progesterone rise (and no temperature shift on a chart).
w: Follicle growth makes estrogen, not progesterone; without a corpus luteum progesterone stays low.
hCG comes from an implanted embryo, not the cycle itself.
Estrogen doesn't drop to zero; withdrawal bleeding can still occur.

q: Normal cells in a dish stop dividing once they cover the surface in a single layer, but cancer cells keep dividing and pile up. Which property have the cancer cells lost?
o: Contact (density-dependent) inhibition
The ability to replicate their own DNA
The ability to build a spindle
The ability to undergo mitosis
e: Normal cells sense crowding by touching neighbors and stop dividing.
Cancer cells ignore these signals and keep growing in heaps; they still replicate DNA and divide.
w: Cancer cells still replicate DNA; they keep dividing.
Cancer cells still form spindles to divide.
Cancer cells still undergo mitosis, more than normal ones.

q: Which feature distinguishes apoptosis from necrosis?
o: Apoptotic cells shrink into fragments that are engulfed without inflammation
Apoptotic cells swell and burst, spilling contents and causing inflammation
Apoptosis occurs only in embryos and never in healthy adult tissues
Necrosis is run by caspases, while apoptosis needs no enzymes at all
e: Apoptosis is an orderly, caspase-driven program: the cell shrinks, its DNA is cut, and it breaks into membrane-bound pieces that phagocytes eat.
Necrosis is uncontrolled: the cell swells, bursts and triggers inflammation.
w: Swelling, bursting and inflammation describe necrosis.
Apoptosis happens throughout life, e.g. in immune cell turnover.
Reversed; caspases drive apoptosis, and necrosis is uncontrolled.
t: Apoptosis is a tidy shrink-and-package; necrosis is a messy swell-and-burst.

q: How many functional eggs does one primary oocyte usually produce?
o: One, plus polar bodies
Four
Two
None until fertilization
e: Unequal cytoplasmic division gives one large ovum and small polar bodies.
Spermatogenesis, by contrast, makes four sperm from each primary spermatocyte.
w: Four functional gametes per primary cell describes spermatogenesis; oogenesis gives one ovum because cytoplasm divides unequally.
Oogenesis doesn't make two eggs; unequal division gives one large ovum and the rest become small polar bodies.
Meiosis I finishes at ovulation.

q: Counting only independent assortment of the 23 chromosome pairs (no crossing over), about how many genetically different gametes can one human make?
o: About 8 × 10⁶ (2²³)
About 530 (23²)
About 7 × 10¹³ (2⁴⁶)
e: Each of 23 pairs can send either homolog to a gamete: 2 choices per pair.
2²³ = 8,388,608 ≈ 8 × 10⁶. Crossing over raises the number enormously.
w: Added instead of using exponent; each pair is an independent 2-way choice.
Squared 23 instead of raising 2 to the 23rd.
Used 46 chromosomes; independent assortment counts 23 pairs.

q: Cohesin holds sister chromatids together until anaphase, when the protease separase cuts it. Separase is held inactive by securin until the anaphase-promoting complex (APC/C) tags securin for destruction. If a drug blocks APC/C, where will dividing cells most likely arrest?
o: At metaphase, with sister chromatids still joined
In G₁, before DNA replication begins
In telophase, after the nuclei have re-formed
In prophase, before the chromosomes condense
e: Without APC/C activity, securin is not destroyed, so separase stays inactive.
Cohesin is never cut, so the sisters cannot separate. Cells reach metaphase with chromosomes aligned but cannot start anaphase.
w: Cells blocked in APC/C activity still pass G₁ and S normally; the block only stops the metaphase-to-anaphase step.
Never reach telophase.
Prophase comes before the APC/C-dependent step, so cells pass through it and stop later, at metaphase.

q: A cell heterozygous (Aa) at a gene completes mitosis. Another Aa cell completes meiosis I with no crossing over near the gene. What do the daughter cells carry?
o: Mitosis: two Aa cells; meiosis I: one AA cell and one aa cell
Mitosis: one AA cell and one aa cell; meiosis I: two Aa cells
Mitosis: two Aa cells; meiosis I: two Aa cells
Mitosis: one A cell and one a cell; meiosis I: four cells
e: After S phase, each chromosome has two identical sister chromatids (A,A and a,a).
In mitosis, sister chromatids separate, so each daughter gets one A and one a.
In meiosis I, homologs separate, so one cell gets both A chromatids and the other both a chromatids.
w: This swaps the two divisions; in mitosis each daughter keeps both homologs.
Meiosis I separates homologs, so the two cells can't both keep A and a without crossing over.
Mitosis keeps the diploid set, and meiosis I yields two cells, not four.
t: Mitosis splits sisters; meiosis I splits homologs.

q: Phosphorylation of nuclear lamins at the start of mitosis breaks down the nuclear envelope. A drug blocks lamin dephosphorylation. Which step is most directly prevented?
o: Re-forming nuclei around each chromosome set
Condensing the chromosomes in prophase
Lining up the chromosomes at metaphase
Separating the sister chromatids at the start of anaphase
e: Lamin phosphorylation in prophase disassembles the nuclear lamina.
At telophase, lamins are dephosphorylated and reassemble, so nuclear envelopes re-form.
Blocking dephosphorylation leaves daughter chromosomes without a proper nucleus.
w: Condensation in prophase happens alongside lamin phosphorylation, not dephosphorylation.
Metaphase alignment depends on the spindle, and the envelope is already gone then.
Sister separation depends on separase cutting cohesin, not on lamins.

q: Which checkpoint ensures that every chromosome is attached to the spindle before anaphase starts?
o: The spindle assembly (M) checkpoint
The G₁/S restriction checkpoint
The G₂/M DNA damage checkpoint
The intra-S replication checkpoint
e: Unattached kinetochores block the start of anaphase.
This prevents chromosome loss or gain in daughter cells.
w: That's before S phase.
That checks DNA damage.
That checks replication.

q: Combined oral contraceptives provide steady levels of estrogen and progestin. How do they mainly prevent pregnancy?
o: Negative feedback suppresses the mid-cycle LH surge
They raise FSH so that many follicles ovulate
They destroy the oocytes stored in the ovaries
They make the corpus luteum form much earlier
e: Steady estrogen and progestin feed back on the hypothalamus and pituitary, lowering GnRH, FSH and LH.
Without an LH surge, ovulation does not occur.
w: Steady estrogen and progestin lower FSH by negative feedback, so follicles are not stimulated to ovulate.
The pill does not harm stored oocytes; it blocks the LH surge so that none of them is ovulated.
A corpus luteum forms only after ovulation, and the pill prevents ovulation rather than changing corpus luteum timing.

q: Frog egg extracts cycle between interphase and mitosis about every 30 minutes. Cycloheximide, which blocks translation, halts the extract in interphase. Adding purified cyclin B protein then drives it into mitosis, even with cycloheximide still present. What is the best conclusion?
o: Cyclin B must be newly made each cycle to trigger mitosis
CDK1 must be newly made each cycle to trigger mitosis
Cycloheximide destroys cyclin B already in the extract
Mitosis requires new synthesis of many unrelated proteins
e: Blocking translation stops cycling, so some protein must be made each time.
Supplying cyclin B alone rescues entry into mitosis, so cyclin B is the protein that must be resynthesized (it is destroyed at the end of each M phase).
w: Purified cyclin B alone rescued mitosis, so CDK1 needn't be remade.
Cycloheximide blocks translation; it doesn't destroy existing cyclin B.
Cyclin B alone was enough; no other new proteins were required.

q: Why can't a normal human body (somatic) cell keep dividing indefinitely in a culture dish?
o: Telomeres shorten with each division until the cell stops dividing (senescence)
Cells use up their DNA nucleotide supply after a fixed number of divisions
Ribosomes wear out after about 50 divisions, permanently halting protein synthesis
Mitochondria are diluted out with each division until ATP runs out
e: DNA polymerase can't fully copy chromosome ends, so telomeres shrink.
Stem cells and cancer cells use telomerase to avoid this limit.
w: Nucleotides are made continuously; supply is not the limit.
Ribosomes are replaced continuously and do not limit division.
Mitochondria replicate and are not diluted out.

q: Fertilization took place 3 days ago, yet a sensitive hCG pregnancy test is negative. What is the best explanation?
o: hCG is made only after the blastocyst implants
hCG is made only in the second trimester
hCG is made by the mother's pituitary gland
hCG is broken down by the corpus luteum
e: hCG is secreted by the trophoblast once the blastocyst implants, about a week after fertilization.
At 3 days the embryo is still a small cleavage-stage ball of cells drifting toward the uterus, so no hCG has been made yet.
w: hCG is made from implantation onward, about a week after fertilization, and peaks in the first trimester.
Made by trophoblast.
The corpus luteum is the target of hCG, which keeps it alive; it does not break hCG down.

q: An experimenter moves a group of early-embryo cells that would normally form part of the neural tube to the belly region, and they form skin (epidermis) like the surrounding ectoderm. What can be concluded?
o: Those cells were not yet determined when they were moved
They were already determined as neural tissue before they were moved
They were totipotent
The experiment caused apoptosis
e: If cells adopt the fate of their new location, they weren't yet committed.
Determined cells would keep their original fate wherever they're placed.
w: They changed fate.
They aren't totipotent.
Apoptotic cells would die, but these cells survived and formed epidermis, so cell death isn't the conclusion.

q: In preimplantation genetic testing, a few cells are removed from the trophectoderm (trophoblast) of a day-5 blastocyst rather than from the inner cell mass. Why?
o: Trophoblast forms the placenta, sparing the embryo
Trophoblast cells have more DNA than the inner cell mass cells
Inner cell mass cells have no nuclei at this stage
Trophoblast cells are the only ones that divide
e: The inner cell mass becomes the embryo itself.
The trophoblast becomes the embryo's part of the placenta and chorion.
Taking cells from the trophoblast tests the same genome while sparing the cells that build the fetus.
w: Both groups carry the same diploid genome.
Inner cell mass cells have nuclei; they are the embryo's founder cells.
Both cell groups are dividing at this stage.

q: When a fetus has no working kidneys, the amniotic sac contains very little fluid later in pregnancy. Why?
o: Fetal urine is the main source of amniotic fluid later on
The kidneys make the amnion membrane
Amniotic fluid is mostly maternal urine
The fetal kidneys pump fluid back out of the amniotic sac
e: The amnion forms a fluid-filled sac that cushions the fetus.
From the second trimester on, most of that fluid is fetal urine.
With no fetal urine, fluid volume falls (oligohydramnios).
w: The amnion forms from embryonic tissue early on, not from the kidneys.
Maternal urine is excreted by the mother and doesn't enter the amniotic sac.
Kidneys add fluid to the sac; they don't remove it.

q: Which pair of cell types share the same germ-layer origin?
o: Alveolar lining cells and thyroid cells
Alveolar lining cells and cardiac muscle cells
Thyroid follicular cells and epidermal cells
Epidermal cells and cardiac muscle cells
e: Lung epithelium buds from the embryonic foregut, which is endoderm.
The thyroid also buds from foregut endoderm (the floor of the pharynx).
Cardiac muscle is mesoderm, and epidermis is ectoderm.
w: Cardiac muscle comes from mesoderm, not endoderm.
Epidermis comes from ectoderm, while thyroid follicles come from endoderm.
These come from ectoderm and mesoderm, two different layers.
t: Endoderm forms the lining of the gut tube and everything that buds from it: lungs, liver, pancreas, thyroid.

q: Which germ layer forms skeletal muscle, bone, blood and the kidneys?
o: Mesoderm
Ectoderm
Endoderm
Trophoblast
e: Mesoderm forms the 'middle' tissues: muscle, bone, connective tissue, the heart and blood, kidneys and gonads.
w: Ectoderm forms skin and nerves.
Endoderm lines the gut.
It forms the placenta.

q: How do substances move between mother and fetus in the placenta?
o: They cross a thin barrier between bloods that don't mix
Maternal blood flows straight into fetal vessels
Fetal blood is pumped into the uterine arteries
They pass only through the umbilical cord wall
e: Maternal blood bathes the chorionic villi, which contain fetal capillaries.
O₂, nutrients and wastes cross the thin villus wall by diffusion or transport, but the two blood supplies stay separate.
w: Bloods don't mix.
Bloods don't mix.
Exchange happens across the walls of the chorionic villi in the placenta; the cord only carries fetal blood to and from it.

q: Why does fetal hemoglobin (HbF) help the fetus get oxygen from the mother?
o: HbF binds O₂ more tightly than adult hemoglobin
HbF binds O₂ less tightly than adult hemoglobin
HbF binds 2,3-BPG more strongly than adult hemoglobin
HbF has more heme groups per molecule than HbA
e: HbF binds 2,3-BPG poorly, so its O₂ curve is left-shifted.
O₂ moves from maternal hemoglobin to fetal hemoglobin across the placenta.
w: This is backwards.
It binds 2,3-BPG weakly.
It has the same four hemes.

q: In a chick embryo, removing a developing limb bud causes many of the motor neurons that would have supplied it to die, while grafting an extra limb bud saves more neurons than usual. What best explains this?
o: Neurons compete for survival factors from their targets
The limb bud itself produces new motor neurons by mitosis
Motor neurons die only when they are physically cut
The extra limb supplies neurons with extra oxygen
e: Embryos make more neurons than they need.
Target tissues release limited neurotrophic factors (such as nerve growth factor for some neurons); neurons that don't get enough undergo apoptosis.
w: Limb buds don't generate motor neurons; neurons come from the spinal cord.
Neurons die from lack of target-derived trophic factors, not cutting.
Survival depends on neurotrophic factors, not extra oxygen.

q: A human blastocyst reaches the uterus but cannot 'hatch' out of its zona pellucida. What is the most likely outcome?
o: It cannot implant in the endometrium
It implants in the fallopian tube instead
It splits to form identical twins
It develops into a fetus without a placenta
e: The zona keeps the trophoblast from touching any tissue.
Hatching normally happens in the uterus, letting the trophoblast contact and invade the endometrium. (The zona is also what stops implantation in the tube.)
w: The zona normally prevents tubal implantation; it doesn't redirect there.
Failure to hatch doesn't cause twinning.
Without hatching it can't implant, so no placenta or fetus develops.

q: The neural tube forms from:
o: Ectoderm, during neurulation
Endoderm, during cleavage
Mesoderm, during implantation
Trophoblast
e: The notochord (mesoderm) signals the overlying ectoderm to fold into the neural tube.
w: Endoderm forms the gut lining and its organs, and cleavage comes before germ layers even exist; the neural tube is ectoderm.
Mesoderm forms the notochord that signals neurulation, but the neural tube itself folds from ectoderm, well after implantation.
It forms the placenta.

q: Tubal ligation blocks each fallopian tube near the uterus. Why does this prevent pregnancy even though the ovaries still ovulate?
o: Sperm can't reach the egg in the tube, where it is fertilized
Without open tubes, the ovaries stop making estrogen and progesterone
The egg can no longer leave the ovary
The uterus can no longer thicken its lining
e: Fertilization normally occurs in the outer part (ampulla) of the fallopian tube.
Sperm travel from the uterus up the tube to get there.
Blocking the tube near the uterus keeps sperm and egg apart.
w: The ovaries' hormone output does not depend on open fallopian tubes.
Ovulation still releases the egg; it just can't meet sperm.
The uterine lining still cycles under ovarian hormones.

q: The vagus nerve contains fibers that slow the heart and fibers that carry stretch information from the aortic arch to the brainstem. How are these two kinds of fibers classified?
o: Heart-slowing fibers are efferent; aortic stretch fibers are afferent
Both are efferent, because both are in the vagus
Heart-slowing fibers are afferent; aortic stretch fibers are efferent
Both are afferent, because both connect to the brainstem
e: Efferent fibers carry signals out from the CNS to effectors such as heart muscle.
Afferent fibers carry sensory signals in to the CNS.
So the heart-slowing fibers are efferent (motor), and the stretch fibers are afferent (sensory).
w: A nerve can carry both directions; the vagus is mixed.
This reverses the directions.
Fibers that act on the heart carry signals away from the brainstem, so they are efferent.

q: Local anesthetics block pain without making a patient unconscious. Based on how they act, where do they work?
o: On voltage-gated Na⁺ channels in local nerve fibers, blocking conduction
On GABA receptors in the brain, dampening conscious awareness of pain
On voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels in muscle, preventing contraction
On opioid receptors in the spinal cord, inhibiting pain transmission
e: They stop action potentials from traveling in nerves near the injection site.
Pain signals never reach the brain.
w: That describes general anesthetics, which cause unconsciousness.
Blocking muscle contraction would not block pain.
That describes opioids, not local anesthetics.

q: Besides speeding conduction, why does myelination reduce the energy a neuron spends on each action potential?
o: Ions cross only at nodes, so pumps restore less
Myelin stores ATP for use by the Na⁺/K⁺ pump
Myelin lets action potentials skip repolarizing
Myelin adds more Na⁺ channels along the axon
e: In a myelinated axon, Na⁺ and K⁺ flow across the membrane only at the nodes of Ranvier.
Fewer ions move per action potential, so the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase uses less ATP to restore the gradients.
w: Myelin doesn't store ATP.
Each node still depolarizes and then repolarizes; myelin saves energy by limiting ion flow to the nodes, not by skipping repolarization.
Myelin has no channels.

q: A patient has blurred vision from optic nerve inflammation and slowed conduction in brain pathways, but nerve conduction studies in the arms and legs are normal. Which cells are most likely under attack?
o: Oligodendrocytes
Schwann cells
Fibrous astrocytes
Lower motor neurons
e: The optic nerve and brain pathways are part of the CNS.
CNS myelin is made by oligodendrocytes, while peripheral myelin is made by Schwann cells.
Slowed CNS conduction with normal peripheral nerves points to oligodendrocyte myelin.
w: Schwann cells myelinate peripheral nerves, which conduct normally here.
Astrocytes support neurons and the blood–brain barrier but don't make myelin.
Losing motor neurons would cause weakness, not slowed conduction in the optic nerve.

q: Cells in the carotid bodies detect a drop in blood O₂ and signal the brainstem to increase breathing. These receptors are best classified as:
o: Chemoreceptors
Mechanoreceptors
Nociceptors
Thermoreceptors
e: Chemoreceptors respond to chemical concentrations, here O₂ (as well as CO₂ and H⁺).
Mechanoreceptors sense stretch or pressure, nociceptors sense harmful stimuli, and thermoreceptors sense temperature.
w: Mechanoreceptors respond to stretch, pressure or touch, not to a drop in blood O₂.
Nociceptors respond to tissue-damaging stimuli that cause pain, not to blood O₂ levels.
Thermoreceptors respond to temperature changes, not to the chemical level of O₂ in blood.

q: In Guillain–Barré syndrome, the immune system attacks myelin made by Schwann cells. Which finding is expected?
o: Slowed conduction in peripheral nerves, with brain tracts spared
Slowed conduction in brain tracts, with peripheral nerves spared
Loss of neuron cell bodies in the primary motor cortex
Faster conduction because the axons are now exposed
e: Schwann cells myelinate only peripheral axons.
Demyelinated PNS axons conduct slowly or fail, causing weakness and lost reflexes; CNS myelin (oligodendrocytes) is untouched.
w: That's CNS myelin.
Cell bodies spared.
Losing myelin slows conduction, because saltatory jumps fail and current leaks out of exposed axons.

q: After a stroke, a patient has normal strength and sensation but overshoots when reaching for a cup, can't do rapid alternating hand movements, and walks with a wide, unsteady gait. Which region is most likely damaged?
o: The cerebellum
The primary motor cortex
The medulla oblongata
The hippocampus
e: Strength and sensation are normal, so motor and sensory pathways work.
The problem is coordination: timing and accuracy of movement, and balance.
These are cerebellar functions.
w: Motor cortex damage causes weakness, which this patient doesn't have.
The medulla controls breathing and heart rate, not coordinated reaching.
The hippocampus forms new memories and doesn't coordinate movement.

q: An MRI shows lesions mainly in the brain's white matter. Which structures make up most of this tissue?
o: Myelinated axon tracts
Neuron cell bodies
Dendrites and synapses
Cerebrospinal fluid spaces
e: White matter looks white because of the fatty myelin wrapped around bundles of axons.
Gray matter is where neuron cell bodies, dendrites and synapses are concentrated.
w: Neuron cell bodies are concentrated in gray matter; white matter is mostly myelinated axons.
Dendrites and synapses are concentrated in gray matter, not in the myelin-rich white matter.
Cerebrospinal fluid fills the ventricles and surrounding spaces; it is not the tissue that makes up white matter.

q: A musician takes propranolol, a β-adrenergic blocker, before a concert. Which stage-fright symptoms is it most likely to reduce?
o: Racing heart and shaky hands
Dry mouth and dilated pupils
Slow heart and constricted pupils
Increased stomach movements
e: Stress activates the sympathetic 'fight or flight' system.
A fast, pounding heartbeat (β₁) and tremor (β₂) are driven by β-adrenergic receptors.
Blocking β receptors blunts these symptoms.
w: Dry mouth and pupil dilation are mainly through α-adrenergic and other pathways, not the main β effects.
A slow heart and small pupils are parasympathetic effects, not stage-fright symptoms.
Sympathetic activity slows gut movements, and propranolol wouldn't increase them.

q: Which brain structure controls body temperature, hunger and the pituitary gland?
o: Hypothalamus
Cerebellum
Amygdala
Hippocampus
e: The hypothalamus is the main link between the nervous and endocrine systems.
w: Balance and coordination.
Fear and emotion.
The hippocampus forms new long-term memories; it doesn't regulate temperature, hunger or the pituitary.

q: During surgery, a curare-like drug that competitively blocks nicotinic ACh receptors keeps a patient's muscles relaxed. Afterward, neostigmine, an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, is given to reverse the paralysis. Why does this work?
o: More ACh builds up and outcompetes the blocker
It breaks down the blocker in the synaptic cleft
It makes muscle fibers fire with no ACh at all
It locks the blocker onto the receptor more tightly
e: A competitive blocker can be overcome by raising the concentration of the natural ligand.
Inhibiting acetylcholinesterase lets ACh accumulate in the cleft, so ACh wins more receptors and contraction returns.
w: Neostigmine inhibits acetylcholinesterase; it doesn't break down the blocker.
Muscle still needs ACh binding to fire.
Raising ACh competes the blocker off; it doesn't bind it tighter.
t: Neostigmine also boosts ACh at muscarinic sites, so a muscarinic blocker is usually given with it.

q: How does myelination by Schwann cells differ from myelination by oligodendrocytes?
o: Each Schwann cell wraps one axon segment; each oligodendrocyte wraps segments of many axons
Schwann cells myelinate CNS axons, while oligodendrocytes myelinate PNS axons instead
Only myelin made by oligodendrocytes has nodes of Ranvier
Schwann cell myelin contains no lipid, unlike oligodendrocyte myelin
e: Schwann cells myelinate axons in the PNS, and each one wraps a single segment of a single axon.
Oligodendrocytes work in the CNS and extend several processes, each myelinating a segment of a different axon. Both kinds of myelin are lipid-rich and leave nodes of Ranvier.
w: This swaps the locations: Schwann cells myelinate PNS axons, and oligodendrocytes myelinate CNS axons.
Both have nodes.
Both are lipid-rich.

q: Cultured cells respond to hormone X by making more of one enzyme over 4 hours. A drug that blocks transcription abolishes the response, but a drug that blocks adenylyl cyclase has no effect. Hormone X is most likely:
o: A steroid such as estradiol acting on an intracellular receptor
A peptide such as glucagon acting through cAMP
A catecholamine such as epinephrine acting through cAMP
A neurotransmitter such as acetylcholine opening an ion channel
e: The response needs new transcription and takes hours, the signature of a hormone–receptor complex acting on DNA.
Glucagon and epinephrine (β receptors) work through adenylyl cyclase and cAMP, so blocking it would have stopped them.
w: Blocking adenylyl cyclase had no effect, so it doesn't act via cAMP.
Epinephrine's β-receptor effects use cAMP, but blocking adenylyl cyclase didn't matter.
Ion channel responses take milliseconds, not hours of new transcription.

q: Peptide hormones like insulin act by:
o: Binding cell-surface receptors and triggering second messengers
Diffusing into the nucleus and binding DNA directly
Crossing the membrane and binding cytoplasmic receptors
Binding intracellular receptors that act as transcription factors
e: Peptides are water-soluble and can't cross the lipid bilayer, so they use surface receptors.
w: Steroids bind DNA receptors.
Peptides can't cross.
Intracellular receptors acting as transcription factors are how steroid hormones work; water-soluble peptides can't cross the membrane.

q: Why is cortisol given as an anti-inflammatory drug?
o: It suppresses the immune and inflammatory responses
It increases white blood cell activity at sites of injury
It increases histamine release
It acts as an antibiotic
e: Glucocorticoids reduce production of inflammatory molecules like prostaglandins and cytokines.
w: It suppresses them.
It reduces it.
It doesn't kill bacteria.

q: Some antipsychotic drugs block dopamine D₂ receptors and can cause milk secretion in patients who are not breastfeeding. What explains this side effect?
o: Dopamine normally holds prolactin down; blocking it lifts the brake
Dopamine stimulates prolactin, so blocking it raises oxytocin instead
The drugs act directly on the breast to make milk
The drugs raise estrogen, which triggers milk release
e: Hypothalamic dopamine travels to the anterior pituitary and inhibits prolactin release.
Blocking D₂ receptors removes this inhibition.
Prolactin rises and stimulates milk production.
w: Dopamine inhibits prolactin, and blocking it doesn't work by raising oxytocin.
The effect goes through the pituitary's prolactin, not directly through the breast.
Raising estrogen isn't the mechanism; the drugs block dopamine at the pituitary.

q: A patient has taken high-dose prednisone, a cortisol-like drug, every day for six months. Which set of findings is expected?
o: High glucose, muscle wasting and low ACTH
Low glucose, weight loss and high ACTH
High glucose, muscle wasting and high ACTH
Low glucose, muscle gain and low ACTH
e: Excess glucocorticoid raises glucose (gluconeogenesis) and breaks down muscle protein.
It also suppresses CRH and ACTH by negative feedback, so ACTH is low.
w: This reverses the effects: excess glucocorticoid raises glucose and suppresses ACTH by negative feedback, rather than lowering glucose and raising ACTH.
ACTH is suppressed.
Muscle is lost.

q: Right after a person loses about 1 L of blood, which hormonal changes help restore blood volume and pressure?
o: ADH and aldosterone rise, while ANP falls
ADH and aldosterone fall, while ANP rises
ADH rises, while aldosterone and ANP fall
ADH falls, while aldosterone and ANP rise
e: Low pressure reduces baroreceptor firing, which boosts ADH release; low kidney perfusion releases renin → angiotensin II → aldosterone.
The atria are stretched less, so ANP (which promotes Na⁺ and water loss) falls.
w: This has every change backwards: blood loss raises ADH and aldosterone and lowers ANP to retain fluid.
Low kidney perfusion activates renin and angiotensin II, so aldosterone rises rather than falls.
Low pressure reduces baroreceptor firing, which raises ADH release rather than lowering it, and ANP falls.

q: In an animal, the posterior pituitary is destroyed but the hypothalamus is left intact. Water loss in urine rises sharply, then partly recovers over weeks. What best explains the recovery?
o: Hypothalamic neurons release ADH from their cut axon ends
The anterior pituitary takes over making and releasing ADH
The kidneys begin making their own ADH
The adrenal cortex releases more ADH
e: ADH is made in hypothalamic neuron cell bodies.
It travels down their axons and is normally released from the posterior pituitary.
After injury, the cut axon ends can still release ADH into nearby blood vessels, restoring some secretion.
w: The anterior pituitary makes its own hormones (such as ACTH and TSH) but not ADH.
The kidneys respond to ADH; they don't make it.
The adrenal cortex makes steroid hormones, not ADH.
t: The posterior pituitary stores and releases; the hypothalamus makes.

q: Aldosterone acts on the kidney to:
o: Increase Na⁺ reabsorption and K⁺ secretion
Increase Na⁺ excretion and K⁺ reabsorption
Increase water excretion and Na⁺ loss
Increase Ca²⁺ reabsorption and phosphate excretion
e: Aldosterone works on the distal tubule and collecting duct.
Water follows the reabsorbed Na⁺, raising blood volume and pressure.
w: This is backwards.
It retains water.
Raising Ca²⁺ reabsorption and phosphate excretion is parathyroid hormone's effect on the kidney, not aldosterone's.

q: Calcitonin and PTH work as antagonists. If blood calcium is too high, which response is expected?
o: More calcitonin and less PTH
More PTH and less calcitonin
More of both
Less of both
e: Calcitonin lowers blood calcium (bone deposition).
PTH raises it, so it would be reduced.
w: That raises calcium.
These oppose each other.
These oppose each other.

q: Type 1 and type 2 diabetes both cause high blood glucose. What is the key difference?
o: Type 1 lacks insulin production; type 2 mainly involves insulin resistance
Type 1 involves too much insulin; type 2 involves too little
Type 1 involves insulin resistance; type 2 lacks insulin production
Type 1 involves excess glucagon; type 2 involves excess cortisol
e: Type 1: autoimmune destruction of β cells.
Type 2: insulin resistance (with later β-cell decline).
w: Type 1 lacks insulin.
This is backwards.
Neither is the cause.

q: A patient's kidney collecting ducts lack working ADH receptors, and blood ADH is high. What will the urine be like?
o: Large volumes of very dilute urine
Small volumes of very concentrated urine
Normal volumes of urine containing glucose
Large volumes of very concentrated urine
e: ADH normally inserts aquaporins into the collecting duct so water is reabsorbed.
Without working receptors, water stays in the tubule, giving copious dilute urine (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus) despite high ADH.
w: ADH can't act.
Glucose in urine comes from high blood glucose, as in diabetes mellitus; a lack of ADH action causes dilute urine, not glycosuria.
Urine is dilute.
t: Diabetes insipidus = lots of dilute, 'tasteless' urine; diabetes mellitus = urine with glucose.

q: Researchers remove both adrenal glands from rats. Rats given plain water die within about two weeks, but rats given 0.9% NaCl to drink survive much longer. Loss of which hormone's effect does the salt water mainly make up for?
o: Aldosterone, which retains Na⁺ in the kidney
Epinephrine, which raises the heart rate
Cortisol, which raises blood glucose
ADH, which retains water in the kidney
e: Without aldosterone, the kidneys keep losing Na⁺, and water follows, so blood volume and pressure fall.
Drinking salt water replaces the lost Na⁺. Cortisol is also missing, which is why survival is still not normal; ADH comes from the hypothalamus, not the adrenals.
w: Epinephrine affects heart rate, not kidney Na⁺ retention that salt replaces.
Cortisol's loss isn't fixed by salt; that's why survival is still not normal.
ADH comes from the hypothalamus/posterior pituitary, not the adrenals.

q: After two days of repeated vomiting, a patient's blood pH is 7.50 and HCO₃⁻ is high. Which respiratory change best helps compensate?
o: Slower, shallower breathing that lets CO₂ rise
Faster, deeper breathing that blows off CO₂
Slower breathing that lowers blood CO₂
Faster breathing that raises blood HCO₃⁻
e: Losing stomach HCl leaves excess HCO₃⁻: a metabolic alkalosis.
Hypoventilation retains CO₂, which forms carbonic acid and pulls pH back down toward 7.4.
w: Blowing off CO₂ raises pH further, worsening alkalosis.
Slower breathing raises, not lowers, blood CO₂.
Faster breathing lowers CO₂; it doesn't raise HCO₃⁻.
t: Vomiting loses acid → alkalosis; severe diarrhea loses bicarbonate → acidosis.

q: Mucus and cilia in the airways:
o: Trap and sweep particles up and out of the airways
Exchange O₂ and CO₂ across the bronchial wall
Produce surfactant that keeps the bronchi open
Absorb water to keep the airway lining dry
e: This 'mucociliary escalator' clears debris; smoking damages it.
w: Alveoli exchange gases.
Type II cells make surfactant.
They keep it moist.

q: A patient's right phrenic nerve is cut during surgery. On an X-ray taken during a deep breath in, what does the right side of the diaphragm do?
o: It stays high instead of moving down
It moves down farther than the left side
It moves down normally, driven by the intercostals
It contracts in spasms
e: The phrenic nerve drives the diaphragm.
During inhalation, the diaphragm contracts and flattens downward, enlarging the chest.
A paralyzed half can't contract, so it stays high (and may even be pulled up).
w: A paralyzed muscle can't move farther than a working one.
The intercostals move the ribs; they can't pull the paralyzed diaphragm down.
Cutting the nerve causes paralysis, not spasm.

q: After several days at high altitude, red blood cells make more 2,3-BPG. How does this help?
o: It lowers Hb's O₂ affinity, so tissues unload more O₂
It raises Hb's O₂ affinity, so tissues unload more O₂
It raises Hb's O₂ affinity, so the lungs load much more O₂
It replaces O₂ at hemoglobin's heme binding sites
e: 2,3-BPG binds deoxyhemoglobin and stabilizes it, shifting the O₂–Hb curve to the right.
Lower affinity means more O₂ is released at tissue P(O₂), offsetting the lower O₂ loaded at altitude.
w: 2,3-BPG lowers hemoglobin's O₂ affinity; it is lower, not higher, affinity that lets tissues unload more O₂.
2,3-BPG lowers rather than raises O₂ affinity, and its benefit is more unloading in tissues, not more loading in the lungs.
Doesn't replace O₂.

q: A patient with a spinal cord injury has paralyzed abdominal muscles but a working diaphragm. Which ability is most impaired?
o: Coughing forcefully
Breathing quietly at rest
Taking a deep breath in
Holding a breath
e: Quiet exhalation is passive, from elastic recoil of the lungs.
Forceful exhalation and coughing use the abdominal muscles and internal intercostals to push air out.
Without abdominal muscles, coughs are weak.
w: Quiet breathing uses the diaphragm and passive recoil, which still work.
Inhalation is driven mainly by the diaphragm, which still works.
Holding a breath doesn't need abdominal muscles.

q: The cartilage rings of the trachea are C-shaped, open at the back, where the trachea lies against the esophagus. What is the advantage of this shape?
o: The esophagus can bulge forward as food passes
The open back lets the trachea collapse during each exhalation
Air can leak out of the gap to the esophagus
It lets the trachea stretch to hold more air
e: The cartilage holds the trachea open against pressure changes during breathing.
The posterior gap is bridged by smooth muscle and connective tissue.
This lets the esophagus expand into the space as a bolus passes, without compressing the airway.
w: The cartilage is there to keep the airway from collapsing, not to let it collapse.
The gap is closed by muscle and connective tissue, so air doesn't leak through.
The trachea is not a storage space; gas exchange happens in the alveoli.

q: Hypoventilation (breathing too slowly) causes:
o: Respiratory acidosis
Respiratory alkalosis
Metabolic alkalosis
No change in pH
e: CO₂ builds up, making more H⁺ through the bicarbonate equilibrium, so pH falls.
w: Respiratory alkalosis comes from hyperventilation blowing off CO₂; breathing too slowly retains CO₂ and lowers pH.
Hypoventilation changes CO₂, so the disturbance is respiratory, and CO₂ buildup makes it acidosis, not alkalosis.
CO₂ changes pH.

q: Two people both have a minute ventilation of 6 L min⁻¹ and a dead space of 150 mL. Person A takes 12 breaths per minute of 500 mL; person B takes 30 breaths per minute of 200 mL. What is each person's alveolar ventilation?
o: A: 4.2 L min⁻¹; B: 1.5 L min⁻¹
Both: 6.0 L min⁻¹
Both: 4.2 L min⁻¹
A: 1.5 L min⁻¹; B: 4.2 L min⁻¹
e: Alveolar ventilation = rate × (tidal volume − dead space).
w: Subtract dead space.
Person B's alveolar ventilation is lower because 30 × (200 − 150) mL gives only 1.5 L min⁻¹, not 4.2.
These values are swapped: Person A, with the bigger 500 mL breaths, gets 4.2 L min⁻¹, and shallow-breathing Person B gets 1.5.
t: Rapid shallow breathing mostly moves dead-space air back and forth.

q: Adding acid to the blood (with P(CO₂) held constant) stimulates breathing mainly through the carotid bodies, while a rise in arterial P(CO₂) acts strongly on central chemoreceptors in the medulla. What explains the difference?
o: CO₂ crosses the blood–brain barrier easily; H⁺ doesn't
H⁺ crosses the blood–brain barrier easily; CO₂ does not
Central chemoreceptors detect only O₂, not acid
The carotid bodies cannot detect changes in CO₂
e: CO₂ is small and nonpolar, so it diffuses into the cerebrospinal fluid and forms H⁺ there, which the central chemoreceptors sense.
Charged H⁺ in the blood crosses the barrier poorly, so blood acid acts mostly on the peripheral (carotid) chemoreceptors.
w: This is backwards: small, nonpolar CO₂ crosses the blood–brain barrier easily, while charged H⁺ crosses it poorly.
They sense CO₂/H⁺.
The carotid bodies do respond to CO₂; the difference is that only CO₂, not blood H⁺, readily reaches the central chemoreceptors.
t: Small, uncharged molecules cross the blood–brain barrier; ions mostly don't.

q: A patient's FVC is 2.0 L (predicted 4.0 L), and her FEV₁ is 1.8 L. Which pattern does this suggest?
o: Restrictive disease, such as pulmonary fibrosis
Obstructive disease, such as asthma or COPD
Normal lungs with a larger-than-usual vital capacity
Mixed obstruction, since FEV₁ is below normal
e: FEV₁/FVC = 1.8 ÷ 2.0 = 0.9, which is normal or high, so air flows out quickly: no obstruction.
But total volume (FVC) is only half of predicted, so the lungs can't expand fully: a restrictive pattern.
w: Ratio is normal.
FVC is low.
FEV₁ is low only because FVC is low; the FEV₁/FVC ratio of 0.9 is normal, which rules out obstruction.
t: Obstructive: FEV₁/FVC low. Restrictive: FVC low, ratio normal or high.

q: A breath of air enters the nose and passes down to the terminal bronchioles. Through this part of the airway, its O₂ and CO₂ content barely changes. Why?
o: These conducting airways have no alveoli
The air moves too fast for any gas to diffuse
The airway walls are impermeable to O₂ but not to CO₂
Mucus absorbs the O₂ before it reaches the alveoli
e: Gas exchange happens across the thin walls of alveoli (and respiratory bronchioles).
The nose, trachea, bronchi and terminal bronchioles only conduct air; they form the anatomic dead space.
Gas there doesn't meet a thin barrier next to capillaries, so its composition stays the same.
w: Speed isn't the reason; even still air in the trachea wouldn't exchange gas, because the walls are too thick.
Conducting airway walls aren't selectively permeable to one gas; they simply lack an exchange surface.
Mucus traps particles; it doesn't absorb O₂.

q: Before a breath-hold dive, a swimmer hyperventilates for a minute. Why is this dangerous?
o: Low CO₂ delays the urge to breathe as O₂ falls too low
It raises CO₂ so high that the diver loses consciousness
It loads hemoglobin with excess O₂, causing O₂ toxicity
It makes the blood acidic, weakening the swimming muscles
e: Hyperventilation blows off CO₂ but adds little O₂, since hemoglobin is already nearly saturated.
CO₂ drives the urge to breathe, so the diver can stay under until O₂ falls low enough to cause blackout without warning.
w: It lowers CO₂.
Not O₂ toxicity.
Blood becomes basic.
t: Hyperventilation lowers CO₂, not raises O₂: it removes the alarm, not the danger.

q: A new drug is not bound to plasma proteins. Its renal clearance is 300 mL min⁻¹, while the patient's GFR is 120 mL min⁻¹. What can be concluded?
o: The drug is filtered and also secreted into the tubules
The drug is filtered and partly reabsorbed
The drug is filtered only, with no other handling
The drug is not filtered at the glomerulus
e: If a drug were only filtered, its clearance would equal GFR (120 mL min⁻¹).
Clearance above GFR (300 > 120) means extra drug is added to the urine by tubular secretion.
Clearance below GFR would point to net reabsorption.
w: Net reabsorption would make clearance lower than GFR.
Filtration only would give clearance equal to GFR (120).
A clearance of 300 shows the drug reaches the urine; unbound drug is freely filtered.
t: Clearance > GFR: net secretion. Clearance < GFR: net reabsorption.

q: A person's GFR is 120 mL min⁻¹. The proximal tubule reabsorbs two-thirds of the filtered water. About how much fluid leaves the proximal tubule each minute?
o: 40 mL
80 mL
120 mL
13 mL
e: Filtered: 120 mL min⁻¹.
Reabsorbed in the proximal tubule: 2/3 × 120 = 80 mL min⁻¹.
Remaining: 120 − 80 = 40 mL min⁻¹ flows on to the loop of Henle.
w: 80 mL is the amount reabsorbed, not what is left.
120 mL is the amount filtered, before any reabsorption.
13 mL is about one-ninth of the filtrate, not the one-third that remains.

q: Fluid is sampled from Bowman's space in a healthy kidney and compared with the plasma entering the glomerulus. Which result is expected?
o: Similar glucose and Na⁺, almost no albumin
Similar albumin, but almost no glucose
Much more glucose than in plasma, and no Na⁺ at all
Red blood cells, but no glucose
e: Filtration begins at the glomerulus, where fluid passes into Bowman's capsule.
The barrier lets water and small solutes such as glucose and Na⁺ through freely.
Large proteins like albumin and blood cells are held back.
w: Albumin is too large and too negatively charged to pass the healthy barrier, while glucose passes freely.
Filtration doesn't concentrate glucose or remove Na⁺; small solutes pass at plasma levels.
Blood cells are far too large to be filtered.

q: A patient with kidney failure develops anemia. Which explanation fits best?
o: The damaged kidneys make too little erythropoietin
The damaged kidneys filter red blood cells out of the blood into the urine
Too much iron is absorbed
Bone marrow makes too many red blood cells
e: EPO drives red blood cell production; patients often receive EPO injections.
w: Kidneys do not filter out red blood cells.
Iron overload does not cause anemia.
Too many red blood cells would cause polycythemia, not anemia.

q: Mean arterial pressure rises from 100 to 140 mmHg, yet GFR barely changes. The afferent arteriole constricts as soon as its wall is stretched. What is this response called?
o: Myogenic autoregulation
Tubuloglomerular feedback
Sympathetic vasodilation
Renin–angiotensin activation
e: Vascular smooth muscle contracts when stretched. This is the myogenic response.
Constricting the afferent arteriole keeps glomerular pressure, and therefore GFR, fairly constant.
w: That's macula densa.
Sympathetic stimulation constricts rather than dilates renal arterioles, and this response is intrinsic to the stretched vessel wall.
The renin–angiotensin system acts too slowly and responds to low pressure, not instant constriction from wall stretch.
t: Stretch → constrict: the myogenic response protects the glomerulus from pressure surges.

q: ADH increases water reabsorption mainly in which part of the nephron?
o: Glomerulus
Proximal convoluted tubule
Descending loop of Henle
Collecting duct
e: ADH binds receptors on collecting duct cells.
This inserts aquaporin channels into their membranes.
More water is reabsorbed, so urine becomes more concentrated.
w: The glomerulus filters; it doesn't reabsorb.
The PCT isn't ADH's main target.
The descending limb isn't ADH's target.
t: ADH = 'anti-diuretic' = less urine. Alcohol blocks ADH, which is why it makes you urinate more.

q: Angiotensin II raises blood pressure by:
o: Constricting arterioles and triggering aldosterone release
Dilating arterioles and triggering aldosterone release
Constricting arterioles and blocking ADH and thirst
Increasing Na⁺ excretion and lowering blood volume
e: It also stimulates thirst and ADH release.
w: Angiotensin II constricts arterioles, which raises pressure; dilating them would lower blood pressure.
It boosts both.
It retains Na⁺.

q: Desert rodents such as kangaroo rats have unusually long loops of Henle. Why does this let them make very concentrated urine?
o: A longer loop builds a steeper salt gradient in the medulla
A longer loop filters more plasma at the glomerulus
A longer loop secretes water into the collecting duct
A longer loop removes the need for ADH
e: The loop of Henle acts as a countercurrent multiplier: each step of salt pumping adds to the gradient.
