A longer loop multiplies more, so the inner medulla becomes saltier, and the collecting duct can draw out more water when ADH is present.
w: Loop length doesn't affect glomerular filtration; the longer loop builds a steeper medullary salt gradient for concentrating urine.
Not water secretion.
Still needs ADH.

q: Which urethral sphincter is under voluntary control, and what kind of muscle is it made of?
o: The external sphincter, made of skeletal muscle
The internal sphincter, made of skeletal muscle
The internal sphincter, made of smooth muscle
The external sphincter, made of smooth muscle
e: The internal sphincter is smooth muscle controlled by the autonomic nervous system.
The external sphincter is skeletal muscle, which is why toilet training is possible.
w: Internal is smooth.
The internal sphincter is smooth muscle under autonomic control, so it isn't the voluntary one.
Skeletal, not smooth.

q: A lung tumor secretes ADH continuously, even when the blood is already dilute. Which pair of findings is expected?
o: Low plasma Na⁺ and concentrated urine
High plasma Na⁺ and dilute urine
Low plasma Na⁺ and dilute urine
High plasma Na⁺ and concentrated urine
e: Constant ADH keeps aquaporins in the collecting duct, so water keeps being reabsorbed.
The retained water dilutes the blood (low Na⁺), while the urine stays inappropriately concentrated.
w: ADH causes water retention, which lowers Na⁺ and concentrates urine.
Dilute urine is the opposite of what constant ADH causes.
Water retention dilutes the blood, lowering Na⁺.

q: A hiker spends hours in hot, dry desert air without drinking, losing a lot of sweat that is more dilute than plasma. Which set of hormone changes is expected?
o: ADH and aldosterone rise; ANP falls
ADH rises; aldosterone and ANP fall
ADH falls; aldosterone and ANP rise
ADH, aldosterone and ANP all fall
e: Losing hypotonic sweat raises plasma osmolarity, so osmoreceptors increase ADH release.
Lower blood volume activates renin → angiotensin II → aldosterone, while less atrial stretch lowers ANP.
w: Low blood volume raises aldosterone, not lowers it.
ADH rises with high osmolarity, and ANP falls with low volume.
Dehydration raises ADH and aldosterone.

q: A patient is severely dehydrated. Which change in urine is expected?
o: Small volume of concentrated urine
Large volume of dilute urine
No change
Large volume of concentrated urine
e: High ADH increases water reabsorption in the collecting duct.
w: ADH is high.
Urine does change: dehydration raises ADH, so more water is reabsorbed and urine becomes small and concentrated.
Urine is concentrated, but high ADH reabsorbs more water, so urine volume falls rather than being large.

q: Plasma is collected with an anticlotting agent, while serum is the fluid left after blood has clotted. Which protein is present in plasma but nearly absent from serum?
o: Fibrinogen
Albumin
Antibodies (IgG)
Glucose
e: During clotting, thrombin converts fibrinogen into fibrin strands.
Fibrin forms the mesh of the clot, which is removed.
So the fibrinogen has been used up, and serum lacks it.
w: Albumin isn't used in clotting, so it stays in serum.
Antibodies remain in serum, which is why serum is used for antibody tests.
Glucose is not a protein and isn't used in clotting.

q: A β₁-blocker drug lowers blood pressure mainly by:
o: Lowering heart rate and contractility
Dilating arterioles through NO release
Blocking aldosterone in the kidney
Raising sympathetic drive to the heart
e: β₁ receptors on the heart respond to norepinephrine and epinephrine by speeding and strengthening the beat.
Blocking them lowers HR and stroke volume, so cardiac output and blood pressure fall (BP = CO × TPR).
w: That's other drugs.
Blocking aldosterone in the kidney is how spironolactone works; β₁-blockers act on heart receptors.
A β₁-blocker blocks sympathetic signals to the heart, the opposite of raising sympathetic drive.

q:
A catheter study gives the values below for four heart chambers. Which chamber pumps oxygenated blood into the systemic circulation?
ChamberPeak pressure (mmHg)O₂ saturation
12575%
212098%
31098%
4575%
o: Chamber 2
Chamber 1
Chamber 3
Chamber 4
e: The systemic pump must have oxygenated blood (98%).
It must also make high pressure to drive the systemic circuit.
Chamber 2 (120 mmHg, 98%) is the left ventricle.
w: Chamber 1 has low pressure and 75% saturation, so it is the right ventricle pumping to the lungs.
Chamber 3 has oxygenated blood but low pressure, so it is the left atrium.
Chamber 4 has low pressure and deoxygenated blood, so it is the right atrium.

q: After a large heart attack, part of the left ventricular wall is replaced by scar tissue. What is the main consequence?
o: Less pumping force, so stroke volume falls
The heart rate is set by the scar
The valves can no longer close
The coronary arteries now carry more blood to the wall
e: The myocardium, made of cardiac muscle, is the layer that contracts.
Scar tissue can't contract.
With less working muscle, the ventricle ejects less blood with each beat.
w: Scar tissue doesn't act as a pacemaker; the SA node still sets the rate.
Valve closure depends on pressure differences and valve tissue, not mainly on wall muscle.
Scarring doesn't increase coronary flow.

q: A person uses 250 mL of O₂ per minute. Arterial blood holds 200 mL O₂ per L, and mixed venous blood holds 150 mL O₂ per L. What is the cardiac output?
o: 5.0 L min⁻¹
1.25 L min⁻¹
0.2 L min⁻¹
12.5 L min⁻¹
e: Each liter of blood gives up 200 − 150 = 50 mL of O₂ to the tissues.
Cardiac output = 250 mL min⁻¹ ÷ 50 mL L⁻¹ = 5.0 L min⁻¹ (the Fick principle).
w: Use the difference.
This is inverted.
Recheck: 250 ÷ 50.

q: Why must the average output of the right ventricle equal that of the left ventricle?
o: The circuits are in series, so a mismatch would pool blood
Both ventricles share one pacemaker, so their volumes match
Both ventricles have walls of the same thickness and force
A hole in the septum lets their volumes equalize each beat
e: Blood from the right ventricle must pass through the lungs to reach the left side, then around the body back to the right.
If one side pumped even slightly more, blood would quickly build up in the other circuit (as in heart failure).
w: One pacemaker sets rate, not volume.
The left ventricle wall is much thicker and stronger than the right; outputs match because the circuits are in series.
No hole normally.

q: A patient's tricuspid valve doesn't close properly. Which finding is expected during ventricular systole?
o: Blood flows back into the right atrium and the neck veins pulse
Blood flows back into the left atrium and the lungs fill with fluid
Blood flows back from the aorta into the left ventricle
Blood flows back from the pulmonary artery into the right ventricle
e: The tricuspid valve lies between the right atrium and right ventricle.
When the right ventricle contracts with a leaky valve, blood is pushed back into the right atrium.
That pressure wave travels up into the systemic veins, such as the jugular veins.
w: Backflow into the left atrium comes from a leaky mitral valve.
Backflow from the aorta happens through a leaky aortic valve, during diastole.
Backflow from the pulmonary artery is through a leaky pulmonary valve, during diastole.

q: An Rh⁻ mother carries an Rh⁺ baby. Why is a second Rh⁺ pregnancy at risk without treatment?
o: Her anti-Rh antibodies from the first birth can cross the placenta and destroy fetal RBCs
Rh⁺ cells from the first baby permanently convert her own blood type to Rh⁺ as well
The fetus's anti-Rh antibodies cross into her blood and destroy her red blood cells
Uterine scarring from the first birth keeps the second placenta from forming properly
e: Exposure at the first delivery makes the mother produce anti-Rh IgG.
RhoGAM given to the mother prevents this sensitization.
w: Blood type doesn't change.
Mother makes the antibodies.
The danger comes from maternal anti-Rh antibodies crossing the placenta, not from uterine scarring affecting placental formation.

q: Each day, a few liters more fluid filter out of the capillaries than are reabsorbed. Where does this excess fluid go?
o: Lymphatic vessels return it to the venous blood
The kidneys excrete it directly from the tissues
It stays in the tissues and slowly evaporates
Sweat glands carry it out through the skin
e: Excess interstitial fluid enters lymphatic capillaries and becomes lymph.
Lymph passes through lymph nodes and empties into the veins near the heart via the thoracic duct.
w: The kidneys filter blood plasma, not tissue fluid directly; excess interstitial fluid returns to the blood through lymphatics first.
Interstitial fluid does not evaporate from tissues; it drains into lymphatic vessels and back to the veins.
Sweat glands make sweat for cooling; they do not collect the excess fluid filtered from capillaries.

q: Which pair consists of a vein that carries O₂-rich blood and an artery that carries O₂-poor blood, listed in that order?
o: Pulmonary veins and umbilical arteries
Venae cavae and the aorta
Pulmonary veins and the aorta
Hepatic portal vein and umbilical arteries
e: Vessels are named by the direction of flow: arteries carry blood away from the heart, veins carry it toward the heart.
Pulmonary veins bring O₂-rich blood from the lungs to the left atrium.
Umbilical arteries carry O₂-poor blood away from the fetal heart to the placenta.
w: The venae cavae carry O₂-poor blood and the aorta O₂-rich blood, the usual pattern.
The pulmonary veins fit, but the aorta carries O₂-rich blood.
The umbilical arteries fit, but the hepatic portal vein carries blood that has already given up O₂ in the gut's capillaries.

q: After a heart attack, a clot forms on the wall of the left ventricle. If a piece breaks off, where is it most likely to lodge?
o: In a systemic artery, such as one in the brain
In a branch of a pulmonary artery deep in the lungs
In the superior vena cava
In the right ventricle
e: Blood leaving the left ventricle goes into the aorta.
From there, it travels to systemic arteries, which narrow downstream.
A clot will lodge where an artery becomes too small, such as in the brain (a stroke).
w: The left ventricle pumps into the aorta, not the pulmonary arteries, so a clot from it travels to the body.
Blood from the left ventricle doesn't return to the vena cava before passing through capillaries.
Blood doesn't flow from the left ventricle to the right one in a normal heart.

q: A ventricle has an end-diastolic volume of 120 mL and an end-systolic volume of 50 mL. What are its stroke volume and ejection fraction?
o: 70 mL and about 58%
70 mL and about 42%
170 mL and about 58%
50 mL and about 42%
e: SV = EDV − ESV = 120 − 50 = 70 mL.
w: Divide by EDV.
Subtract, don't add.
50 mL is the end-systolic volume, and 42% is ESV ÷ EDV; stroke volume is 120 − 50 = 70 mL.
t: EF uses EDV in the denominator, not ESV.

q: Why doesn't pepsin digest the stomach's own lining?
o: It's secreted as inactive pepsinogen, and mucus protects the lining
The lining is made mostly of lipids, which pepsin can't digest
Pepsin is active only at neutral pH, so stomach acid keeps it inactive
Parietal cells secrete a pepsin inhibitor into the lumen
e: Pepsinogen is activated by acid in the stomach's lumen.
Bicarbonate-rich mucus protects the epithelial cells.
w: The lining is protein.
Pepsin works in acid.
No such inhibitor.

q: A patient's salivary glands were damaged by radiation, so she makes almost no saliva. Yet she still digests starch nearly normally. Why?
o: Most starch is digested in the small intestine
Pepsin digests starch in the stomach instead of the mouth
Stomach acid breaks starch into glucose
Colon bacteria absorb starch for her
e: Salivary amylase starts starch digestion in the mouth.
But food stays there only briefly, and stomach acid soon stops the enzyme.
Pancreatic amylase in the small intestine does most of the work.
w: Pepsin digests protein, not starch.
Stomach acid doesn't break starch into glucose.
Colon bacteria ferment leftover starch but don't absorb it for the person.

q: A patient has severe watery diarrhea for several days. Which acid–base disturbance is most likely to develop?
o: Metabolic acidosis from lost bicarbonate
Metabolic alkalosis from losing stomach acid
Respiratory acidosis from slowed breathing
Respiratory alkalosis from losing gut CO₂
e: Intestinal and pancreatic secretions are rich in HCO₃⁻.
Losing them in stool lowers blood HCO₃⁻, causing metabolic acidosis. Vomiting, which loses HCl, causes the opposite.
w: Metabolic alkalosis follows vomiting, which loses stomach HCl; diarrhea loses bicarbonate and causes acidosis.
Diarrhea doesn't slow breathing; it causes metabolic acidosis by losing bicarbonate-rich intestinal fluid.
Gut CO₂ loss isn't significant here; losing bicarbonate in stool makes the blood more acidic, not alkaline.

q: An infant has a thickened pyloric sphincter and vomits forcefully after every feeding. The vomit contains stomach contents but no bile. Blood tests show a high pH and high HCO₃⁻. What explains the acid–base change?
o: Loss of stomach HCl leaves extra bicarbonate in the blood
Swallowed air causes the infant to retain extra CO₂
Vomiting removes pancreatic bicarbonate from the body
The kidneys stop excreting bicarbonate after feeding
e: Each H⁺ that parietal cells secrete into the stomach leaves an HCO₃⁻ in the blood.
Normally that H⁺ is later neutralized in the duodenum; when it is vomited instead, the extra HCO₃⁻ remains, causing metabolic alkalosis.
No bile in the vomit fits a blockage before the duodenum.
w: Swallowed air doesn't cause CO₂ retention or explain high HCO₃⁻.
Bile-free vomit means the block is before the duodenum, so pancreatic fluid isn't lost.
The kidneys excrete extra HCO₃⁻; the cause is lost stomach acid.

q: A person's insulin response is much larger after swallowing 50 g of glucose than after receiving IV glucose that produces the same blood glucose level. Which explanation fits best?
o: The gut releases hormones that boost insulin secretion
Oral glucose is absorbed faster than IV glucose
IV glucose is broken down before reaching the pancreas
The stomach secretes insulin when glucose is swallowed
e: Blood glucose was matched, so glucose alone can't explain the difference.
Glucose in the intestine triggers incretins (GLP-1 and GIP), which amplify insulin release from pancreatic β cells.
w: Blood glucose levels were matched in both cases, so absorption speed can't explain the bigger insulin response to oral glucose.
IV glucose isn't degraded on the way to the pancreas; it simply lacks the gut incretin signal that oral glucose triggers.
Stomach doesn't make insulin.

q: A segment of guinea pig intestine is removed and placed in a warm salt bath, with no connection to the brain or spinal cord. A small bolus inside it still triggers contraction behind it and relaxation ahead. What does this show?
o: The gut's own enteric neurons can drive peristalsis
Peristalsis needs signals from the vagus nerve
Smooth muscle contracts only when hormones arrive in the blood
Skeletal muscle in the gut wall controls peristalsis
e: The isolated segment has no outside nerve or blood supply.
Yet the coordinated peristaltic reflex still happens.
So the enteric nervous system in the gut wall can generate it on its own.
w: The vagus is cut off in this preparation, yet peristalsis still occurs.
There is no circulating blood, so hormones can't be the trigger.
The intestine wall has smooth muscle, not skeletal muscle.

q: To treat severe ulcers, a surgeon cuts the vagus nerve branches to the stomach. What is the expected effect on the stomach?
o: Less acid secretion and slower stomach emptying
More acid secretion and faster stomach emptying
No change, since only hormones control the stomach
More acid secretion but slower stomach emptying
e: The vagus nerve carries parasympathetic signals that stimulate acid secretion and stomach motility.
Cutting it lowers acid output, but it also weakens contractions, so the stomach empties more slowly.
w: Cutting the vagus removes parasympathetic stimulation, so both acid secretion and stomach emptying fall rather than rise.
The vagus nerve directly stimulates acid secretion and motility, so cutting it does change stomach function, not just hormonal control.
Emptying does slow, but acid secretion falls too, because vagal input normally stimulates parietal cells.

q: After gallbladder removal, bile still enters the duodenum. Why?
o: The liver keeps making bile, which drains continuously
The pancreas takes over making bile
The duodenum begins to make bile
Bile is no longer needed for digestion after this surgery
e: The liver makes bile.
The gallbladder only stores and concentrates it between meals.
Without the gallbladder, bile flows from the liver into the duodenum continuously.
w: The pancreas makes digestive enzymes and bicarbonate, not bile.
The duodenum receives bile; it doesn't make it.
Bile is still needed to emulsify fats.

q: Proton pump inhibitors (like omeprazole) reduce stomach acid by blocking:
o: The H⁺/K⁺-ATPase in parietal cells
Histamine H₂ receptors on gastric parietal cells
Pepsinogen secretion by chief cells
The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase in parietal cells
e: This pump moves H⁺ into the stomach in exchange for K⁺.
w: That's H₂ blockers.
Pepsinogen from chief cells is a protease precursor, not acid; PPIs block the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase that secretes H⁺.
The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase is in nearly every cell and doesn't secrete acid; PPIs block the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase.

q: Shortly after a large meal, blood pH rises slightly (the 'alkaline tide'). Which explanation fits best?
o: Parietal cells send H⁺ into the stomach and HCO₃⁻ into the blood
Pancreatic bicarbonate is absorbed directly into the blood
Breathing speeds up after eating, blowing off extra CO₂
Digested amino acids act as strong bases once they reach the blood
e: Inside parietal cells, carbonic anhydrase makes H⁺ and HCO₃⁻ from CO₂ and H₂O.
H⁺ is pumped into the stomach, while HCO₃⁻ leaves the other side of the cell (in exchange for Cl⁻) and enters the blood.
w: Pancreatic bicarbonate is secreted into the duodenum to neutralize chyme, not absorbed directly into the blood after meals.
Breathing doesn't speed up after a meal to explain the rise; it comes from parietal cells releasing HCO₃⁻ into the blood while secreting acid.
Amino acids aren't strong bases.

q: A small gallstone gets stuck where the common bile duct and the main pancreatic duct join and enter the duodenum. Which pair of problems can this cause?
o: Jaundice and pancreatitis
Jaundice and stomach ulcers
Pancreatitis and vitamin B₁₂ deficiency
Stomach ulcers and lactose intolerance
e: The common bile duct and pancreatic duct share an outlet into the duodenum.
A stone there blocks bile flow (causing jaundice).
It also blocks pancreatic juice, which can back up and inflame the pancreas.
w: The blocked ducts don't drain the stomach, so ulcers aren't the result.
B₁₂ absorption depends on intrinsic factor and the ileum.
Neither ulcers nor lactose intolerance follow from blocking these ducts.

q: Inside a parietal cell, the pH is about 7.2, while the stomach fluid it secretes into can reach pH 1.0. About how many times higher is the H⁺ concentration in the stomach?
o: About 10⁶ times
About 7 times
About 10³ times
About 6 times
e: Each pH unit is a 10-fold change in H⁺.
Pumping against this steep gradient needs ATP, supplied to the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase.
w: 7 comes from dividing the pH values (7.2 / 1.0), but pH is a log scale.
10³ uses half the pH difference.
6 is the pH difference itself, not the fold change.

q: When a B cell switches from making IgM to making IgG against the same pathogen, what changes?
o: The constant region; specificity stays the same
The variable region, so it binds a new antigen
Only the light chains, so it binds a new antigen
Nothing; IgM and IgG are the same protein
e: Class switching swaps the heavy-chain constant region, changing what the antibody does (e.g. crossing the placenta).
The variable regions that bind the antigen are unchanged. Helper T cell signals drive the switch.
w: Class switching keeps the variable region, so the antibody still binds the same antigen; only the constant region changes.
Light chains stay.
IgM and IgG have different heavy-chain constant regions, so class switching does change the antibody.

q: Researchers deplete CD8⁺ T cells in mice, then infect one group with a virus that grows inside cells and another with bacteria that grow outside cells. Which result is most likely?
o: Viral clearance is impaired much more than bacterial clearance
Bacterial clearance is impaired much more than viral clearance
Both are cleared normally because B cells take over the job
Neither is cleared, because no antibodies can be made at all
e: CD8⁺ T cells kill infected host cells, which is key for clearing intracellular viruses.
Extracellular bacteria are handled mainly by antibodies, complement and phagocytes, which still work (B cells need CD4⁺, not CD8⁺, help).
w: Extracellular bacteria are cleared mainly by antibodies and phagocytes, not CD8⁺ cells.
B cells don't kill virus-infected cells; CD8⁺ T cells do.
Antibody production needs CD4⁺ help, which is intact.

q: In a wound, neutrophils dominate on the first day, but by day 3 most of the immune cells are macrophages. Where do these macrophages come from?
o: Blood monocytes that entered and differentiated
Neutrophils that changed into macrophages in the tissue
B cells that switched to phagocytosis
Red blood cells that lost their hemoglobin
e: Monocytes circulate in the blood.
After leaving the blood and entering tissue, they differentiate into macrophages.
They arrive after neutrophils and can live much longer.
w: Neutrophils are short-lived and don't become macrophages.
B cells make antibodies; they don't become macrophages.
Red blood cells have no nucleus and can't become immune cells.

q: Helper T cells (CD4⁺) recognize antigen presented on:
o: MHC class II molecules
MHC class I molecules
Red blood cells
Antibodies
e: MHC II is found on antigen-presenting cells (macrophages, dendritic cells, B cells).
CD8⁺ cytotoxic T cells recognize MHC I, found on all nucleated cells.
w: That's for CD8⁺.
RBCs lack MHC.
Antibodies don't present.
t: Rule of 8: CD4 × MHC II = 8; CD8 × MHC I = 8.

q: Mice lacking Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) survive an injection of bacterial lipopolysaccharide (LPS) that kills normal mice. What best explains this?
o: TLR4 senses LPS and triggers the cytokine surge of shock
TLR4 is the receptor LPS uses to kill cells directly
Without TLR4, the mice make far more protective antibody against LPS
TLR4 normally blocks the liver from clearing LPS
e: TLR4 on macrophages recognizes LPS, a molecule shared by Gram-negative bacteria.
Activation triggers release of inflammatory cytokines.
A huge, body-wide cytokine release causes the shock; without TLR4, it doesn't happen.
w: LPS harms the host mainly by triggering the host's own response, not by killing cells directly.
Antibody responses take days, too slow to explain survival from a single injection.
TLR4 is a detection receptor; it doesn't block LPS clearance.

q: Complement proteins help fight bacteria by:
o: Forming pores in bacterial membranes and tagging them for phagocytosis
Being secreted by plasma cells to bind specific bacterial antigens
Presenting bacterial peptides to helper T cells via MHC II molecules
Digesting bacterial toxins inside the lysosomes of neutrophils
e: Complement forms the membrane attack complex and opsonizes (coats) bacteria.
w: Proteins secreted by plasma cells to bind specific antigens are antibodies; complement proteins are made mainly by the liver.
Presenting peptides on MHC II to helper T cells is the job of antigen-presenting cells, not complement proteins.
Not their role.

q: A baby is born without a thymus. Which problem is most expected?
o: Few T cells and frequent viral and fungal infections
No neutrophils, but normal T cell and B cell function
Too many T cells attacking the baby's own tissues
Normal T cells, but no complement proteins at all
e: T cells must mature in the thymus, so few functional T cells exist.
Without T cells, defense against viruses and fungi fails, and antibody responses that need helper T cells are weak too.
w: Neutrophils are fine.
Too few T cells.
Complement is fine.

q: Regulatory T cells help prevent autoimmune disease by:
o: Suppressing self-reactive lymphocytes out in the tissues
Killing every body cell that displays MHC class I molecules
Producing antibodies that coat and hide self-antigens
Deleting self-reactive T cells during thymic development
e: Some self-reactive cells escape deletion in the thymus.
Regulatory T cells (often CD4⁺CD25⁺) release inhibitory signals that keep these cells in check in the periphery (peripheral tolerance).
w: Not killing all.
Antibodies are made by B cells; regulatory T cells act by releasing inhibitory signals that suppress self-reactive lymphocytes.
That is central tolerance.

q: Why can't the same antibody fight both measles and chickenpox?
o: Each antibody binds a specific antigen shape (epitope)
Antibodies are made only by neutrophils, which cannot switch targets
Antibodies work only on bacteria
Antibodies change shape randomly
e: Antibody specificity comes from the variable regions, which match one epitope.
w: Made by plasma cells.
They also target viruses.
Shape is fixed.

q: Live attenuated viral vaccines usually trigger stronger CD8⁺ T cell responses than killed-virus vaccines. Why?
o: Their proteins are made inside cells and shown on MHC I
Killed viruses cannot be taken up by any phagocytes
Live viruses are presented only on MHC II molecules
CD8⁺ T cells recognize whole live virus in the blood
e: CD8⁺ T cells are activated by peptides from proteins made inside cells, shown on MHC I.
A weakened live virus infects cells and makes its proteins there; killed virus is mostly taken up and shown on MHC II to helper T cells.
w: They can be taken up.
Live virus uses MHC I.
They need MHC I.
t: Inside the cell → MHC I → CD8⁺. Taken in from outside → MHC II → CD4⁺.

q: Some tumors display PD-L1, which binds the inhibitory receptor PD-1 on T cells. Drugs that block PD-1 can shrink tumors but sometimes cause autoimmune colitis or thyroiditis. Why?
o: Removing the brake also unleashes self-reactive T cells
The drug is an antigen that collects in the thyroid
Blocking PD-1 destroys all antibodies in the gut
Tumor cells release thyroid hormone after treatment
e: PD-1 is an 'off switch' that limits T cell activity; tumors exploit it to escape attack.
Blocking it reactivates anti-tumor T cells, but it also frees T cells that react to self, which normal PD-1 signaling keeps in check.
w: Not an antigen.
No antibodies lost.
The thyroiditis isn't from tumor-made hormone; blocking PD-1 frees self-reactive T cells to attack the thyroid.

q: Which cells capture antigen in the tissues, travel to lymph nodes, and are the most effective at activating naive T cells?
o: Dendritic cells
Neutrophils
Plasma cells
Mast cells
e: Dendritic cells engulf antigen, migrate through lymph to nodes, and present peptides on MHC with costimulatory signals.
They bridge innate and adaptive immunity.
w: Neutrophils are short-lived phagocytes that kill microbes on site; they do not carry antigen to lymph nodes to activate naive T cells.
Plasma cells are differentiated B cells that secrete antibodies; they do not present antigen to naive T cells.
Mast cells release histamine in allergy and inflammation; they are not the main activators of naive T cells.

q: How do osteoclasts break down bone?
o: They seal onto bone and secrete acid and proteases
They release calcitonin, which dissolves the mineral
They divide inside the matrix and absorb collagen
They convert hydroxyapatite into new cartilage
e: Osteoclasts are large, multinucleated cells from the monocyte/macrophage lineage.
They pump H⁺ into a sealed space to dissolve the mineral, and secrete enzymes that digest collagen.
w: Calcitonin is a thyroid hormone that inhibits osteoclasts; osteoclasts dissolve bone themselves with acid and proteases.
They don't divide there.
Osteoclasts dissolve hydroxyapatite and digest collagen; they don't convert bone mineral into cartilage.

q: Low blood Ca²⁺ causes muscle twitching and spasms (tetany), even though muscle contraction requires Ca²⁺. Why?
o: Low outside Ca²⁺ makes nerve Na⁺ channels open more easily
Muscles store extra Ca²⁺ when blood levels are low
Low Ca²⁺ blocks acetylcholinesterase at the synapse
Low Ca²⁺ makes myosin bind actin without any signal
e: Extracellular Ca²⁺ normally stabilizes voltage-gated Na⁺ channels.
When it falls, nerves reach threshold more easily and fire on their own, causing spasms; contraction still uses Ca²⁺ stored inside muscle cells.
w: Muscle fibers don't stockpile Ca²⁺ in response to low blood levels; tetany comes from nerves firing too easily when outside Ca²⁺ falls.
Low Ca²⁺ doesn't block acetylcholinesterase; it destabilizes nerve Na⁺ channels so neurons reach threshold and fire spontaneously.
Myosin still needs Ca²⁺ bound to troponin inside the cell; spasms arise because low outside Ca²⁺ makes nerves overexcitable.

q: In a sarcomere, each thin filament is 1.0 µm long and the thick filaments are 1.6 µm long. If the sarcomere shortens from 2.4 µm to 2.2 µm, what is the new width of the H zone?
o: 0.2 µm
0.4 µm
0.6 µm
1.6 µm
e: The H zone is the central region with thick filaments but no thin filaments.
Thin filaments extend 1.0 µm from each Z line, covering 2 × 1.0 = 2.0 µm.
H zone = 2.2 − 2.0 = 0.2 µm (it was 2.4 − 2.0 = 0.4 µm before).
w: 0.4 µm is the H zone at the original 2.4 µm length; at 2.2 µm it narrows to 0.2 µm.
0.6 µm is too wide; the thin filaments cover 2.0 µm, leaving only 2.2 − 2.0 = 0.2 µm.
1.6 µm is the thick filament length, which is the A band, not the H zone.

q: A worker's leg is crushed under heavy machinery for several hours. After rescue, his urine is dark brown and his blood K⁺ is dangerously high. Which explanation fits both findings?
o: Damaged muscle cells release myoglobin and K⁺ into the blood
Crushed bone marrow releases large amounts of hemoglobin
The kidneys stop secreting K⁺ because ADH levels are low
Pain triggers aldosterone release, which raises blood K⁺
e: Crushed muscle fibers break open (rhabdomyolysis). K⁺ is the main cation inside cells, so it floods into the blood.
Myoglobin is filtered by the kidneys, turns the urine dark and can injure the tubules.
w: Bone marrow isn't the source; crushed muscle releases myoglobin and K⁺.
ADH doesn't control K⁺ secretion.
Aldosterone lowers blood K⁺ by increasing its excretion.
t: Aldosterone lowers blood K⁺, so it can't explain hyperkalemia.

q: A patient with a parathyroid tumor makes too much PTH. She has bone pain and develops kidney stones. Which explanation links these findings?
o: Bone resorption raises blood Ca²⁺, so more Ca²⁺ reaches the urine
Calcium is deposited in bone, so the kidney traps the excess
PTH blocks the kidney from filtering any Ca²⁺
Low blood Ca²⁺ causes bone pain and stone formation
e: Excess PTH drives osteoclasts to resorb bone (causing pain) and raises blood Ca²⁺.
Although PTH boosts Ca²⁺ reabsorption, so much Ca²⁺ is filtered that urine Ca²⁺ rises and can form stones.
w: PTH removes calcium from bone; it doesn't deposit it.
PTH doesn't stop Ca²⁺ filtration; the load is high.
PTH excess raises blood Ca²⁺, not lowers it.
t: Classic hyperparathyroidism: 'bones, stones, groans and moans'.

q: Osteocytes are trapped in mineralized bone, yet they stay alive for years. How do they get nutrients and communicate?
o: Through tiny canals joining their processes
By diffusion straight through the solid mineral matrix
Through blood vessels that enter every lacuna
Through lymph vessels running through the matrix
e: Osteocytes sit in small spaces (lacunae) within hard matrix.
Their long processes run through tiny canals (canaliculi) and connect by gap junctions.
Nutrients and signals pass along this network to the central canal of the osteon.
w: Mineralized matrix is too dense for nutrients to diffuse through.
Blood vessels run in central canals, not into every lacuna.
Bone matrix doesn't have lymph vessels running through it.

q: Sweat is first made in the gland's coil with about the same NaCl concentration as plasma. As it travels up the duct, Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are reabsorbed, with Cl⁻ crossing through CFTR channels. Why is sweat very salty in people with cystic fibrosis?
o: Cl⁻ can't be reabsorbed in the duct, so NaCl stays in the sweat
Extra Cl⁻ is secreted into the coil, which raises the salt in sweat
The sweat glands make far more water, diluting less salt
Na⁺ is pumped into the duct by overactive Na⁺/K⁺-ATPases
e: Defective CFTR blocks Cl⁻ reabsorption in the duct.
With Cl⁻ stuck in the lumen, Na⁺ reabsorption also falls (to stay electrically neutral), so sweat stays salty. This is the basis of the sweat chloride test.
w: Defective CFTR stops Cl⁻ reabsorption in the duct; the salt stays because it isn't reclaimed, not because extra is secreted.
Not more water.
Not pumped in.

q: Osteoporosis in older women after menopause is linked mainly to:
o: Lower estrogen, which increases bone resorption
Higher estrogen, which increases bone resorption
Excess calcitonin, which blocks bone formation
Excess vitamin D, which leaches calcium from bone
e: Estrogen normally restrains osteoclasts.
When it drops, resorption outpaces bone formation.
w: Estrogen falls after menopause, not rises, and estrogen normally restrains osteoclasts rather than increasing resorption.
Calcitonin isn't the cause.
Not vitamin D excess.

q: During a slow, easy walk, which motor units in the calf muscles are most likely to be firing?
o: Small motor units made of slow, fatigue-resistant fibers
Large motor units made of fast glycolytic fibers that fatigue quickly
All motor units at once, each at a low rate
Only the largest motor units, for maximum force
e: Motor units are recruited in order of size, smallest first (the size principle).
Small units contain slow oxidative fibers, which are ideal for gentle, sustained activity. Large, fast units join only as more force is needed.
w: Large fast glycolytic units are recruited only for high force; a gentle walk uses small slow units first.
Motor units aren't all activated together at low rates; they are recruited smallest first, by the size principle.
The largest motor units are recruited last, only when maximal force is needed, not for an easy walk.

q: A biopsy shows long cylindrical muscle cells with striations, many nuclei at their edges, and no intercalated discs. How is this muscle controlled?
o: Voluntarily, by somatic motor neurons
Involuntarily, by the autonomic system
By its own pacemaker cells
By hormones alone, without nerves
e: Striations, many peripheral nuclei and no intercalated discs identify skeletal muscle.
Skeletal muscle contracts only when somatic motor neurons stimulate it.
That makes it voluntary.
w: Autonomic control is typical of smooth and cardiac muscle.
Pacemaker cells are a feature of cardiac muscle, which has intercalated discs.
Skeletal muscle needs nerve input to contract.

q: Chemotherapy drugs kill rapidly dividing cells. Which epidermal layer is most directly affected, and what results?
o: Stratum basale, so the skin renews more slowly
Stratum corneum, so dead surface cells divide less
The dermis, so sweat glands stop working
Stratum corneum, so melanin production rises
e: New skin cells are made by division in the stratum basale, the deepest epidermal layer.
These cells push upward and replace those lost at the surface.
Killing dividing basal cells slows renewal, so the skin becomes thin and heals slowly.
w: The stratum corneum is made of dead cells, which don't divide.
The dermis isn't the epidermal layer that divides to renew the skin.
Dead surface cells don't make melanin; melanocytes sit in the basal layer.

q: Osteoclast activity increases when blood calcium is low. Which hormone drives this?
o: Parathyroid hormone
Calcitonin from the thyroid
Insulin from the pancreas
Glucagon
e: PTH indirectly activates osteoclasts to release calcium from bone.
w: It lowers calcium.
Insulin regulates blood glucose and doesn't drive osteoclasts to release calcium; PTH does.
Glucagon raises blood glucose, not blood calcium, and doesn't activate osteoclasts.

q: Researchers mark three regions of an early embryo with a harmless dye before gastrulation and later find the dye in the tissues shown. Cells from which regions moved into the embryo's interior during gastrulation?
o: Regions 2 and 3
Regions 1 and 2
Region 1 only
Region 3 only
e: Region 1 became ectoderm derivatives, which stay on the outside.
Regions 2 (mesoderm: heart, vessels, kidney) and 3 (endoderm: gut lining, liver) moved inward through the blastopore or primitive streak.
w: Region 1 gave epidermis and brain (ectoderm), which stays outside.
Region 1 is ectoderm, which doesn't move inward.
Region 2 (mesoderm) also moved inward.

q: Rats are tested before and after surgery that cuts the nerves from the carotid bodies. Ventilation is measured while they breathe low-O₂ air or air with extra CO₂ (table). What best explains the results?
o: Carotid bodies drive the hypoxic response; central sensors drive most of the CO₂ response
Carotid bodies drive the CO₂ response; central sensors drive most of the response to hypoxia
The surgery damaged the medulla's breathing rhythm generator
The carotid bodies play no role in controlling breathing
e: After denervation, the response to low O₂ nearly disappears (200% → 105%), so it depends on the carotid bodies.
The CO₂ response stays large (300% → 250%), so most of it comes from the central chemoreceptors in the medulla.
w: Reversed; the hypoxic response vanished after denervation.
Normal breathing persisted with only partial CO₂ reduction, so the medulla works.
Losing the hypoxic response shows carotid bodies matter.

q: Three patients undergo a water deprivation test, and then each receives desmopressin (a synthetic ADH). The results are shown. Which patient most likely has nephrogenic diabetes insipidus?
o: Patient R, because desmopressin barely changes the urine
Patient Q, because desmopressin greatly concentrates the urine
Patient P, because the urine stays concentrated throughout
Patient Q, because the urine is dilute after deprivation
e: P concentrates urine normally when deprived of water.
Q can't concentrate on his own but responds to ADH: he makes no ADH (central DI).
R stays dilute even with ADH: his kidneys don't respond to it (nephrogenic DI).
w: Q's strong response to desmopressin means the kidneys work but no ADH is made, which is central diabetes insipidus.
Patient P concentrates urine normally during water deprivation, so P has no diabetes insipidus.
Dilute urine after deprivation fits both types, but Q then responds to desmopressin, which points to central, not nephrogenic, DI.

q: Serum samples from a sick patient are serially diluted and tested for antibody against a virus (+ = positive). The titer is the highest dilution that is still positive. What do the results show?
o: A 16-fold rise in titer, suggesting a current infection
A 4-fold drop in titer, suggesting a past infection
A 300-fold rise in titer, suggesting a current infection
No change in titer, since both samples were positive
e: Day 1 titer = 1:20; day 21 titer = 1:320.
320 ÷ 20 = 16, a 16-fold (four-dilution) rise. A rise of 4-fold or more between paired samples points to an active, current infection.
w: The titer rose from 1:20 to 1:320, so it is a 16-fold increase, not a drop.
Recheck: 320 ÷ 20.
Both samples were positive, but the highest positive dilution rose from 1:20 to 1:320, so the titer changed 16-fold.

q: The graph shows blood pressure along the systemic circulation. Where does pressure drop most steeply?
o: Across the arterioles
Across the large arteries
Across the large veins
Inside the aorta
e: Arterioles have the greatest resistance, so the biggest pressure drop occurs there.
Their smooth muscle adjusts resistance to control flow to organs.
w: Large arteries have low resistance, so pressure drops only a little across them; the steep drop is across the arterioles.
Large veins have low resistance, and pressure is already low by then, so little drop occurs there.
The aorta has very low resistance, so pressure barely falls inside it; the steepest drop is across the arterioles.

q: In the left ventricular pressure–volume loop shown, the loop runs counterclockwise from point 1. Which segment represents isovolumetric relaxation?
e: Isovolumetric means volume is constant: the two vertical segments.
At 3 the aortic valve closes; pressure then falls with all valves shut until the mitral valve opens at 4. (1 → 2 is isovolumetric contraction, 2 → 3 ejection, 4 → 1 filling.)
w: Segment 1 → 2 is isovolumetric contraction, when pressure rises with all valves closed before ejection begins.
Segment 2 → 3 is ejection, when volume falls as blood leaves through the open aortic valve.
Segment 4 → 1 is filling, when volume rises after the mitral valve opens, so volume is not constant.

q: In Gibson and Walk's visual cliff studies, most crawling infants (about 6–14 months old) would not cross onto the glass over the 'deep' side, even when their mothers called. Why can't this result alone prove that depth perception is innate?
o: The infants had months of visual experience before testing
The infants could feel the glass, so vision was irrelevant
The mothers' calls made the infants too anxious to move
Too few infants were tested to support any conclusion
e: Infants can't be tested until they can crawl, and by then they have had months to learn about depth.
So the study shows depth perception is present by crawling age, not that it was there at birth.
w: The visual cliff is covered by solid glass on both sides, so the infants' refusal reflected what they saw, not what they felt.
Mothers' calls were meant to encourage crossing; the problem with proving innateness is the infants' prior visual experience.
Not the issue.

q: A patient whose cochlear hair cells were destroyed by a toxic antibiotic receives a cochlear implant. The device restores some hearing because it:
o: Stimulates the auditory nerve directly with electrodes
Amplifies sound so the remaining hair cells respond
Replaces the small bones of the middle ear
Sends sound vibrations through the skull bones
e: Losing hair cells causes sensorineural hearing loss, so making sound louder doesn't help much.
The implant bypasses hair cells: electrodes along the cochlea stimulate auditory nerve fibers, with different positions signaling different pitches (place coding).
w: Hair cells are gone.
Not middle ear.
Not bone conduction.

q: After staring at a red image, a person sees a green afterimage on a white wall. Which theory best explains this?
o: Opponent-process theory
Trichromatic (Young–Helmholtz) theory
Place theory
Frequency theory
e: Red–green, blue–yellow and black–white work as opposing pairs.
Fatigue on one side produces the opposite color when it rebounds.
w: It doesn't explain afterimages.
Place theory explains how the cochlea codes pitch, so it says nothing about color afterimages.
Frequency theory explains pitch coding by neural firing rate in hearing, not color afterimages.

q: A cook barely notices adding 1 g of salt to 50 g of seasoning. According to Weber's law, how much must be added to 200 g to be noticed?
o: 4 g
1 g
2 g
8 g
e: The JND is a constant proportion: 1/50 = 2%.
w: The JND scales with size.
Recheck: 2% of 200 g.
Recheck: 2% of 200 g.

q: In a hearing test, a patient says "I hear a tone" on a trial when no tone was played. In signal detection theory, this response is a:
o: Hit
Miss
False alarm
Correct rejection
e: Signal absent + response "yes" = false alarm.
Signal present + "yes" = hit; signal present + "no" = miss.
Signal absent + "no" = correct rejection.
w: A hit needs a real signal.
A miss is saying no to a real signal.
Correct rejection is saying no to no signal.
t: Draw the 2 × 2 grid (signal present/absent × yes/no). It answers every version of this question.

q: The semicircular canals detect:
o: Rotational movement of the head
Linear acceleration and gravity
Sound frequency and loudness
Body position from muscle stretch
e: They're part of the vestibular system, which supports balance.
w: That's the otolith organs.
That's the cochlea.
Sensing body position from muscle stretch is proprioception, which uses muscle and joint receptors, not the semicircular canals.

q: In what order does a visual signal pass through the cells of the retina on its way to the brain?
o: Photoreceptors → bipolar cells → ganglion cells
Ganglion cells → bipolar cells → photoreceptors
Bipolar cells → photoreceptors → ganglion cells
Photoreceptors → ganglion cells → bipolar cells
e: Rods and cones transduce light, then signal bipolar cells, which signal ganglion cells.
Ganglion cell axons bundle into the optic nerve.
w: This order is reversed: light is transduced by photoreceptors first, and ganglion cells send the final output.
Bipolar cells cannot come first because only photoreceptors transduce light; bipolar cells sit between photoreceptors and ganglion cells.
Photoreceptors signal bipolar cells, not ganglion cells directly; bipolar cells are the middle layer.
t: Trap: light physically passes through the ganglion and bipolar layers first, but the neural SIGNAL starts at the photoreceptors.

q: A patient with a growing pituitary tumor keeps bumping into door frames on both sides, though his central vision is clear. The tumor presses upward on the middle of the optic chiasm. Which visual field loss is expected?
o: Loss of the outer (temporal) half of each eye's visual field
Complete blindness in one eye, while the other eye stays normal
Loss of the left half of the visual field in both eyes
Loss of the inner (nasal) half of each eye's visual field
e: At the optic chiasm, only fibers from the nasal (inner) half of each retina cross.
The nasal retina receives light from the temporal (outer) visual field, so pressing on the crossing fibers causes bitemporal hemianopia, or 'tunnel vision.'
w: Chiasm compression affects both eyes, not just one.
Left homonymous hemianopia comes from damage behind the chiasm (right optic tract).
Nasal fields come from temporal retina fibers, which don't cross.
t: Nasal retina sees the temporal field: retina and field are mirror images.

q: In a hearing test, a patient says 'yes' often, catching every real tone but also giving many false alarms. In signal detection terms, this person has:
o: A liberal response criterion
A conservative response criterion
Perfect sensitivity
No ability to hear
e: A liberal criterion means a willingness to say 'yes' even when unsure.
Sensitivity (d′) and response bias are separate.
w: They say 'yes' often.
False alarms show errors.
They hear tones.

q: A person can just barely tell that a 100 g weight is heavier when 2 g is added. According to Weber's law, about how much must be added to a 500 g weight to notice a difference?
o: 2 g
5 g
e: Weber's law: the just-noticeable difference (JND) is a constant fraction of the original stimulus.
Here the fraction is 2 g ÷ 100 g = 2%.
w: This ignores the proportion.
This uses 1%, not 2%.
This uses 10%, not 2%.
t: Weber's law is a proportion problem. Find the fraction first, then scale it.

q: A man lacks working medium-wavelength ('green') cones and confuses reds with greens, yet his vision is otherwise normal. Which theory does his condition most directly support?
o: Trichromatic theory
Opponent-process theory
Place theory
Gate control theory
e: Trichromatic (Young–Helmholtz) theory says color vision depends on three cone types.
Missing one type leaves only two (dichromacy), which predicts exactly this kind of color confusion.
w: Opponent-process theory explains afterimages and paired color channels, not color confusion from a missing cone type.
Place theory explains how the cochlea codes pitch, not color vision.
Gate control theory explains how pain signals are modulated in the spinal cord, not color vision.

q: Astronauts in orbit often report losing any sense of which way is 'down,' even though they can still feel when their heads rotate. Which vestibular signal is most changed in orbit?
o: Otolith signals about tilt relative to gravity
Semicircular canal signals about head rotation
Cochlear signals about sound frequency and pitch
Muscle spindle signals about stretch in the limbs
e: The otolith organs (utricle and saccule) sense linear acceleration and tilt by how gravity pulls on tiny crystals.
In free fall there is no steady gravitational pull to signal tilt, so the sense of 'down' is lost.
The semicircular canals sense rotation through fluid movement, which still works.
w: The astronauts can still feel head rotation, so the semicircular canals are still working.
The cochlea codes sound, not orientation.
Muscle spindles signal limb stretch, not the direction of gravity.

q: After a concussion, a football player cannot remember the 30 minutes before the hit, but his memories from the previous week and from childhood are intact. What does this pattern suggest?
o: His most recent memories had not yet been fully consolidated
He has anterograde amnesia caused by the surgical removal of his hippocampus
His older memories are held in sensory memory
His older memories are held in short-term memory
e: Losing memories from before an injury is retrograde amnesia.
Recent memories are lost first because consolidation into stable long-term storage takes time; older memories are more resistant.
w: That's new-memory loss.
Sensory memory lasts only seconds, so it cannot hold memories from last week or from childhood.
Short-term memory lasts only about 20–30 seconds, so it cannot hold week-old or childhood memories.

q: Children receiving chemotherapy are given an unusual-flavored candy just before each infusion. Later they avoid the candy but keep eating their usual foods. What best explains why the candy protects their normal diet?
o: Novel tastes become conditioned stimuli more easily than familiar ones
The candy is an unconditioned stimulus that cancels the drug's nausea
The children habituate to nausea, so no foods become aversive at all
Familiar foods are unconditioned stimuli and cannot become conditioned
e: Nausea after chemotherapy can create a taste aversion to recently eaten food.
Familiar foods condition less readily (latent inhibition), and a novel, salient taste overshadows them.
So the aversion attaches to the candy instead of the children's usual meals.
w: The candy does not reduce nausea; it becomes the target of the learned aversion.
The children do develop an aversion, to the candy, so no-aversion habituation doesn't fit.
Familiar foods can become conditioned stimuli; they simply condition less readily than novel tastes.

q: In the sea slug Aplysia, gentle touches to the siphon cause the gill to withdraw, but the response weakens with repetition. Recordings show the sensory neurons still fire to each touch. What most likely causes the weakening?
o: Sensory neurons release less transmitter onto motor neurons
Touch receptors on the siphon stop responding to repeated touches
The gill muscle becomes fatigued and can no longer contract fully
New synapses form between the sensory neurons and the motor neurons
e: The shrinking response to a repeated harmless stimulus is habituation.
Because the sensory neurons still fire, the change is at the synapse: each touch releases less transmitter.
w: Recordings show the sensory neurons still fire, so the receptors have not stopped responding.
Muscle fatigue is unlikely, since a strong new stimulus can restore the full response.
Forming new synapses would strengthen the response, not weaken it.

q: Participants verify 'A canary can sing' faster than 'A canary has skin.' According to Collins and Quillian's hierarchical network model of semantic memory, why?
o: 'Has skin' is stored at a more distant level (animal)
'Has skin' is actually a false statement about canaries
Shorter sentences are always verified faster
Singing is stored in procedural memory instead
e: The model stores each property at the most general level that it applies to: 'can sing' with canary, 'can fly' with bird, 'has skin' with animal.
Verifying 'has skin' requires moving up two levels in the network, which takes extra time.
w: "A canary has skin" is true; it takes longer because the property is stored at the more general animal level.
Sentence length is not the reason; the model explains the delay by distance in the semantic hierarchy.
Singing is a stored fact about canaries in semantic memory, not a procedural skill.

q:
Participants hear lists and repeat them back in order. Average span (items recalled correctly) is shown.
List typeAverage span
Single digits7
One-syllable words6
Five-syllable words3
Which conclusion fits best?
o: Span depends partly on how long items take to say
Span is fixed at exactly 7 items for any material
Longer words are stored in long-term memory instead
Five-syllable words are less familiar, so span is 0
e: Miller described a span of about 7 ± 2 items.
Here the span drops from 6 to 3 as words get longer, even though the number of items is what is counted.
So short-term memory capacity depends partly on how much can be rehearsed in a short time (the word-length effect).
w: Span varies from 3 to 7 here, so it is not fixed for all material.
Immediate ordered repetition relies on short-term memory, not long-term storage.
The span for five-syllable words is 3, not 0.

q: A teenager comes home after curfew, so his parents take away his car keys for a week, and he stops coming home late. This is:
o: Negative punishment
Negative reinforcement
Positive punishment
Extinction
e: Something desirable (car access) is REMOVED, so it is negative.
The late behavior DECREASES, so it is punishment.
w: Negative reinforcement removes something unpleasant to increase a behavior, but here a privilege is removed and lateness decreases.
Positive punishment adds an unpleasant consequence, while here something desirable (car keys) is taken away.
Extinction is withholding the reinforcer that maintained a behavior, not taking away an unrelated privilege as a consequence.
t: Positive/negative = add/remove; reinforcement/punishment = behavior goes up/down.

q: A child bitten by one dog becomes afraid of all dogs. This is:
o: Stimulus generalization
Stimulus discrimination
Extinction
Spontaneous recovery
e: The response spreads to stimuli similar to the original conditioned stimulus.
w: That's telling apart.
Extinction is the weakening of a conditioned response, not its spread from one dog to all dogs.
That's the response returning.

q: A factory worker is paid $5 for every 10 garments she finishes. Which reinforcement schedule is this?
o: Fixed-ratio
Fixed-interval
Variable-ratio
Variable-interval
e: Reinforcement comes after a set NUMBER of responses (10 garments), so it is a ratio schedule.
The number never changes, so it is fixed. Fixed-ratio schedules produce high response rates with short pauses after each reward.
w: A fixed-interval schedule rewards the first response after a set time, but this pay depends on the number of garments.
A variable-ratio schedule rewards after an unpredictable number of responses, while here it is always 10 garments.
A variable-interval schedule rewards after unpredictable time periods, while this pay depends on a fixed count.

q: While solving problems, participants rate every 15 seconds how close they feel to the answer. For algebra problems, ratings rise steadily before a solution. For riddle-like problems, ratings stay low and then jump just before the answer. What does this suggest about the riddle-like problems?
o: They are solved by insight, with no sense of gradual progress
They are solved by trial and error, with steady gradual progress
They are solved by following an algorithm one step at a time
They are solved by recalling the answer from a past experience
e: Steady gains in 'closeness' fit step-by-step solving.
Low ratings followed by a sudden jump fit insight: the solution comes all at once, as in Köhler's chimpanzee Sultan.
So the riddle-like problems are solved by insight.
w: Trial and error produces gradual improvement, which the riddle ratings do not show.
Following an algorithm would make people feel steadily closer to the answer.
Recalling a known answer would make it feel close from the start, not after a sudden jump.

q: A child loves video games but dislikes reading. His parents allow 30 minutes of gaming only after he reads for 30 minutes, and his reading time increases. Which principle explains this?
o: The Premack principle
Stimulus generalization
Classical conditioning
Latent learning
e: The Premack principle: a more preferred activity can reinforce a less preferred one.
Gaming (preferred) is made contingent on reading (less preferred), so reading increases.
w: Stimulus generalization is responding to stimuli that resemble a conditioned stimulus.
Reading is a voluntary behavior strengthened by its consequence, which is operant, not classical, conditioning.
Latent learning is learning that stays hidden until a reward appears, not using one activity to reward another.

q: Eyewitnesses who heard the word 'smashed' estimated higher car speeds than those who heard 'hit'. This illustrates:
o: The misinformation effect
Proactive interference
State-dependent memory
Flashbulb memory
e: Information after an event can change how the event is remembered.
w: That's old info blocking new.
That's internal state.
That's vivid memory.

q: Rats drank sweet water while each lick also triggered a flash of light and a click. Then one group was made ill by X-ray exposure, and another received foot shocks. Later, the ill rats avoided the sweet taste but not the light and click, while the shocked rats avoided the light and click but not the taste. What does this show?
o: Animals are biologically prepared to link certain cues to certain outcomes
Any stimulus can be paired equally well with any consequence, whatever its type
Taste aversions need many separate pairings before they appear
Rats cannot detect lights and sounds while they are drinking
e: If all pairings were equal, each group would avoid both the taste and the light-and-click.
Instead, taste was linked to illness and light-and-click to pain, so evolution has prepared some associations (Garcia and Koelling's finding).
w: Each cue paired best with one outcome; pairings weren't equal.
Garcia showed taste aversions can form after a single pairing.
Shocked rats avoided the light and click, so they detected them.
t: Taste goes with nausea; sights and sounds go with pain.

q: A sleep lab compares healthy 20-year-olds with healthy 70-year-olds. Which EEG difference is most likely?
o: The older adults show much less high-amplitude delta activity
The older adults show much more high-amplitude delta activity
The older adults show no REM sleep at all during the night
The two groups show the same amount of each stage across the night
e: High-amplitude, low-frequency delta waves mark stage N3 (slow-wave sleep).
N3 declines steeply with age, while lighter N1/N2 sleep and night awakenings increase.
w: Delta (N3) sleep decreases with age rather than increasing.
REM declines only modestly with age; healthy older adults still have REM periods.
Sleep architecture changes with age, most clearly the loss of N3.
t: Deep sleep is a young person's luxury: N3 shrinks with age.

q: A patient after a stroke speaks slowly in short, effortful phrases but understands what others say. Which brain area was most likely damaged?
o: Wernicke's area
Broca's area
Occipital lobe
Cerebellum
e: Broca's area (frontal lobe) is involved in speech production.
Damage causes non-fluent (Broca's) aphasia, with comprehension mostly spared.
Wernicke's aphasia is the opposite: fluent speech that makes little sense, with poor comprehension.
w: Wernicke's damage hurts comprehension.
The occipital lobe handles vision.
The cerebellum handles coordination.
t: Broca's = Broken speech. Wernicke's = Wordy but makes no sense.

q: A theorist argues that a gifted dancer, a skilled counselor and a math prodigy each show a different kind of intelligence that IQ tests miss. This view best matches:
o: Gardner's theory of multiple intelligences
Spearman's general intelligence (g) factor
Chomsky's language acquisition device
Cattell's fluid–crystallized distinction
e: Gardner proposed several separate intelligences, such as bodily-kinesthetic, interpersonal and logical-mathematical.
Spearman instead argued that one general factor (g) underlies performance on all mental tests.
w: One general factor.
Chomsky's language acquisition device is an innate capacity for grammar, not a theory of multiple intelligences.
Two types only.

q: In Piaget's three-mountain task, a 4-year-old is asked what a doll on the far side of a mountain model can see, and she describes her own view. This reflects:
o: Egocentrism in the preoperational stage
Missing object permanence in the sensorimotor stage
Failed conservation in the formal operational stage
Abstract reasoning in the concrete operational stage
e: Preoperational children (about ages 2–7) have trouble taking another person's point of view.
Describing her own view as the doll's shows egocentrism.
w: She has object permanence.
Conservation failure is a preoperational trait, and formal operational thinkers have long since mastered conservation.
Concrete operational children reason logically about concrete objects; they are not defined by abstract reasoning, and this child is egocentric.

q: A student who scrolls on her phone in bed until 1 a.m. has trouble falling asleep. Which explanation is best supported by research on circadian rhythms?
o: Bright, blue-rich light suppresses evening melatonin release
Screen light raises melatonin levels and then causes REM rebound later at night
Darkness signals the SCN to stop releasing melatonin
Phone use causes narcolepsy-like sleep attacks
e: Light-sensitive retinal ganglion cells, most responsive to blue light, signal the SCN.
The SCN then suppresses melatonin from the pineal gland, delaying the body's 'time to sleep' signal.
w: Light lowers melatonin.
Darkness raises it.
Narcolepsy is a neurological disorder of sudden sleep attacks, not trouble falling asleep after screen use.

q: A clinician reasons: 'All patients with this mutation develop the disease. This patient has the mutation. So this patient will develop the disease.' This is:
o: Deductive reasoning
Inductive reasoning
The availability heuristic
Belief perseverance
e: Deductive reasoning moves from general premises to a specific, logically certain conclusion.
Inductive reasoning goes the other way, building a general rule from specific cases.
w: Specific to general.
Not a heuristic.
Belief perseverance is clinging to a belief after it is discredited, not drawing a certain conclusion from general premises.

q: A 19-year-old falls asleep in class several times a day and sometimes collapses with weak knees when she laughs. In a sleep lab she enters REM within 5 minutes of falling asleep. Which diagnosis and mechanism fit best?
o: Narcolepsy, linked to loss of orexin-producing neurons
Obstructive sleep apnea, from repeated airway collapse
Insomnia disorder, from heightened arousal at night
REM sleep behavior disorder, from loss of REM paralysis
e: Daytime sleep attacks, emotion-triggered weakness (cataplexy) and REM soon after sleep onset are signs of narcolepsy.
Narcolepsy type 1 is linked to loss of hypothalamic neurons that make orexin (hypocretin).
w: Sleep apnea causes daytime sleepiness, but not cataplexy or REM right at sleep onset.
Insomnia involves trouble getting or staying asleep, not sudden sleep attacks.
REM sleep behavior disorder involves acting out dreams, not cataplexy while awake.

q: Which drug class slows central nervous system activity?
o: Depressants (like alcohol and benzodiazepines)
Stimulants (like cocaine and amphetamines)
Hallucinogens (like LSD and psilocybin)
Mild stimulants (like caffeine and nicotine)
e: Depressants often enhance GABA activity.
w: These speed it up.
These alter perception.
These speed it up.

q: Chomsky's sentence 'Colorless green ideas sleep furiously' sounds grammatical to English speakers even though it means nothing. It shows that:
o: Syntax can be judged separately from meaning
Meaning is needed to judge whether grammar is correct
Phonemes carry the meaning of whole sentences
Language determines how speakers perceive colors
e: Syntax is the set of rules for combining words; semantics is meaning.
The sentence follows English word-order rules but makes no sense, so people can judge grammar without meaning.
w: The sentence shows grammar can be judged without meaning, so meaning is not needed.
Phonemes are sounds.
The sentence demonstrates syntax versus meaning; it has nothing to do with language shaping color perception.

q: According to the activation-synthesis hypothesis, dreams are:
o: The brain's attempt to interpret random neural activity in REM
Disguised expressions of unconscious wishes and conflicts
A process for consolidating memories formed during the previous day
Mental rehearsal of threats to prepare for waking life
e: Freud's theory, by contrast, sees dreams as disguised wishes.
w: Dreams as disguised unconscious wishes is Freud's psychoanalytic view, not activation-synthesis.
That's memory consolidation.
That's threat simulation.

q: A volunteer's EEG shows alpha waves giving way to low-amplitude theta waves, with slow, rolling eye movements. If she is woken at this moment, what is she most likely to say?
o: That she was only dozing or not asleep at all
That she was having a long, vivid, story-like dream
Nothing clear, since she is groggy and confused
That she was paralyzed and couldn't move her arms
e: Theta waves with slow eye movements mark stage N1, the lightest sleep.
People woken from N1 often deny having been asleep.
w: Long, vivid dreams are typical of REM sleep.
Grogginess and confusion on waking are typical of N3 (slow-wave sleep).
Muscle paralysis (atonia) is a feature of REM sleep.

q: According to Piaget, a child who understands that pouring water into a taller glass doesn't change its amount has reached the:
o: Concrete operational stage
Sensorimotor stage
Preoperational stage
Formal operational stage
e: Conservation develops around ages 7–11.
w: The sensorimotor stage (birth to about age 2) centers on object permanence, not conservation.
No conservation yet.
The formal operational stage adds abstract and hypothetical reasoning; conservation is already mastered earlier.

q: In an fMRI study, participants look at a flickering black-and-white checkerboard, then at a plain gray screen. Which region would show the largest increase in activity during the checkerboard?
o: The occipital lobe, around the calcarine sulcus
The frontal lobe, in front of the central sulcus
The temporal lobe, along the superior temporal gyrus
The parietal lobe, just behind the central sulcus
e: A high-contrast flickering pattern strongly drives the primary visual cortex.
The primary visual cortex lies in the occipital lobe along the calcarine sulcus.
w: The area just in front of the central sulcus is the primary motor cortex, which controls movement.
The superior temporal gyrus contains the primary auditory cortex.
The area just behind the central sulcus is the primary somatosensory cortex, which processes touch.

q: A patient has trouble recognizing familiar faces but can recognize people by their voices. Damage to which area is most likely?
o: The fusiform gyrus (temporal–occipital region)
Broca's area (left inferior frontal lobe region)
The hippocampus (medial temporal lobe)
The somatosensory cortex (parietal lobe)
e: This condition is called prosopagnosia.
The fusiform face area is specialized for face recognition.
w: Broca's area governs speech production.
The hippocampus forms new memories, not face perception.
Somatosensory cortex processes touch.

q: Stroking the sole of a 3-month-old's foot makes her big toe extend upward and her other toes fan out (the Babinski sign). If an adult showed this same response, it would most likely indicate:
o: Damage to the motor pathway from the brain
A normal, fully mature spinal reflex
Overactive pain receptors in the foot
Damage limited to receptors in the skin
e: In infants the corticospinal (motor) tracts are still maturing, so the Babinski sign is normal.
In healthy adults the toes curl downward; an upward big toe signals damage to the motor pathway from the brain (upper motor neurons).
w: Not in adults.
Not pain receptors.
The Babinski sign reflects damage to the motor pathway from the brain, not damage limited to skin receptors.
t: Babinski: normal in babies, a red flag in adults.

q: Adoption studies are useful in behavioral genetics because they:
o: Separate genes (from biological parents) from environment (from adoptive parents)
Show that the shared rearing environment is the main source of traits
Hold genes constant by studying only adopted identical twin pairs
Remove all environmental effects so that genetic effects can be measured directly
e: Comparing adopted children to both sets of parents helps tease apart nature and nurture.
w: They test genes vs. environment.
That's twin studies.
Environment still acts.

q: Which brain imaging technique best shows which brain regions are active during a task?
o: Functional MRI (fMRI)
Standard X-ray
CT scan
Structural MRI only
e: fMRI tracks changes in blood oxygen (BOLD signal) that follow neural activity.
CT and structural MRI mainly show anatomy.
w: Shows bone, not activity.
A CT scan shows structural anatomy using X-rays; it does not track which regions are active during a task.
Shows anatomy only.

q: A cook touches a hot pan and jerks her hand away before she feels any pain. Why does the movement come before the sensation?
o: The withdrawal reflex loops through the spinal cord without waiting for the brain
Pain receptors in the skin also contract the arm muscles directly, without any synapse
The brain decides to move first and creates the pain afterward
Pain signals travel faster than motor signals to the arm
e: In a withdrawal reflex, sensory neurons enter the spinal cord, where interneurons immediately activate the motor neurons that pull the arm away.
The pain signal has to travel up to the brain and be processed before it is felt, which takes longer. So the hand is already moving by the time she notices the pain.
w: Receptors don't contract muscle.
Brain isn't first.
Pain fibers actually conduct more slowly than motor fibers; the hand moves first because the reflex loops through the spinal cord without waiting for the brain.
t: Reflexes are wired in the spinal cord; feeling needs the brain.

q: Brain scans of experienced London taxi drivers, who memorize the city's complex street layout, showed larger posterior hippocampi than in controls, and size increased with years on the job. This best supports:
o: Experience-driven plasticity in a region used for spatial memory
Hippocampal size is fixed by genes before adulthood and cannot change
The hippocampus controls the motor skills of driving
Spatial memory is stored mainly in the cerebellum
e: The hippocampus is important for spatial navigation and memory.
Because size grew with years of driving, the finding suggests that heavy use can reshape brain structure (neuroplasticity), although the study is correlational.
w: It grew with use.
The hippocampus supports spatial memory for navigation; the motor skills of driving rely on other areas.
The study found that the hippocampus, not the cerebellum, was larger with spatial experience.

q: Neurons in the locus coeruleus of the pons project widely through the brain and become very active during alertness and stress. Which neurotransmitter do they mainly release?
o: Norepinephrine
Dopamine
Acetylcholine
Serotonin (5-HT)
e: The locus coeruleus is the brain's main source of norepinephrine, which raises arousal and vigilance.
For comparison: raphe nuclei → serotonin; substantia nigra and VTA → dopamine.
w: Dopamine comes mainly from the substantia nigra and VTA, not the locus coeruleus.
Acetylcholine in the brain comes mainly from the basal forebrain, not the locus coeruleus.
Serotonin comes mainly from the raphe nuclei, not the locus coeruleus.
t: Locus coeruleus = 'blue spot' = norepinephrine alarm center.

q: During surgery, a patient receives a drug that blocks only the muscle-type nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction. Which function would be lost while the drug acts?
o: Voluntary movement of the limbs
Speeding of the heart during stress
Constriction of the pupils in bright light
Peristalsis of the small intestine
e: The neuromuscular junction is where somatic motor neurons release acetylcholine onto skeletal muscle.
Blocking it paralyzes voluntary skeletal muscle.
Autonomic targets such as heart, pupils and gut are not served by this synapse.
w: Heart rate is controlled by the autonomic nervous system, which does not use the neuromuscular junction.
Pupil constriction is a parasympathetic reflex acting on smooth muscle.
Peristalsis is driven by the enteric and autonomic systems acting on smooth muscle.

q: A patient has damage to the reticular formation in the brainstem. Which problem is most likely?
o: Impaired wakefulness and arousal, possibly coma
Inability to recognize familiar faces
Inability to form new explicit memories of events
Loss of fine coordination of movement
e: The reticular formation (reticular activating system) projects through the thalamus to the cortex and keeps the brain alert.
Damage can reduce arousal and even cause coma. Faces depend on the fusiform gyrus, new memories on the hippocampus and coordination on the cerebellum.
w: Recognizing familiar faces depends on the fusiform gyrus, not the brainstem reticular formation.
Forming new explicit memories depends on the hippocampus, not the reticular formation.
Fine coordination of movement depends on the cerebellum, not the reticular formation.

q: In a long-term New Zealand study, Caspi and colleagues reported that people carrying one or two short versions of a serotonin transporter gene variant were more likely to become depressed after many stressful life events than people with two long versions. With few stressful events, depression rates were similar. What does this pattern illustrate?
o: A gene–environment interaction
A purely genetic cause of depression
A purely environmental cause of depression
Synaptic pruning during adolescence
e: The gene variant mattered mainly when stress was high, and stress mattered more for people with the short variant.
When the effect of one factor depends on the level of another, that is an interaction. (Later attempts to replicate this specific finding have had mixed results.)
w: Depression rose mainly with many stressful events, so stress mattered and the cause was not purely genetic.
The gene variant changed how strongly stress affected depression, so the cause was not purely environmental.
Synaptic pruning is removing unused connections during development, not a gene effect that depends on stress.

q: Researchers apply transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) over a volunteer's left motor cortex, and her right thumb twitches. What key advantage does TMS have over fMRI for studying brain function?
o: It alters brain activity directly, so it can test causation
It measures blood flow more precisely than fMRI
It records single neurons directly through the intact skull
It gives detailed images of brain structure
e: fMRI shows which areas are active during a task, which is correlational.
TMS briefly excites or disrupts a cortical area; if behavior changes, that area plays a causal role.
w: Doesn't measure flow.
Not single neurons.
TMS stimulates or disrupts brain activity; it does not produce detailed images of brain structure.

q: In Selye's general adaptation syndrome, which stage comes after alarm?
o: Resistance
Exhaustion
Recovery
Denial
e: Alarm → resistance → exhaustion.
Long-term stress depletes the body's resources.
w: Exhaustion is the final stage of Selye's syndrome, coming after resistance rather than directly after alarm.
Not a stage.
Not a stage.

q: Which brain structure, besides the amygdala, is especially important in regulating emotion through planning and reasoning?
o: Prefrontal cortex
Occipital lobe
Cerebellum
Medulla
e: The prefrontal cortex helps control emotional reactions and impulses.
w: The occipital lobe processes vision, not emotion regulation through planning and reasoning.
The cerebellum coordinates movement and balance rather than regulating emotion through reasoning.
The medulla controls vital functions like breathing and heart rate, not emotional regulation.

q: The Cannon–Bard theory says that:
o: Arousal and emotional experience occur simultaneously and independently
Emotional experience follows from the perception of bodily arousal
Emotion results from arousal plus a cognitive label for it
Emotion begins with a cognitive appraisal before any arousal
e: The thalamus sends signals to the cortex and body at once.
w: Emotion following the perception of bodily arousal is the James–Lange theory, not Cannon–Bard.
Arousal plus a cognitive label is the Schachter–Singer two-factor theory.
Cognitive appraisal coming before arousal is Lazarus's appraisal theory, not Cannon–Bard.

q: A patient with an incurable illness cannot change her diagnosis, so she practices meditation, journals and focuses on the meaning she finds in her family. This is an example of:
o: Emotion-focused coping
Problem-focused coping
Displacement
Approach–avoidance conflict
e: Emotion-focused coping manages the emotional response to a stressor rather than changing the stressor itself.
It is especially useful when the stressor cannot be controlled, as with an incurable diagnosis.
w: Changing the stressor.
Displacement redirects an impulse toward a safer target, while meditation and journaling manage emotion directly.
Not a conflict.

q: A goose sees an egg outside its nest and rolls it back with the underside of its bill. If a researcher removes the egg partway, the goose completes the rolling motion anyway. Which view of motivation does this best support?
o: Instinct theory: inborn action patterns run to completion
Incentive theory: the egg is a reward that pulls behavior
Drive-reduction theory: the goose acts to reduce hunger
Arousal theory: the goose seeks an optimal level of stimulation
e: The behavior is unlearned and, once triggered, runs to the end even without the egg.
This is a fixed action pattern, the kind of inborn behavior instinct theory uses to explain motivation.
w: If the egg itself were pulling the behavior, removing it would stop the motion.
Rolling an egg does not reduce a biological need such as hunger.
The goose is not seeking stimulation; it is carrying out a fixed sequence.

q: A researcher studying fear records a participant's skin conductance, codes her facial expressions from video, and asks her to rate how afraid she feels. Which emotion components do these three measures target, in order?
o: Physiological, behavioral, cognitive
Behavioral, physiological, cognitive
Cognitive, behavioral, physiological
Physiological, cognitive, behavioral
e: Skin conductance measures bodily arousal (physiological).
Facial expression is observable action (behavioral).
Rating one's own fear reflects subjective appraisal and experience (cognitive).
w: Skin conductance is a bodily response, so it is physiological, not behavioral.
