q:
Passage: The biologist described a wetland as a filter, not because it physically screens out every contaminant, but because microbial and chemical processes transform or trap many substances before water reaches a river.

In context, “filter” is best understood as:
o: A metaphor for several contaminant-removal processes
An explanation of how water evaporates from the wetland only
A mechanical mesh installed underground
A device that removes every chemical
e: The passage explicitly treats filtration as a broader functional analogy.
w: Evaporation isn't mentioned.
There's no physical mesh.
The passage says it doesn't remove everything.

q:
Passage: In the eighteenth century, novels were widely condemned as a frivolous and even dangerous pastime, especially for young readers. Today, schools assign novels as serious reading and worry instead about how much time students spend playing video games.

Which conclusion is best supported by the passage?
o: Judgments about which pastimes are harmful can shift over time
Video games will be assigned as school reading within a century
Eighteenth-century novels were lower in quality than modern ones
Young readers have always preferred novels to any other pastime
e: The passage shows one pastime moving from condemned to assigned while worry shifts to a new one.
The video-game prediction goes too far: the passage makes no prediction.
w: The passage only contrasts past and present attitudes; it makes no prediction about video games being assigned in the future.
The passage says novels were condemned as frivolous, not that they were worse than modern novels; quality is never compared.
The passage says nothing about what young readers preferred, only how adults judged novels and video games.

q:
Passage: A critic argues that a poet's late work is weaker than her early work because she wrote it after moving to a large city, far from the coastal landscapes that inspired her first poems.

The critic's argument assumes that:
o: The landscape, rather than other life changes, was central to the early poems' strength
The poet's late work was written more quickly than her early work had been
Readers generally prefer poems about nature to poems about cities and crowds
Poets who stay in one place their whole lives tend to write their best work late in life
e: The critic links the decline to the move; that only works if the landscape, and not aging, illness or other changes, drove the early quality.
w: Speed isn't the issue.
Reader taste isn't needed.
The critic's argument is about one poet's move away from her inspiring landscape; it needs no claim about poets who never move.

q:
Passage: An economist observes that state lotteries are often promoted as a way to fund schools. In several states, she notes, legislatures then cut regular school budgets by roughly the amount the lottery raised, so schools gained little. 'The money is real,' she writes, 'but the promise attached to it often is not.'

The economist's attitude toward the claim that lotteries fund schools is best described as:
o: Skeptical that the promise brings schools any real gain
Certain that lotteries raise no money for anything
Enthusiastic about lotteries as a reliable funding source
Neutral, since she reaches no conclusion about schools
e: 'The promise … often is not [real]' signals skepticism about the benefit to schools.
The 'raise no money for anything' option is too extreme: she says 'The money is real.'
w: Too extreme: she writes that 'the money is real'; her doubt is about whether schools actually gain from it.
She shows legislatures cutting school budgets by the lottery amount, so she is doubtful, not enthusiastic.
She does reach a conclusion: the promise attached to lottery money 'often is not' real for schools.

q:
Passage: An engineer argues that adding more lanes to a highway rarely reduces traffic for long, because the new capacity encourages more people to drive until congestion returns.

Which situation is most similar to the engineer's argument?
o: A hospital adds parking, and more people drive there until it fills
A road adds a toll, and drivers switch to other routes
A school hires more teachers, and class sizes shrink and stay small permanently
A city adds buses, and rush-hour traffic briefly eases
e: Added capacity attracts more use, cancelling the benefit.
w: Traffic diverts, not grows.
The engineer's point is that added capacity draws new use until the benefit vanishes; here the gain lasts permanently.
Only brief relief.

q:
Passage: A biographer notes that a diarist's surviving journals contain no entries for the two years in which he was most active in politics. Pages appear to have been cut from the bound volumes, and the entries just before and after the gap are unusually brief.

Which conclusion is best supported by the passage?
o: Someone may have removed the diarist's records of his political years
The diarist stopped keeping a journal during his political career
The diarist's political activities during those years were illegal
The biographer cut out those pages in order to protect the diarist's good name
e: Pages 'cut from the bound volumes' point to removal of entries that once existed.
The 'stopped keeping a journal' option fits the gap but ignores the cut pages; the 'illegal' option goes beyond anything stated.
w: Ignores cut pages.
Goes beyond the text.
The passage never says who cut the pages, so naming the biographer as the culprit goes beyond the text.

q:
Passage: Many architects praise open-plan offices for encouraging collaboration. Studies, however, have found that workers in such offices often send more emails and talk face to face less. The walls came down, but people built new ones out of headphones and screens.

The final sentence mainly serves to:
o: Restate the finding as an image of workers creating their own barriers
Introduce new evidence that open offices really do increase teamwork after all
Argue that headphones and screens should be banned from workplaces
Concede that the architects' original praise was largely justified
e: The 'new walls' are a figurative summary of the study: people withdrew into email and headphones.
No new data or policy is offered in that sentence.
w: Not new evidence.
No ban proposed.
Not a concession.

q:
Passage: A linguist notes that every generation complains that young people are ruining the language. Yet, she observes, languages have always changed, and the 'errors' of one century are often the standard grammar of the next.

The linguist's attitude toward complaints about young people's language is best described as:
o: Skeptical
Strongly supportive
Fearful
Indifferent to language
e: She suggests the complaints are historically common and often mistaken.
w: She questions them.
She isn't afraid.
She cares about language.

q:
Passage: A literary scholar observes that readers in different decades have taken a famous short poem to be about war, about lost love and about religious doubt. Rather than concluding that the poem means nothing, she argues that its compressed images are what let each generation find its own concerns in it.

The scholar would most likely agree that:
o: A poem's openness to many readings can help explain its lasting appeal
The poem has no real meaning, since readers disagree about its subject
Only the poem's earliest readers understood what it was actually about
Compressed images make poems harder to enjoy for most modern readers
e: She ties the poem's survival across generations to images that invite new readings.
She explicitly rejects 'the poem means nothing.'
w: She rejects this.
The scholar treats each generation's reading as a valid response to the poem; she never privileges the earliest readers.
She credits the compressed images with letting each generation find its own concerns, the opposite of making poems harder to enjoy.

q:
Passage: A linguist argues that a language's lack of a single word for a concept does not stop its speakers from thinking about that concept. Speakers, she says, simply describe it with a longer phrase when they need to.

Which finding would most STRENGTHEN the linguist's argument?
o: Speakers of a language with no word for 'jealousy' readily spot it in stories
Some languages have many separate words for different kinds of falling snow
Languages often borrow useful words from the languages of their neighbors
Speakers of most languages tend to prefer short words over longer phrases
e: Recognizing a concept that has no single word shows the concept is still available to thought.
The snow example concerns having many words, not lacking one.
w: Many words, not none.
Borrowing words from neighbors is about how vocabulary grows, not whether speakers can think about a concept that lacks a word.
A preference for short words does not show whether speakers without a word can still think about the concept.

q:
Passage: A historian argues that the printing press spread new religious ideas quickly not only because books became cheaper, but because short, inexpensive pamphlets could be printed overnight and passed hand to hand before authorities had time to respond.

Based on this reasoning, which feature would most help a new idea spread?
o: A format that is quick to produce and easy to share before it can be stopped
A long and costly volume carrying the official approval of the authorities
A single handwritten manuscript kept safely in one well-guarded library
A formal public decree read aloud to the population once every year
e: The historian stresses speed and hand-to-hand sharing that outpaced suppression.
w: Slow and approved.
A single manuscript locked in one library cannot be passed hand to hand, the feature the historian says drove the spread.
A once-a-year official decree is slow and controlled by authorities, the opposite of overnight pamphlets that outran them.

q:
Passage: A music historian argues that the slow tempo of a famous symphony's second movement in modern concerts is a twentieth-century habit rather than the composer's intention. She points to the composer's own metronome markings, which call for a much faster pace.

Which finding would most STRENGTHEN the historian's argument?
o: Reviews of the premiere describe the second movement as brisk and lively
Surveys show that modern audiences strongly prefer the slower tempo
Dozens of conductors have recorded the symphony over the past century
Metronomes of the composer's era were often poorly calibrated mechanical devices
e: Independent evidence that the original performance was fast supports the markings.
Faulty metronomes would weaken the argument by casting doubt on her key evidence.
w: Taste isn't intent.
Doesn't show tempo.
Poorly calibrated metronomes would cast doubt on the composer's markings, the historian's key evidence, so this weakens her case.

q:
Passage: A labor economist argues that raising the wages of home health aides could partly pay for itself. Agencies now lose many aides each year, she notes, and every departure means recruiting and training a replacement, costs that would shrink if better pay kept aides in their jobs.

Which situation follows the same reasoning as the economist's argument?
o: A restaurant pays cooks more and saves on the cost of constantly hiring new cooks
A restaurant cuts cooks' pay and saves money until several of them decide to quit
A restaurant raises menu prices to cover the higher wages it has to pay its cooks
A restaurant hires more cooks so that each one can work fewer hours every week
e: The pattern is a higher wage offset by lower turnover costs; the restaurant case repeats it.
The 'raises menu prices' option pays for higher wages by charging customers, not by savings from retention.
w: That's cutting pay and losing workers, the opposite pattern.
Covering wages by raising prices isn't savings from retention.
Hiring more cooks increases staffing, not savings from lower turnover.

q:
Passage: A historian argues that literacy was widespread among eighteenth-century artisans, citing wills in which many of them left books to their heirs. A critic replies that owning books is not the same as reading them, since books were also valued as property and as signs of respectability.

The critic's reply challenges the historian's argument by:
o: Suggesting the evidence fits another explanation besides literacy
Denying that artisans of the period ever owned any books at all
Arguing that the wills were forged long after the artisans died
Claiming that artisans were wealthier than the historian assumes
e: The critic accepts that artisans owned books but offers another reason they might have: property and respectability.
The 'never owned any books' option contradicts the critic, who grants the ownership and disputes only what it shows.
w: Critic grants ownership.
The critic never questions the wills themselves; the reply accepts the book ownership and disputes what it shows.
The critic's point is about why artisans might own books, not how wealthy they were.

q:
Passage: A director argues that staging old plays in their original pronunciation cannot let audiences hear them as first audiences did, since today's listeners hear the accent as strange where the original audiences heard it as ordinary. Still, she favors such productions, because they restore rhymes and puns that modern pronunciation hides.

The director's reasons for favoring these productions imply that:
o: A performance can have value without recreating the original audience's experience
Modern audiences cannot enjoy old plays performed with modern pronunciation
The rhymes and puns are the most important features of these old plays
Original pronunciation makes old plays easier for modern listeners to follow and enjoy
e: She denies that such productions recreate the first audiences' hearing, yet still favors them for restoring rhymes and puns, so their value must lie elsewhere.
The 'most important features' option overstates her claim; she names rhymes and puns as a reason, not as the chief value of the plays.
w: She says nothing about modern pronunciation preventing enjoyment.
Overstates her claim; rhymes and puns are a reason, not the chief value.
She says the accent sounds strange to modern ears, not easier to follow.

q:
Passage: A philosopher contends that a fair rule should apply equally to people in similar circumstances. She adds that equality of application does not imply ignoring relevant differences between situations.

Which policy best reflects the philosopher’s position?
o: Apply the same criteria while accounting for relevant circumstances
Give every person identical outcomes regardless of their circumstances or needs
Ignore all contextual evidence
Create different rules for each individual without reasons
e: Fair application can be uniform in principle without treating meaningfully different situations as identical.
w: She doesn't call for identical outcomes.
She says relevant differences matter.
She wants rules applied equally.

q:
Passage: A historian argues that the canal-building boom of the early nineteenth century is usually remembered as a failure because railroads replaced canals within a few decades. But the canals, she notes, trained a generation of engineers, created the first large construction firms and taught investors how to fund huge public works, lessons the railroads then put to use.

The historian's central claim is that:
o: Canals mattered for the skills and institutions they passed on to railroads
Canals moved freight more efficiently than the railroads that replaced them
Railroads failed because they depended too heavily on lessons from canals
Investors lost interest in funding public works after the canals declined
e: The 'But' sentence lists what canals left behind and says railroads 'put [it] to use.'
The efficiency option is out of scope: the passage never compares freight performance.
w: The passage never compares how well canals and railroads moved freight; it stresses the skills and firms canals left behind.
The historian says railroads put the canals' lessons to use, not that relying on them made railroads fail.
The passage says canals taught investors how to fund huge public works, not that investors lost interest afterward.

q:
Passage: A philosopher grants that nostalgia is a natural response to change and usually harmless. But she warns that nostalgia edits as it remembers, keeping a past era's comforts while discarding its hardships, and that a politics built on it promises a return to a place that never existed.

The philosopher's attitude toward nostalgia is best described as:
o: Sympathetic to it as a feeling, but wary of it as a guide to action
Wholly hostile to nostalgia in every one of the many forms it can take
Convinced that the past really was better than the present
Unconcerned about what influence nostalgia has on politics
e: 'Natural' and 'usually harmless' show sympathy; the warning about a politics built on nostalgia shows wariness.
The 'wholly hostile' option ignores the opening concession.
w: Ignores the concession.
Not her view.
She warns about it.

q:
Passage: A museum replaced chronological displays with thematic rooms. Visitors reported finding connections among distant cultures, but some said it became harder to understand how ideas changed over time. The curator argued that neither layout was neutral: each invites a different kind of comparison.

What is the passage’s central claim?
o: Exhibition organization shapes interpretation
Thematic displays are always superior
Visitors dislike all museums
Chronological displays contain fewer objects
e: The curator emphasizes that both arrangements frame comparisons differently.
w: The passage doesn't rank the layouts.
Visitors found connections; they didn't dislike museums.
Object counts aren't discussed.

q:
Passage: A historian of mapmaking notes that medieval world maps often placed Jerusalem at the center and filled distant regions with monsters. Modern viewers call these maps inaccurate, but she argues they were never meant for travel; they were diagrams of a moral and religious world, and judged by that purpose they were carefully made.

What is the historian's main point?
o: Medieval maps should be judged by the purpose they were made to serve
Medieval mapmakers were more skilled at navigation than modern mapmakers
Medieval maps were more accurate than the maps people use today
Modern viewers dislike the religious imagery found in medieval art
e: 'Judged by that purpose they were carefully made' is the conclusion; the maps were 'never meant for travel.'
w: The historian never compares navigation skill; she says the maps were never meant for travel at all.
Not more accurate.
Not her claim.

q:
Passage: A demographer notes that in several European regions birth rates began falling decades before modern contraceptives were available. She concludes that the decision to have fewer children came first, and that new methods mostly made an existing choice easier.

Which statement can be most reasonably inferred from the passage?
o: Families found ways to limit births even before modern contraceptives existed
Modern contraceptives had no effect at all on European birth rates
Birth rates fell first in the regions where modern contraceptives were invented
European families wanted more children once contraceptives became common
e: If birth rates fell before modern methods, people must have limited births some other way.
The 'no effect at all' option is too extreme; she says new methods made the choice 'easier.'
w: Too extreme: she says new methods made an existing choice 'easier,' which implies they had some effect.
The passage never says where modern contraceptives were invented or links that to where birth rates fell first.
The passage says families had already chosen fewer children; nothing suggests they wanted more once contraceptives arrived.

q:
Passage: A political scientist argues that a state's decision to mail ballots to every registered voter raised turnout. He notes that turnout rose eight percentage points in the first election after the change.

Which finding would most weaken the argument?
o: Turnout rose by a similar amount that year in neighboring states that did not mail ballots
Most voters in the state returned their ballots by mail rather than voting in person
Turnout among older voters in the state rose much more than turnout among younger voters
The state had relied only on in-person voting for several decades before the change
e: A similar rise without the policy suggests something else, such as a high-interest election, explains the increase.
How voters returned ballots doesn't show whether the policy changed how many voted.
w: Not about turnout.
Not about the policy.
How long the state used in-person voting does not show whether mailing ballots caused the eight-point rise.

q:
Passage: An author argues that early photography changed painting. Since cameras could record realistic detail cheaply, painters were freed to explore color, emotion and abstraction instead of exact likeness.

Which development would the author's reasoning most likely predict?
o: Some artists will focus on what AI image tools do poorly
Artists will compete with AI tools on exact detail
AI images will become more abstract than painting
Artists will copy AI images exactly
e: New technology that takes over one task pushes artists toward others.
w: They'd move away from what the tool does well.
The author's reasoning is about how artists respond to a new tool, not about how the tool's own output will change.
They'd move away from copying.

q:
Passage: A historian argues that hospitals in the nineteenth century became safer not mainly because of new medicines but because of cleaner water, better ventilation and handwashing. She notes that death rates fell in several hospitals before any new drugs were introduced.

Which statement best expresses the historian's claim?
o: Hygiene, more than medicine, made hospitals safer
New medicines made hospitals safer
Drugs and hygiene contributed equally to safety
Death rates fell only after new drugs arrived
e: The passage contrasts hygiene with medicines and favors hygiene.
w: She favors hygiene.
She favors hygiene.
Deaths fell before new drugs.

q:
Passage: A critic argues that a novel’s fragmented timeline initially confuses readers but eventually encourages them to piece together the narrator’s memories. According to the critic, the difficulty is therefore part of the novel’s artistic method.

Which description best captures the critic’s attitude?
o: Unqualified rejection of the novel
Qualified approval of the narrative difficulty
Concern only about printing costs
Indifference to literary style and narrative structure
e: The critic recognizes initial confusion but interprets it as purposeful.
w: The critic approves.
Costs aren't discussed.
The critic cares about style.

q:
Passage: A city council found that building a bridge shortened commute times. Yet, a year later, average travel times were nearly unchanged because more commuters chose to drive. Officials described this outcome as an unintended result of increased road capacity.

Which new observation most supports the officials’ explanation?
o: Vehicle counts rose substantially after the bridge opened
The city population declined slightly after the bridge opened
Bus ridership on the bridge route rose after it opened
Commute times fell sharply in the first month after opening
e: More cars using the roads is consistent with induced driving demand offsetting time savings.
w: Fewer people would ease traffic.
More bus use wouldn't explain more driving.
An early drop doesn't explain later traffic.

q:
Passage: A study found that students who took handwritten notes remembered more than those who typed. The authors suggest that writing by hand forces students to summarize, since they cannot write as fast as a lecturer speaks.

Which finding would most strengthen the authors' explanation?
o: Typists told to summarize remembered as much as handwriters
Most students said they preferred taking notes on laptops
Handwritten notes were longer than typed notes
Typed notes contained more spelling and grammar errors
e: If summarizing is the key, typing with summarizing should work equally well.
w: Preference isn't the mechanism.
Length doesn't show summarizing.
Errors aren't the mechanism.

q:
Passage: The mayor claims that the new bike lanes reduced traffic accidents, since accidents fell 20% in the year after they opened. A council member notes that the same year, the city also lowered speed limits citywide.

The council member's point mainly suggests that:
o: Another change could explain the drop in accidents
Bike lanes actually increased the number of accidents
Lower speed limits rarely change accident rates
The accident statistics were probably recorded incorrectly
e: A second change is a possible confounding explanation.
w: The council member offers another cause for the drop; nothing suggests bike lanes raised accidents.
The council member implies speed limits might explain the drop, the opposite of saying they rarely matter.
The council member questions the cause of the 20% drop, not whether the accident numbers were recorded correctly.

q:
Passage: A reviewer praises a documentary for presenting both farmers and environmental groups fairly, but faults it for never asking consumers why they buy cheap food.

The reviewer's overall attitude toward the documentary is:
o: Generally positive, with a specific criticism
Entirely negative
Entirely uncritical
Mostly critical, with only minor praise for the film
e: Praise followed by 'but faults it' shows a mixed but mostly favorable view.
w: The reviewer praises the film for presenting farmers and environmental groups fairly, so the view is not entirely negative.
There's a criticism.
The praise covers the film's main approach (fairness to both sides), and the one fault is narrow, so praise dominates.

q:
Passage: An archaeologist claims that a distinctive style of painted pottery spread across a region through trade rather than migration. If people had moved, she reasons, their house designs, burial customs and tools would have spread too, yet only the pottery appears in the new areas.

Which finding would most strengthen her claim?
o: Tests show the pots in new areas were made from clay found only in the original region
The pottery style remained popular for several centuries in its original home region
Houses in the new areas were built in the same style as houses in the original region
Painted pottery of various styles has been found at many other ancient sites worldwide
e: Pots made of the home region's clay must have been carried in, which fits trade.
The house-style option would weaken her claim, since it suggests people moved.
w: How long the style stayed popular at home says nothing about whether it reached new areas by trade or migration.
Matching house styles in the new areas would suggest people moved there, which undercuts her trade explanation.
Pottery found worldwide is too general; it says nothing about how this particular style spread across the region.

q:
Passage: A sociologist studying retail work notes that many stores now call their clerks 'associates' or 'team members.' The new titles suggest partnership and a share in the company's success, she writes, but for most workers the title is 'a promise the paycheck doesn't keep.'

In context, the phrase 'a promise the paycheck doesn't keep' suggests that:
o: The titles imply a partnership that the workers' pay does not reflect
Stores often fail to pay their workers on the dates they have promised
Workers dislike their new titles more than they dislike their low pay
Workers with the new titles earn more than clerks used to in the past
e: The titles 'suggest partnership and a share in the company's success'; the paycheck shows no such share.
The 'pay on the dates promised' option reads the metaphor literally.
w: This reads the metaphor literally; the 'promise' is the partnership implied by the title, not a pay date.
The sociologist never compares how workers feel about titles versus pay; she contrasts the title's promise with the pay.
The phrase says the paycheck fails to match the title's promise, which implies pay has not risen, the opposite of this.

q:
Passage: An art historian argues that the gleaming white marble of ancient statues, admired for centuries as a sign of classical restraint, misleads us. Traces of pigment show that many were once painted in vivid colors. Later admirers, she suggests, built an ideal of purity on what was really the work of weathering.

The historian's main point is that:
o: A long-admired classical ideal rested partly on the effects of weathering
Ancient sculptors generally preferred bright paint to the natural look of marble
Painted statues are more beautiful than statues of plain white marble
Museums should repaint ancient statues in their original bright colors
e: The final sentence states the point: an 'ideal of purity' was built on 'the work of weathering.'
The 'sculptors preferred paint' option overreaches: the passage says many statues were painted, not that sculptors ranked paint above marble. Repainting is never proposed.
w: The passage says many statues were painted, not that sculptors ranked paint above the natural look of marble.
The historian makes no judgment about which is more beautiful; her point is that the white ideal rested on weathering.
The passage never proposes repainting statues; it is about how later admirers misread their white surfaces.

q:
Passage: A philosopher argues that being honest does not require telling every truth. A doctor who chooses not to list every rare side effect, she says, may still be fully honest if nothing she says is false and she answers every question truthfully.

The philosopher distinguishes between:
o: Not lying and disclosing everything
Doctors and patients
Rare side effects and common side effects
Questions and answers
e: Honesty, in her view, doesn't require total disclosure.
w: Not the distinction.
Not the distinction.
Not the distinction.

q:
Passage: A composer claims that new instruments do not automatically lead to new musical ideas. They expand the available possibilities, but the imaginative choices of performers and composers determine which possibilities matter.

What role does the second sentence play?
o: It offers an unrelated definition
It rejects the first sentence
It proves that all instruments, old and new, sound essentially alike
It qualifies the potential influence of new instruments
e: The sentence clarifies that technical possibility alone does not determine artistic significance.
w: It's directly related.
It refines, not rejects, the first sentence.
It says nothing about sound.

q:
Passage: A critic argues that public art funded by cities tends to be bland because selection committees choose works that no one will object to. As evidence, she notes that most city-funded sculptures she surveyed were abstract shapes in neutral colors.

Which finding would most WEAKEN the critic's explanation?
o: Privately funded sculptures in the same cities were just as often abstract and neutral
Many residents of these cities say that they enjoy the abstract sculptures they see
Selection committees in these cities review hundreds of proposals every single year
Most of the surveyed sculptures were installed in parks rather than in downtown plazas
e: If works chosen without committees look the same, committees are not the cause of the blandness.
Residents' enjoyment speaks to whether the art is liked, not why it looks the way it does.
w: Residents enjoying the sculptures says whether the art is liked, not why committees produce abstract, neutral works.
How many proposals committees review does not test whether committee caution causes the blandness.
Where the sculptures stand says nothing about whether committee selection explains their abstract, neutral style.

q:
Passage: An education researcher reports that average grades at many colleges have risen steadily for decades. Because so large a share of students now earn the highest grade, she argues, employers and graduate schools increasingly ignore transcripts and rely on test scores and recommendations instead.

Which inference is best supported by the passage?
o: Grades lose value as a signal when most students receive the top mark
Students today learn less than students did several decades ago
Recommendation letters judge ability more accurately than test scores
Colleges raised grades on purpose to help their students find jobs
e: Readers of transcripts turn elsewhere because top grades no longer distinguish students.
The learning option is out of scope: the passage says nothing about how much students learn.
w: Out of scope.
The passage says employers turn to test scores and recommendations but never ranks one as more accurate than the other.
The passage reports that grades have risen but gives no motive, so a deliberate job-placement plan is not supported.

q:
Passage: A historian argues that medieval craft guilds required apprenticeships of seven years or more not mainly to ensure skill, since many trades could be learned far faster, but to limit how many rivals each master would face.

Which modern situation most closely parallels the historian's argument?
o: A profession requires years of training beyond what the work demands, keeping newcomers few
A hospital requires surgeons to practice for many years because surgery is so difficult to learn
A company trains new hires briefly so they can start earning money for it quickly
A university lets students finish degrees faster by taking extra classes each term
e: The parallel needs a long requirement whose real function is to restrict competition rather than to build skill.
The surgeon option has long training justified by real difficulty, the very explanation the historian rejects.
w: Training fits difficulty.
Brief training to start earning quickly is the opposite of the long requirement the historian says guilds used to limit rivals.
Faster, not longer.

q:
Passage: A political theorist argues that juries reach better verdicts than single judges because twelve people bring a wider range of experience to the evidence. She acknowledges that juries are slower and more costly than judges. Still, she maintains, the quality of the decision is worth the added time and expense.

What is the function of the second sentence in the argument?
o: It admits a drawback without giving up the main claim
It offers the main evidence that juries decide better
It shows that the theorist has come to prefer judges
It raises a claim that the theorist later disproves
e: 'Acknowledges' followed by 'Still' marks a concession that leaves the thesis intact.
She never disproves the cost point; she argues it is outweighed.
w: The second sentence concedes that juries are slower and costlier; it is a drawback, not evidence that they decide better.
She still prefers juries.
She never disproves the cost point; after 'Still,' she grants it and argues the better verdicts are worth it.

q:
Passage: A political scientist argues that town meetings which vote by show of hands understate disagreement. Residents who oppose a popular measure, she reasons, may keep their hands down rather than be seen voting against their neighbors.

Which finding would most STRENGTHEN her argument?
o: When one town switched to secret ballots, 'no' votes on similar measures rose
Most residents of the towns said that they enjoyed attending the monthly town meetings
Towns that vote by hand pass about as many measures as towns that do not
Fewer residents attend town meetings now than attended thirty years ago
e: Her claim is that visibility suppresses opposition; more 'no' votes once voting became private supports exactly that.
The 'pass about as many measures' option, if anything, cuts against her claim and does not isolate the effect of visibility.
w: Enjoying meetings doesn't address whether visibility hides opposition.
Similar passage rates don't isolate visibility and may cut against her claim.
Attendance trends don't show whether hand votes suppress dissent.
t: Strengthen questions reward a comparison that changes only the factor the author blames.

q:
Passage: A historian writes that a celebrated inventor deserves credit for building the first practical version of his device, but that popular accounts erase the dozen earlier tinkerers whose failed designs taught him what not to do. Genius, she suggests, is often a crowd remembered as one person.

The historian's attitude toward the inventor is best described as:
o: Crediting his achievement while rejecting the lone-genius story
Dismissing his achievement as something stolen from the others
Celebrating him as the person solely responsible for the device
Treating the earlier tinkerers' failures as historically trivial
e: She says he 'deserves credit' but faults accounts that 'erase' his predecessors.
'Stolen' is too extreme; she never accuses him of taking their work.
w: Too extreme: she says he deserves credit for the first practical version and never accuses him of stealing others' work.
She rejects this.
She values them.

q:
Passage: A historian of science argues that the early microscope did not at once transform biology. Its lenses revealed tiny creatures in pond water, but observers had no agreed categories for them, and drawings of the same sample by different viewers often looked nothing alike. Only when shared methods of preparing and describing samples emerged did the instrument's images begin to count as evidence.

The historian's argument suggests that observations become scientific evidence when:
o: Observers share practices that let them agree on what they are seeing
An instrument is powerful enough to reveal previously invisible things
Individual observers become highly skilled at drawing what they see
Naturalists apply categories inherited unchanged from earlier eras
e: The final sentence ties evidence to 'shared methods of preparing and describing samples.'
The 'powerful enough to reveal' option is the trap: the lenses already revealed the creatures, yet the images did not yet count as evidence.
w: The lenses already revealed creatures, yet the images weren't evidence.
Individual skill isn't enough; the passage stresses shared methods.
Observers lacked agreed categories; inherited categories aren't the solution.
t: When an author says 'not at once' and 'only when,' the answer is the condition after 'only when.'

q:
Passage: A sports historian argues that records set in an era of shorter seasons should not be dismissed as lesser, since players then faced rough fields and heavy equipment that made every game harder.

How would the historian most likely view a modern sprinter's time that beats one run in the 1930s on a loose cinder track?
o: The comparison should weigh how much track conditions have changed since then
The modern time proves today's sprinters are more naturally gifted
Times from different eras can never be compared in any meaningful way at all
The older time should count for more simply because it is older
e: The historian judges records by the conditions under which they were set; a loose cinder track is exactly such a condition.

The 'never be compared' option is too extreme: the historian does compare eras, adjusting for their conditions. The 'count for more because it is older' option ignores that age alone is not the historian's reason.
w: The historian weighs the conditions records were set under, so crediting talent while ignoring the cinder track goes against that view.
Too extreme: the historian does compare eras, adjusting for conditions like rough fields and heavy equipment.
Not the reason.

q:
Passage: An urban planner proposed planting more street trees to lower summer temperatures. A critic noted that trees also require water and maintenance, and that narrow sidewalks may not accommodate roots. The planner replied that selecting species and sites carefully could reduce these costs.

Which finding most strengthens the planner’s response?
o: A survey found residents prefer tree-lined streets to bare ones
A study found that street trees lower summer temperatures in most large cities
A trial found drought-tolerant trees reduced heat without damaging sidewalks
A report found many cities lack funds to water new street trees
e: The trial addresses both the proposed benefit and the critic’s feasibility objections.
w: Preference doesn't address the costs.
This supports the benefit, not the reply about costs.
This supports the critic.

q:
Passage: A researcher reports that countries with more paid public holidays tend to have workers who rate their lives as more satisfying. He concludes that the holidays themselves make workers happier by giving them more rest.

Which finding would most WEAKEN the researcher's conclusion?
o: Countries whose workers were already more satisfied tended to add holidays later
Workers in countries with many holidays often travel during their time off
Some countries with few holidays offer generous paid vacation time instead
Satisfaction surveys in all of these countries asked exactly the same questions each year
e: If satisfied workforces came first and holidays followed, the causation may run the other way.
The 'generous paid vacation' option complicates the comparison but does not show that holidays fail to cause satisfaction.
w: Workers traveling on their days off is consistent with holidays making them happier, so it does not weaken the conclusion.
Complicates, not weakens.
Consistent survey questions make the data more reliable; they do not challenge the claim that holidays cause satisfaction.
t: Correlation questions: look for reverse causation or a third factor.

q:
Passage: A museum director argues that the museum's new audio guide improves visitors' understanding of the art. Her evidence is that visitors who rented the guide spent twice as long in the galleries as visitors who did not.

Which is the most serious weakness in the director's argument?
o: Spending more time in the galleries does not show that visitors understood more
Producing a high-quality audio guide costs the museum a good deal of money
Some visitors would rather read printed wall labels than listen to recorded commentary
The museum's galleries differ in size, so some take longer to walk through
e: The evidence measures time, but the conclusion is about understanding; the director assumes one implies the other.
Cost and preference are irrelevant to whether the guide improves understanding.
w: Cost doesn't bear on whether understanding improved.
Preferences don't address whether the guide improves understanding.
Gallery size affects everyone's time; it doesn't explain the gap between guide users and non-users.
t: Check whether the evidence measures the same thing the conclusion claims.

q:
Passage: A museum director argues that free admission increases visits by families with low incomes. Critics reply that after one museum went free, most new visitors were people who already visited other museums often.

The critics' reply mainly challenges:
o: Whether free admission reaches the intended visitors
Whether museums should charge any admission at all
Whether families with low incomes enjoy art
Whether museum attendance has risen in recent years
e: It questions who actually benefited.
w: Not the question.
Not the question.
Not the question.

q:
Passage: An analyst argues that a referendum is not more democratic than a legislative vote simply because citizens vote directly. A ballot question offers only yes or no, she notes, while legislators can amend, bargain and combine proposals. In a referendum, the power to write the question may matter more than the power to answer it.

The analyst's main point is that:
o: Direct votes can hand real power to whoever writes the question
Legislatures should be replaced by regular national referendums
Citizens are poorly informed about the questions they vote on
Legislators are more honest than the voters who elect them
e: The final sentence states the point: framing the question 'may matter more than' voting on it.
Voter knowledge and honesty are never discussed, so those options are out of scope.
w: She critiques referendums; she doesn't advocate replacing legislatures with them.
Voter knowledge is never discussed.
Honesty isn't discussed; she compares voting structures.

q:
Passage: A city stopped charging fines for overdue library books. Over the next year, more books were returned, and the library director concluded that fines had been keeping people away: borrowers who owed money had avoided the library, and the books they held, rather than face the charge.

The director's conclusion assumes that:
o: The extra returns came largely from people who had been staying away over fines
Most borrowers in the city had never owed any money to the library at all
The library collected little revenue from fines before they were abolished
Borrowers prefer to visit libraries that have no strict rules about return dates
e: The conclusion links the rise in returns to people avoiding fines; that only works if the new returns came from those avoiders.
The 'little revenue' option may be true but is not needed for the causal claim about why returns rose.
w: The director's claim does not need most borrowers to be debt-free; it needs the new returns to come from fine-avoiders.
How much revenue fines raised is irrelevant to why returns rose after fines ended.
A general taste for libraries with loose rules is not needed; the claim is specifically about people avoiding fines they owed.
t: An assumption is the unstated link the conclusion needs; test it by imagining it false.

q:
Passage: An urban historian writes that the city's first public parks were designed as 'lungs' for crowded neighborhoods. Planners believed open space would improve the health and even the character of factory workers, although the parks were often built far from the districts where those workers lived.

The final clause of the passage most strongly suggests that:
o: The parks did not fully reach the people they were meant to benefit
Factory workers did not want to have parks built near their homes
The planners' beliefs about open space and health were proven right
The parks were deliberately hidden from the city's wealthier residents
e: 'Although … far from the districts where those workers lived' signals a gap between intent and result.
Nothing indicates what workers wanted, so the 'did not want parks near their homes' option is unsupported.
w: The passage says nothing about what workers wanted.
The clause points to a gap; it doesn't confirm the planners' beliefs.
Nothing suggests hiding the parks from anyone.

q:
Passage: A management consultant claims that letting employees write their own job titles raises job satisfaction, because a self-chosen title signals respect. She points to a firm where satisfaction scores rose in the two years after it adopted the policy.

Which finding would most WEAKEN the consultant's claim?
o: The firm's satisfaction scores had begun rising a year before the new policy
Employees at the firm chose titles that were longer and grander than their old ones
Several other firms adopted the same policy during those same two years
Some employees at the firm kept the titles they had been given before
e: If satisfaction was already rising before the policy, the policy cannot easily take credit for the rise.
The 'other firms adopted' option says nothing about whether the policy caused this firm's change.
w: Grander titles don't test cause.
Other firms don't test cause.
Some employees keeping old titles neither shows nor rules out that self-chosen titles raised satisfaction.

q:
Passage: A music historian proposes that a medieval chant tradition developed its long, slow melodies partly because it was sung in stone churches with very long echoes, which blur rapid notes into one another.

Which finding would most strengthen the historian's proposal?
o: Chant traditions that grew up in small wooden chapels used faster, busier melodies
Singers in the chant tradition often trained for many years before performing in public
The stone churches of the period often took several decades to build
Modern choirs sometimes perform medieval chant more slowly than before
e: If echo caused slow melodies, places without long echoes should show faster ones; this comparison supports the causal claim.
The 'trained for many years' and 'decades to build' options are true-sounding but say nothing about echo and tempo.
w: Not about echo.
Not about echo.
How modern choirs perform chant says nothing about why medieval melodies developed to suit long church echoes.

q:
Passage: A reviewer calls a new opera production 'ambitious in every direction at once.' The sets are lavish, the cast enormous and the score reorchestrated; yet, she writes, by the third act it is hard to remember what story all this splendor was meant to serve.

The reviewer's attitude toward the production is best described as:
o: Critical of an excess that buries the story
Admiring of its ambition without reservation
Hostile toward opera as an entire art form
Neutral, simply listing the staging choices
e: 'Yet … hard to remember what story all this splendor was meant to serve' turns the praise of ambition into criticism.
Her complaint is about this production, not about opera in general.
w: She has reservations.
Only this production.
She judges it.
t: Words like 'yet' often mark where the author's real judgment appears.

q:
Passage: A critic writes that a novel's slow opening chapters frustrate many readers but are necessary: they build the quiet world that the later violence destroys. Without them, she argues, the ending would shock but not grieve.

The critic's view of the slow opening is best described as:
o: It is frustrating but essential to the novel's emotional effect
It is a flaw that the author should have removed from the final draft
It distracts readers from the novel's central violence
It makes the ending more shocking but less meaningful
e: 'Frustrate … but are necessary' signals qualified approval.
w: She calls it necessary.
She calls it necessary.
It makes the ending grieve.

q:
Passage: An ecologist found that two neighboring forests supported different bird populations. One forest had more mature trees and deadwood, while the other had recently been cleared and replanted. The ecologist cautioned against attributing the difference to tree age alone.

Which observation most directly justifies the caution?
o: The forests also differ in pesticide exposure
Both forests contain similar numbers of tree species
The mature forest's trees are much older on average
Both forests receive similar annual rainfall
e: A second ecological difference could confound a simple age-based explanation.
w: Similar species numbers don't suggest a confound.
Older trees support the age idea.
Similar rainfall rules out a confound.

q:
Passage: A literary scholar argues that a novelist wrote her final book in great haste, pointing to its many inconsistencies in characters' names, ages and dates.

Which finding would most weaken the scholar's argument?
o: Her earlier, slowly written novels contain just as many such inconsistencies
Her final book sold more copies than any of her earlier novels
Readers at the time rarely noticed the inconsistencies in her books
Her final book is much shorter than most of the novels that she wrote before it
e: If slowly written books have the same errors, the errors do not show haste.
Sales figures and readers' attention say nothing about how quickly the book was written.
w: Sales don't show speed.
Notice doesn't show speed.
Length doesn't show speed.

q:
Passage: A reviewer writes that a new report on education in prisons is the most careful study of the subject yet published. Its interviews with former inmates are thorough and humane. Its cost estimates, however, assume that every graduate will find steady work within a year, an assumption the reviewer calls 'hopeful at best.'

The reviewer's attitude toward the report is best described as:
o: Admiring of its research, but doubtful about its financial claims
Hostile, because the report misleads readers about prison costs
Uncritical, because the report is the most careful study published
Indifferent, since the reviewer sees little value in prison education
e: Praise ('most careful,' 'thorough and humane') is followed by 'however' and doubt about the cost estimates.
The 'uncritical' option ignores the reviewer's objection; 'hopeful at best' is mild skepticism, not hostility.
w: She praises it.
She objects to costs.
She values it.

q:
Passage: An economist argues that when a government caps apartment rents below what the market would charge, landlords have less reason to maintain their buildings, since they cannot raise rents to recover the cost of repairs.

If the economist is correct, which result would be expected after a strict rent cap takes effect?
o: Repairs and upkeep in capped buildings decline over time
Landlords spend more on repairs in order to attract tenants
Rents in capped buildings rise above the market rate
Tenants in capped buildings move out much more often
e: Less incentive to maintain buildings predicts less maintenance.
The rent-rise option contradicts the premise that rents are capped.
w: The economist says capped rents remove landlords' reason to maintain buildings, so spending more on repairs is the opposite.
Rents are capped.
The economist's reasoning concerns landlords' upkeep, not tenant turnover; tenants moving out is never predicted.

q:
Passage: An economist argues that raising the price of cigarettes reduces smoking among teenagers more than among adults, because teenagers have less money and are less addicted.

If the economist is correct, which result would be expected after a large cigarette tax?
o: Teen smoking falls by a larger percentage than adult smoking
Adult smoking falls by a larger percentage than teen smoking
Both groups' smoking falls by about the same percentage
Teen smoking rises as teens switch to cheaper brands
e: Apply the stated reasoning to the new situation.
w: Teens should drop more.
Teens should drop more.
The economist predicts teens will cut back because they have less money; switching brands and smoking more contradicts that.

q:
Passage: A historian observes that surviving letters from merchants are abundant, whereas letters from farm laborers are scarce. She warns that the historical record may exaggerate the concerns of people whose writing was most likely to be preserved.

What inference is most justified?
o: Farm laborers had no concerns
Merchants wrote nearly all of the historical records of the period
The historian opposes studying letters
The archive may overrepresent merchant perspectives
e: Different rates of preservation can bias apparent representation.
w: Scarce letters don't mean no concerns.
Nothing says merchants wrote nearly all records.
She warns about bias, not against letters.

q:
Passage: An essayist claims that the decline of letter writing has made people less reflective. Composing a letter, she argues, required slowing down to choose one's words, whereas text messages are typed and sent in seconds.

The essayist's argument assumes that:
o: People have not moved that slow reflection into some other activity
Text messages are always shorter than the letters people used to write
People once wrote more letters than they now send texts
Reflective people tend to prefer letters to other media
e: If people now reflect while journaling or drafting emails, losing letters would not make them less reflective; the argument needs that not to have happened.
The 'always shorter' option is too extreme and is not needed: the argument rests on speed of composition, not length.
w: Too extreme: the argument rests on how fast texts are written, not on texts always being shorter.
The argument is about how texts are composed, not about how many letters or texts people send.
The argument claims letter writing builds reflection, not that reflective people choose letters; that link is not needed.
